events.ageText: 4567.3 Ma · ± 0.2 Ma · radiometric (uranium–lead) on the grains themselves; one group argues for about 4568.4
events.ageHow: radiometric (uranium-lead) on the grains themselves; one group argues for about 4568.4
events.knownFrom: white grains inside meteorites, the oldest solid things in the solar system

placeNow.name: Pueblito de Allende, Chihuahua, Mexico (26.97 N, 105.32 W), where the meteorite fell

events.summary: About 4.57 billion years ago. Around the young Sun, in a flat disc of gas and dust, the oldest solid grains we know of formed. Some survive as white specks inside meteorites.

paragraphs: A little after one o'clock in the morning on 8 February 1969, a fireball lit the sky over the state of Chihuahua, in northern Mexico, and broke apart. Thousands of stones fell around the village of Pueblito de Allende and along a strip of country about fifty kilometres long. People from the villages, and later from museums, picked them up for years, and together they gathered two tonnes or more.

The stones are called the Allende meteorite. A meteorite is a piece of rock from space that reaches the ground, and most of them come from asteroids, small worlds that never grew into planets. Some of those worlds, like the one Allende came from, have hardly changed since they formed. Broken open, a piece of Allende is dark grey, and scattered through it are white specks, some of them as big as a fingernail.
The white specks are older than the Earth.

Before there was a Sun, there was a cloud of gas and dust. Part of the cloud fell in on itself, the middle grew hot enough to shine, and around it a flat disc of gas and dust went round and round. Close to the young Sun the disc was so hot that only a few stubborn substances, rich in calcium and aluminium, could turn solid. The white specks are made of those.

Their age comes from uranium, which slowly turns into lead at a rate that never changes. Measure how much of each a speck holds, and you can work out when it formed: about 4.567 billion years ago, give or take a couple of hundred thousand years. One group of scientists thinks the specks are a million years older than that, and the argument is still going.
People who study the solar system use the age of these specks as its birthday.

Robert Hazen, a mineralogist, reckons there were only about a dozen kinds of mineral in the dust of the cloud the Sun was born from. Today the list of minerals known on Earth has more than six thousand names, and it grows every year.

references: James Connelly and others, "The absolute chronology and thermal processing of solids in the solar protoplanetary disk," *Science*, 2012. The age, 4,567.30 ± 0.16 million years.
Roy Clarke Jr. and others, "Allende, Mexico, meteorite shower," *Smithsonian Contributions to the Earth Sciences* 5, 1971. The fall: time, strewn field, tonnage.
Robert Hazen and others, "Mineral evolution," *American Mineralogist*, 2008. "Approximately a dozen" minerals in the dust before the planets.
Robert Hazen, *The Story of Earth* (Viking, 2012), chapter "Birth". For a parent.

events.label: Gathering
events.ageText: 4540 Ma · ± 50 Ma · a model age, from lead in the Earth's oldest ores compared with lead in meteorites
events.ageHow: a model age, from lead in the Earth's oldest ores compared with lead in meteorites
events.knownFrom: tungsten and lead in rocks and meteorites, and computer models; no rock survives
events.summary: About 4.54 billion years ago. Dust, pebbles and small worlds circling the young Sun had gathered into a planet, the Earth, hot enough to melt. Its iron sank to the middle and made the core.

paragraphs: In many museums there is a slab of metal from space, sawn flat, polished, and washed with acid. The acid brings out a pattern of crossing bands, like woven straw, which forms only when once-melted iron and nickel cool very slowly, over millions of years.
A slab like that is a piece of the core of a small world.

The disc of gas and dust around the young Sun did not stay dust for long. The grains stuck together into pebbles, the pebbles into bodies kilometres across, and those crashed into each other and grew. Many grew big enough, and hot enough inside, to melt. When a small world melts, its iron, which is heavier than rock, sinks to the middle. Some of those small worlds were later smashed apart, and their cores come down to us as iron meteorites.

The Earth was built the same way, from many such bodies, and the crashes kept it hot enough to melt. Its iron sank, too, and made the core, which is still there under our feet, about 2,900 kilometres down.
How long did the gathering take?

There is a clock for it. A rare metal called hafnium slowly turns into tungsten, and hafnium stays in rock while tungsten goes with iron. So the tungsten left in the rock of the Earth's mantle says when the iron left for the core. By that clock, which two teams read in 2002, the core had formed within about thirty million years. Some scientists in Copenhagen think the Earth grew most of the way in only five million years, from pebbles; others think the last crashes went on for a hundred million. Each side has good evidence.

The iron at the centre is partly liquid still, and its churning makes the Earth's magnetic field, the one a compass needle feels. When the field began is another argument, and the oldest rocks that seem to record it are in Greenland, 3.7 billion years old.

events.picturesWanted: a polished, etched slice of an iron meteorite showing the crossing bands (Commons; licence to check).
references: Thorsten Kleine and others, "Rapid accretion and early core formation on asteroids and the terrestrial planets from Hf–W chronometry," *Nature*, 2002. The core within about thirty million years.
Qingzhu Yin and others, "A short timescale for terrestrial planet formation from Hf–W chronometry of meteorites," *Nature*, 2002. The same, from a second team.
Martin Schiller, Martin Bizzarro and others, "Iron isotope evidence for very rapid accretion and differentiation of the proto-Earth," *Science Advances*, 2020. The fast view.
G. Brent Dalrymple, "The age of the Earth in the twentieth century: a problem (mostly) solved," Geological Society of London Special Publication 190, 2001. 4.54 billion, ± 50 million.

placeNow.name: Lunar Sample Laboratory Facility, Johnson Space Center, Houston, Texas (29.56 N, 95.08 W)

events.summary: About 4.5 billion years ago. Something perhaps the size of Mars probably hit the young Earth, and rock flung into space gathered into the Moon. When it happened, and how big the something was, are still argued.

paragraphs: In a building in Houston, Texas, the rocks the Apollo astronauts brought back from the Moon are kept in steel cabinets filled with pure nitrogen, which keeps the air from changing them. People handle them through thick gloves set into the cabinet walls.
The rocks raised a puzzle at once. In some ways the Moon is very like the Earth's rock and in others not like it at all.

Oxygen comes in kinds that weigh slightly different amounts, and the planets and asteroids we have pieces of each have their own mix, almost like a fingerprint. The Moon's mix matches the Earth's, so closely that the best measurements, in 2025, could find no difference. Yet the Moon has only a small iron core, and the Earth has a big one.

The idea most scientists favour is a crash. Near the end of the Earth's gathering, a body perhaps the size of Mars hit it a glancing blow. Rock from the outside of both was flung into space, and it gathered into the Moon within about a year. The iron of both stayed in the Earth. Some people call the body Theia. Nobody knows its size, and other models have two half-Earths colliding, or an Earth spinning so fast that a day lasted two or three hours.
Each model can explain the fingerprint only by asking for something special, and scientists still argue over which to believe.
The newborn Moon was perhaps fifteen or twenty times closer than it is now, and it would have looked that many times wider in the sky. The day was about five hours long.

When the crash happened is argued too. Crystals from Apollo 14 rocks say at least 4.51 billion years ago; other moon rocks say about 4.35. In 2024 one team suggested that the Earth's pull on the young Moon heated and reset the younger rocks.
The Moon is still moving away, about 3.8 centimetres a year. We know because Apollo crews left mirrors on the Moon, and people on Earth still bounce laser light off them.

events.picturesWanted: a moon rock in a nitrogen cabinet at the Johnson Space Center (NASA, public domain); the full Moon.
references: Robin Canup and Erik Asphaug, "Origin of the Moon in a giant impact near the end of the Earth's formation," *Nature*, 2001. The Mars-sized body; the five-hour day.
Melanie Barboni and others, "Early formation of the Moon 4.51 billion years ago," *Science Advances*, 2017. The old date.
Francis Nimmo and others, "Tidally driven remelting around 4.35 billion years ago indicates the Moon is old," *Nature*, 2024. The reconciliation.
Shigeru Ida, Robin Canup and Glen Stewart, "Lunar accretion from an impact-generated disk," *Nature*, 1997. The Moon forming close in, within about a year.
Robert Hazen, *The Story of Earth* (Viking, 2012), chapter "The Big Thwack". The label is his.

events.label: Black Earth
events.ageText: 4450 Ma · ± 50 Ma · an estimate; nothing from the time survives to be dated
events.ageHow: an estimate; nothing from the time survives to be dated
events.knownFrom: nothing that survives from the time; computer models, and chemical traces in younger rocks
events.summary: About 4.45 billion years ago. After the crash that made the Moon, the Earth's melted surface probably cooled into a crust of dark rock under an air thick with steam. No rock from this time survives.

paragraphs: Nobody can see this part.

No rock from this time is left anywhere on Earth. The planet's skin has been melted, broken, sunk and remade so many times since that every piece of it has gone. What we know comes from computer models, built by scientists who start from the laws of heat and gas and work forward, and from a few chemical traces in much younger rocks.
Here is what one careful model says. Kevin Zahnle, a planetary scientist at NASA, and his colleagues worked it out in 2007.

After the crash that made the Moon, the Earth's surface was melted rock, glowing. The air was full of rock vapour, and from space the Earth would have looked like a small star wrapped in burning cloud. As it cooled, the melted surface froze, and that took only about two million years. Later a thick layer of basalt, the dark rock that lava sets into, built up on top, and its heavy bottom kept breaking off and sinking into the hot rock below.

The air above it was steam and carbon dioxide, breathed out by the rock. When the surface was cool enough, the steam fell as rain, about a metre a year, until the oceans were full. What was left was an air of carbon dioxide so thick that it pressed down about a hundred times as hard as our air does, at a temperature over two hundred degrees Celsius.
Other models give other numbers. Some have the surface staying melted much longer, under a thick blanket of air. Nobody can check any of them against a rock.
Robert Hazen calls this time Black Earth.

The closest anyone has come to it is in Greenland. Rocks near Isua, about 3.8 billion years old, carry a faint chemical signature showing that the inside of the Earth had already sorted itself into layers in its first few hundred million years.

events.picturesWanted: none that would be honest as a photograph. A drawing, plainly a drawing, of a dark crust cracking over glowing rock (to be drawn for CW; Michael has offered black-earth textures for the globe).
references: Kevin Zahnle and others, "Emergence of a habitable planet," *Space Science Reviews*, 2007. The rock-vapour air, the two million years, the rain at a metre a year, the hundred-times air.
Keiko Hamano, Yutaka Abe and Hidenori Genda, "Emergence of two types of terrestrial planet on solidification of magma ocean," *Nature*, 2013. How long a melted surface lasts.
Guillaume Caro and others, "146Sm–142Nd evidence from Isua metamorphosed sediments for early differentiation of the Earth's mantle," *Nature*, 2003. The trace at Isua.
Robert Hazen, *The Story of Earth* (Viking, 2012), chapter "Black Earth: the first basalt crust". The name.

placeNow.name: Erawondoo Hill, Jack Hills, Murchison, Western Australia (26.18 S, 116.93 E)

events.summary: About 4.4 billion years ago. A tiny crystal formed that still survives, in a hill in Western Australia. It is the oldest piece of the Earth yet found, and its oxygen hints at liquid water.

dateLine.tail: and probably begun by 4.5 billion years ago

paragraphs: Erawondoo Hill is a low hill in the Jack Hills, in the Murchison country of Western Australia. Along it runs a band of old river rock: pebbles of quartz set in sand that a river laid down about three billion years ago.
In the sand are tiny crystals of a mineral called zircon.

Zircon grows in melted rock as it cools, and it is very hard, so it outlasts the rock it grew in. When that rock wears away, the zircons wash out into rivers and settle somewhere new. Zircon also takes in uranium as it grows and shuts out lead, so any lead inside a zircon came from its uranium, and the zircon is a clock.

Geologists crush the river rock, sort out the zircons, and set them in a disc of plastic. Then a beam of charged atoms, fired from a machine called an ion microprobe, digs a hole in each crystal too small to see and weighs what comes out.

In 2001 Simon Wilde, a geologist at Curtin University in Perth, and his colleagues reported a crystal about as wide as two hairs that had formed 4.404 billion years ago. It is the oldest piece of the Earth yet found.

Its oxygen tells something more. The crystal is slightly rich in the heavier kind of oxygen, and that usually happens when rock has sat at the surface in cool liquid water before being buried and melted. So there was probably water at the surface, perhaps oceans, less than a hundred and fifty million years after the Earth formed.

Not everyone agrees. Some geologists think water could have changed the crystal much later. In 2024 a study picked out more than a hundred of these zircons that later water had not touched, and they still held the heavy oxygen. Many geologists now think the water was there.
At the Australian National University, a machine has looked through more than a hundred thousand zircons from these hills. About one in twenty is older than four billion years.
Robert Hazen calls this time Blue Earth.

events.picturesWanted: the crystal itself, glowing in a cathodoluminescence picture (John Valley, University of Wisconsin; licence to ask); Erawondoo Hill (Commons or GSWA; licence to check).
references: Simon Wilde, John Valley, William Peck and Colin Graham, "Evidence from detrital zircons for the existence of continental crust and oceans on the Earth 4.4 Gyr ago," *Nature*, 2001. The age and the oxygen.
John Valley and others, "Hadean age for a post-magma-ocean zircon confirmed by atom-probe tomography," *Nature Geoscience*, 2014. That the lead has not moved.
John Valley, William Peck, Elizabeth King and Simon Wilde, "A cool early Earth," *Geology*, 2002. Water and mild conditions from 4.4 billion.
Robert Hazen, *The Story of Earth* (Viking, 2012). For a parent.

placeNow.name: Acasta River, Northwest Territories, Canada (65.17 N, 115.57 W)

events.summary: About 4.03 billion years ago. Rock formed that still survives, beside the Acasta River in northern Canada. It is the oldest rock that nearly every geologist accepts. Rock in Nunavik may be older; that is still argued.

dateLine.tail: and probably begun by 4.4 billion years ago

paragraphs: About three hundred kilometres north of Yellowknife, on the Acasta River, there is an outcrop of grey rock striped light and dark, with a few small garnets in it. It is a gneiss ("nice"), a rock that has been squeezed and heated deep underground until its minerals lined up in bands.

In 1989 Samuel Bowring, an American geologist, and his colleagues dated zircons from the outcrop, and later work put the oldest of the rock at 4.031 billion years. Nothing older that everyone accepts has been found anywhere.
The oldest part of it is called the Idiwhaa gneiss. *Idiwhaa* is a Tłı̨chǫ word, and it means "ancient."

The Earth's first crust was basalt, the dark, heavy rock that lava sets into. Granite is different: pale, lighter, and made when older rock, basalt among it, is melted again, often with water. Because granite is lighter it rides higher, the way a thick, light raft floats higher than a thin heavy one, and continents are made mostly of rock like it. The Idiwhaa gneiss was made when hot melt rose close to the surface and melted in older dark rock that water had already soaked, much as new rock is made in Iceland today.
But is it the oldest rock?

On the east shore of Hudson Bay, near Inukjuak, in Nunavik, there is a belt of old rock called Nuvvuagittuq. In 2008 a team led by Jonathan O'Neil, a Canadian geologist, dated it at 4.28 billion years by one method. Other geologists, using zircons, said 3.8. In 2025 O'Neil's team dated rock that cuts through the old rock, at about 4.16 billion, by two methods that agree. If they are right, the rock it cuts through is older still. Not everyone is convinced yet.

In 2024 the Inuit of Inukjuak, through their landholding corporation, stopped geologists taking any more rock from the site, because so much had been chipped away, and some of it had turned up for sale online.

events.label: Bombardment
events.ageText: 3900 Ma · argued, from about 4200 to 3500 Ma · radiometric on moon rocks melted by impacts; how to read those dates is the argument
events.ageHow: argued, from about 4200 to 3500 Ma · radiometric on moon rocks melted by impacts; how to read those dates is the argument
events.knownFrom: the Moon's craters and the ages of moon rocks; on Earth, beds of tiny glass beads from later impacts
events.summary: About 3.9 billion years ago. Moon rocks once seemed to say that a storm of huge rocks from space hit the Moon and the Earth all at once. Many scientists now doubt the storm.

paragraphs: On the Moon there is a dark plain about 1,200 kilometres across. It is a crater, later filled with lava. It is called Mare Imbrium, the Sea of Showers.

In 1974, three scientists at Caltech, in California, dated rocks the Apollo crews had brought back. Many of the rocks had been melted by impacts, and the melting had reset their clocks. Again and again they gave the same age: about 3.9 billion years.

The scientists, Fouad Tera, Dimitri Papanastassiou and Gerald Wasserburg, suggested that something had sent a storm of huge rocks through the inner solar system, all within a short time. They called it a cataclysm. If it hit the Moon, it hit the Earth too, and the Earth is the bigger target.
In 1989 four American scientists worked out what such hits would have done to the Earth. A rock a few hundred kilometres across, they said, would boil the oceans away.
For many years the storm was in the books.

Then people looked again at where the Apollo rocks came from. Mare Imbrium is close to several of the landing sites, and the blow that made it threw melted rock across a great part of the Moon. So many of the rocks that said "3.9 billion" may record one blow, not a storm. Other scientists argued that the way the rocks were dated could make a spike that was not there.

Many scientists now think the hits came over a long time, slowly growing fewer, perhaps with a burst somewhere in it. The size of rock needed to boil the oceans has grown too: in 2022 it was put at more than seven hundred kilometres across.

The Earth has kept no crater from this time. The oldest signs of big hits are thin layers of tiny round beads, each about the size of a fine grain of sand, made when rock vaporised by an impact cooled and fell like hail, in rocks in South Africa and Western Australia. Those are about 3.5 to 3.2 billion years old, and nobody knows how many older ones have been lost.

events.picturesWanted: the full Moon with Mare Imbrium marked (NASA, public domain); glass spherules from the Barberton beds under a microscope (licence to check).
references: Fouad Tera, Dimitri Papanastassiou and Gerald Wasserburg, "Isotopic evidence for a terminal lunar cataclysm," *Earth and Planetary Science Letters*, 1974. The storm.
Norman Sleep, Kevin Zahnle, James Kasting and Harold Morowitz, "Annihilation of ecosystems by large asteroid impacts on the early Earth," *Nature*, 1989. Boiling the oceans.
William Bottke and Marc Norman, "The Late Heavy Bombardment," *Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences*, 2017. The doubt, and the long decline.
Robert Citron and Sarah Stewart, "Large impacts onto the early Earth: planetary sterilization and iron delivery," *Planetary Science Journal*, 2022. The bigger rock.

events.knownFrom: layered mounds in rock in the Pilbara, and older, disputed traces in Greenland, Labrador, Nunavik and a single zircon

placeNow.name: Strelley Pool, Trendall Locality, East Pilbara, Western Australia (21.21 S, 119.31 E)

events.summary: About 3.43 billion years ago. In shallow water in what is now the Pilbara, in Western Australia, mats of microbes built layered mounds of stone. They are the oldest signs of life that nearly everyone accepts.

dateLine.tail: and probably begun by 4.1 billion years ago

paragraphs: West of Marble Bar, in the Pilbara, Six Mile Creek cuts through a band of grey and white rock. In the rock are shapes: low domes, steep cones, waves, and something that looks like the bottom of an egg carton. They run for more than ten kilometres.
The shapes are stromatolites ("stro-MAT-o-lites").

A stromatolite is built by microbes, living things so small that millions fit on a fingernail. They grow in a mat on the bottom of shallow water, and the mat is sticky. Sand and mud settle on it and stick, and the microbes grow up through the new layer toward the light, and the next layer settles on them. Layer by layer, over years, the mat builds a mound of stone.

Stromatolites are still being built today in Hamelin Pool, in Shark Bay, on the coast of Western Australia, where the water is about twice as salty as the sea and few animals can live to graze on the mats.

In 2006 Abigail Allwood, an Australian geologist, and her colleagues described seven different kinds of shape at Strelley Pool. They argued that so many shapes, each suited to its place on an old shallow seafloor, could only have been built by living things. Nearly everyone now agrees. Rocks above and below the mounds show they are between about 3.43 and 3.35 billion years old.
Is life older than that?

Probably. Several older finds have been claimed, and every one is argued over. In Greenland, small peaks in 3.7-billion-year-old rock were called stromatolites in 2016, and two years later another team showed they could be folds made by squeezing. In Labrador and in Nunavik there are traces of carbon and tiny tubes in rock at least 3.7 billion years old, and perhaps much older. And in 2015 a team found a speck of carbon sealed inside a zircon from the Jack Hills, 4.1 billion years old, that looks like carbon left by life. They called it "potentially" life, and that is as far as anyone can go.

events.picturesWanted: the Strelley Pool cones and egg-carton forms (Allwood 2006 figures, or GSWA; licence to ask); living stromatolites at Hamelin Pool (Commons or DBCA; licence to check).

events.label: Kenorland
events.ageText: 2700 Ma · ± 50 Ma · an estimate, from the ages of mountain building and of dykes in the old pieces
events.ageHow: an estimate, from the ages of mountain building and of dykes in the old pieces
events.knownFrom: the ages of old mountain belts and dykes, and the direction of magnetism frozen into old rock

placeNow.short: about a position on the ancient Earth

events.summary: About 2.7 billion years ago. Many old pieces of continent came together. Some geologists think they made one great continent, called Kenorland. Others think they made several smaller ones.

paragraphs: Kenora is a town on Lake of the Woods, in northwestern Ontario. The Anishinaabe name for the place is Wauzhushk Onigum, "the portage to the country of the muskrats," and the town was once called Rat Portage. In 1905 the town took a new name, made from the first letters of Keewatin, Norman and Rat Portage.

The rock under the town is very old. It belongs to the Superior craton, the largest of the very old pieces of continent left on Earth. A craton ("CRAY-ton") is the old, stable heart of a continent, a piece that has survived since it formed while the land around it was broken up and remade. Mountains were built here about 2.7 billion years ago, and geologists named that time of mountain building the Kenoran, after the town.
In 1991 a group of geologists suggested that the Superior craton and the other old cratons had then been joined into one great continent. They called it Kenorland.
How could anyone tell?

When a continent is pulled apart, melted rock rises into the cracks and freezes there as walls of dark rock called dykes. So if two cratons were once one, their dykes should match: the same ages, in the same order. Rock also keeps a little magnetism from the time it froze, pointing the way the Earth's field pointed, and that can say how far north or south a piece once lay.

In 2003 Wouter Bleeker, a geologist at the Geological Survey of Canada, looked at the dykes. The Superior craton has dykes about 2.45 billion years old. The Slave craton, the old rock around Yellowknife, has none of those, and has dykes about 2.2 billion years old instead. So the two broke away from their neighbours at different times. Bleeker thought there were several smaller groups, not one continent.
He called his paper "a puzzle in ca. 35 pieces," because that is about how many pieces of crust that old survive. Nobody has fitted them together yet.

events.summary: About 2.5 billion years ago. Tiny living things in the sea were probably already splitting water with sunlight and giving off oxygen. A drill core from Western Australia may hold a whiff of it. How much earlier, nobody knows.

dateLine.tail: and probably begun by 3 billion years ago

paragraphs: In 2004 a drilling rig in the Hamersley Range, in the Pilbara, drilled down through old seafloor and brought up a long stick of rock, a core, nearly a kilometre of it. Between about a hundred and two hundred metres down, the core passes through dark shale, mud that settled on a seafloor about 2.5 billion years ago and turned to stone.
The scientists were looking for oxygen.

Almost all the oxygen in the air today was made by living things, and the first to make it were probably cyanobacteria ("sigh-AN-o-bacteria"), tiny cells that live in water and use sunlight to make food. To do it they need hydrogen, and they pull it out of water, which is hydrogen and oxygen joined. The oxygen is thrown away.

For a long time, the oxygen they threw away vanished. Iron dissolved in the sea took it, and so did the gases from volcanoes and the fresh rock of the land. Only when those were used up could oxygen stay in the air, and in rock that is plain from about 2.4 billion years ago.
So when did the oxygen-making start?

In 2007 a team led by Ariel Anbar, a geochemist in Arizona, reported metals in the shale that rivers carry to the sea only when oxygen in the air is wearing away the rocks. They called it a whiff of oxygen, about seventy million years before oxygen first built up in the air. In 2022 another team looked at the same core and said the metals had been added much later, after the mud had become rock. In 2023 Anbar's team answered. Nobody has won.

Older evidence has had a harder time. Chemicals found in 1999 in rocks 2.7 billion years old, said to come from cyanobacteria, turned out in 2015 to have got into the rock much later. Rocks in South Africa, nearly 3 billion years old, hold signs of oxygen in shallow water, and that evidence has so far held up. The clocks in living cells' genes say somewhere between 3.4 and 2.9 billion years.

placeNow.name: Joffre Gorge, Karijini National Park, Western Australia (22.39 S, 118.27 E)

events.summary: About 2.46 billion years ago. A day lasted about 17 hours, and the Moon was closer than it is now. The measurement comes from the rhythm of the layers in a rock in Karijini, Western Australia.

paragraphs: In Karijini National Park, in the Pilbara of Western Australia, Joffre Gorge cuts down through rock striped red, grey and black. The rock is banded iron: thin layers rich in iron and layers richer in clay, laid down one on another on a seafloor about 2.46 billion years ago.
The stripes are not all alike. Thin layers gather into bundles, and the bundles come round again and again, like a beat.
So what kept the beat?

The Earth spins like a top, and like a top it wobbles, so that its axis slowly traces a circle. Together with slow changes in the Earth's path around the Sun, the wobble changes how sunlight falls on the Earth through the year, and so the climate changes in a slow rhythm too. Today the rhythm takes about 21,000 years to come round. The climate changed what settled on the seafloor, and the rock kept the beat.
How fast the Earth wobbles depends on how fast it spins and on how close the Moon is. So if you can measure the beat in very old rock, you can work out how long a day was then.

In 2022 Margriet Lantink, a geologist at Utrecht University, and her colleagues did that with the layers at Joffre Gorge, which they dated by tiny zircon crystals in a thin layer of shale. Their answer was a day of about 16.9 hours, with the Moon about 321,800 kilometres away, a little more than four-fifths as far as it is now.

The day has been growing longer ever since, and the Moon has been moving away. The Moon's pull raises tides in the sea, and the tides drag on the spinning Earth like a hand on a turning wheel, slowing it. As the Earth slows, the Moon is pushed outward, and today it moves away by about four centimetres a year.
Before 2022, the oldest measurement of the day made this way came from rock in northern China about 1.4 billion years old, and it gave a day of nearly 19 hours.

placeNow.name: Gowganda, Ontario, Canada (47.63 N, 80.79 W)

events.summary: About 2.45 billion years ago. Ice spread over the Earth, came and went at least four times in more than two hundred million years, and once reached near the equator. It began about when oxygen first reached the air.

paragraphs: Near Gowganda, in northern Ontario, there is grey rock packed with stones of every size, from grains of sand to boulders, jumbled together. Rivers and waves sort stones by size. Ice does not. A glacier picks up whatever it slides over and drops the lot in a heap when it melts.

The rock at Gowganda is glacier rubble that turned to stone, about 2.3 billion years old. It is the youngest of three such layers north of Lake Huron, one above another; the oldest, called the Ramsay Lake, was laid down about 2.45 billion years ago. Rocks in South Africa hold others. Dated by the ash and lava between the layers, the rocks of the two countries say that ice came and went at least four times between about 2.45 and 2.22 billion years ago.
How far did the ice reach?

In South Africa, in the Northern Cape, a layer of glacier rubble called the Makganyene lies under old lava. When lava cools, tiny grains of iron in it line up with the Earth's magnetism and stay that way, and how steeply they point says how far from the equator the lava was. In 1997 David Evans, Nicolas Beukes and Joseph Kirschvink measured the lava above the Makganyene and found it had formed about 11 degrees from the equator. Kirschvink and his colleagues argued that the whole Earth had frozen. Not everyone is convinced.
Why then?

The ice came at about the same time as oxygen first reached the air. Before that, the air probably held methane, a gas made by tiny living things, which traps the Sun's heat even better than carbon dioxide does. Oxygen destroys methane. One idea is that when oxygen arrived, the methane went, and the Earth cooled until it froze. Many geologists think the timing is no coincidence. One study argues that the oxygen came first, but the question is not settled.
This was not the Earth's first ice age. Rubble in South Africa shows that glaciers were already at work about 2.9 billion years ago, but nobody knows how far that ice reached.

events.summary: About 2.43 billion years ago. Oxygen first stayed in the air, though only a trace of it. For about two hundred million years it seems to have come and gone, until about 2.22 billion years ago it stayed for good.

paragraphs: Long sticks of rock drilled from the ground in South Africa hold grey shale, mud that settled on a seafloor between about 2.35 and 2.2 billion years ago. Inside the shale are tiny grains of pyrite, a mineral made of iron and sulphur, and the sulphur in them tells whether the air above that sea held oxygen.
How can sulphur tell?

Sulphur atoms come in a few weights, some slightly heavier than others. Volcanoes breathe out sulphur gas, and high in the air the Sun's ultraviolet light breaks the gas apart. With no oxygen in the air, the ultraviolet reaches all the way down, and the breaking sorts the sulphur atoms by weight in an odd way that nothing else on Earth does. Rain carries the sulphur into the sea, and the rocks keep the odd mix. But even a trace of oxygen, about a hundred-thousandth of what the air holds now, is enough to end it.
In 2000 James Farquhar and his colleagues measured sulphur in rocks of many ages and found that the odd mix vanishes between about 2.45 and 2.09 billion years ago.

Other rocks show oxygen first reaching the air about 2.43 billion years ago. In 2021 Simon Poulton, a geochemist at the University of Leeds, and his colleagues looked closely at younger rocks from the Transvaal of South Africa. They found the odd mix coming back after oxygen had arrived, then vanishing again, more than once. Only about 2.22 billion years ago did oxygen stay for good.

Why did it rise then, and not before? The tiny living things that make oxygen were probably at work hundreds of millions of years earlier. Geologists have several ideas: that more volcanoes were on land instead of under the sea, that hydrogen leaking away into space slowly cleared the way, or that the living things that made methane ran short of the nickel they need. None has won.
Since then, oxygen has never left the air, though for more than another billion years there was far less of it than there is now.

events.summary: About 2.31 billion years ago. Sand on land rusted red. It is the oldest red rock on land that has been found, and it means there was oxygen in the air to make rust.

dateLine.tail: and probably begun by 2.43 billion years ago

paragraphs: Around the town of Cobalt, in northern Ontario near the Quebec border, there is a sandstone called the Lorrain. Look at it under a microscope and its grains of quartz, clear as glass on their own, are coated with a thin skin of red dust. The dust is hematite, a kind of rust.

In 2024 a team of geologists in Canada found that the red skin formed soon after the sand was laid down on land, as rainwater soaked through it, a little more than 2.31 billion years ago. They say it is the oldest red rock on land that anyone has found.
Rust is iron joined with oxygen. Iron on land rusts only if there is oxygen in the air.
So what did the land look like before?

At Blind River, also in Ontario, and in South Africa, there are older gravels, laid down by rivers, that hold grains of pyrite, a shiny yellow mineral of iron and sulphur often called fool's gold. Oxygen destroys pyrite. Those grains were tumbled down rivers and survived, so the air they tumbled through had almost no oxygen in it.

Rust is a mineral, and once there was oxygen, the Earth could make many minerals it had never made before. Robert Hazen, a mineralogist in Washington, has spent years counting. In 2008 he and his colleagues worked out that the dust the solar system formed from held only about a dozen kinds of mineral, and that by the time the first continents formed there may have been about 1,500. Of the 4,300 kinds then known, they argued, most exist only because of living things, chiefly because of the oxygen that living things made.
Mineralogists keep finding new kinds. In September 2026 the official list held 6,239.

placeNow.name: the Hull–Rust–Mahoning mine, Hibbing, Minnesota, USA (47.46 N, 92.95 W)

events.summary: About 1.88 billion years ago. For the last time on such a scale, the iron dissolved in the sea fell as rust, in layers. The layers are now the iron ore of Minnesota, Michigan and Ontario.

paragraphs: At Hibbing, in Minnesota, there is a hole in the ground about five kilometres long, three wide and more than 160 metres deep. It is the Hull–Rust–Mahoning mine, and people have been digging iron ore out of it since 1895. The mine lies along the Mesabi Range, a name that comes from the Ojibwe *Misaabe Wajiw*, "Big Man Mountain."

The ore is banded iron, rock in thin layers, some dark and rich in iron and some paler and made of silica, the stuff of quartz and flint. The layers settled on a seafloor about 1.88 billion years ago.
How does a sea make iron ore?

Iron dissolves in seawater only when there is little or no oxygen in it. Join that iron with oxygen and it becomes rust, which cannot stay dissolved, so it sinks to the bottom. Layer after layer of rust, with layers of silica between, became banded iron. What did the joining is argued: oxygen made by tiny living things, other tiny living things that use iron directly, or sunlight.

Banded iron is old. The oldest, in Greenland, is more than 3.7 billion years old, and the greatest of all was laid down in Western Australia about 2.47 to 2.45 billion years ago. The iron around Lake Superior, in Minnesota, Michigan and Ontario, was one last great pulse. Then the seas almost stopped making banded iron for more than a billion years.

Why did it stop? Some geologists think the deep sea gained oxygen, so iron could no longer travel through it dissolved. Others think the deep sea filled instead with sulphur, which locked the iron away as pyrite. Others point to a huge asteroid that hit near what is now Sudbury, Ontario, about 1.85 billion years ago, and stirred the oceans.
Most of the iron ore mined in the world today is banded iron, and most of the iron ore mined in the United States comes from Minnesota.

events.summary: About 1.8 billion years ago. Most of the land may have come together into one great continent, which lasted hundreds of millions of years. Geologists call it Nuna, or Columbia. Nobody is sure what shape it was.

dateLine.tail: and probably begun by 2.1 billion years ago

paragraphs: Under the town of Flin Flon, and across a wide belt of northern Manitoba and Saskatchewan, lie the roots of mountains. Geologists call the belt the Trans-Hudson. About 1.8 billion years ago, two old pieces of what is now North America pushed into each other here, the way India is pushing into Asia today, and the edges crumpled up into mountains. The mountains wore away long ago; the roots remain.

Belts like this one, from about 2.1 to 1.8 billion years old, are found on nearly every continent. In 2002 two groups of geologists argued that they were the seams of one supercontinent, made when most of the land on Earth came together.

They gave it different names. John Rogers and M. Santosh called it Columbia, after the Columbia region of North America, which in their map lay next to India. But Paul Hoffman had already, in 1997, called the joined core of North America and northern and eastern Europe Nuna, from an Inuit word for the lands bordering the northern oceans, and many geologists now use his name.
How do you fit together a continent nobody has seen?

One way is to match the seams, like the torn edges of a map. Another is the magnetism of rocks. When rock forms, tiny grains of iron in it line up with the Earth's magnetism and stay that way, and how steeply they point says how far the rock was from the equator. But the grains cannot say how far east or west the rock was, so a piece of continent can slide sideways on the map without breaking any evidence.

So the shape is argued. Siberia may have been part of Nuna, but nobody has proved it, and for parts of South America and Africa there is no strong evidence that they were part of it. Many geologists think Nuna was together by about 1.8 billion years ago, others say somewhat later, and it seems to have held together until somewhere around 1.5 to 1.4 billion.
Nobody has drawn a map of Nuna that everyone accepts.

events.summary: About 1.64 billion years ago. Fossils in China may be the oldest cells of the kind animals and plants are made of, with a nucleus. They were probably here earlier, and certainly by 1.05 billion years ago.

dateLine.tail: and probably begun by 1.9 billion years ago
dateLine.sure: and certainly here by 1.05 billion years ago

paragraphs: Every animal, every plant, every mushroom and every seaweed is made of cells of one kind. Each has a nucleus, a small bag that holds the cell's genes. Each also holds tiny parts called mitochondria ("my-toe-KON-dree-uh"), which use oxygen to make the energy the cell runs on. Bacteria have neither.

The mitochondria were once bacteria themselves. Long ago a cell swallowed a bacterium and, instead of digesting it, kept it, and the two lived on as one. Lynn Margulis, an American biologist, argued this in 1967, and many journals turned her paper down before one printed it. It is now accepted.
But when did it happen?

In the Yanshan mountains of North China there are rocks called the Chuanlinggou, made of mud that settled about 1.64 billion years ago. In them, under the microscope, are fossils of single cells with walls patterned and built in ways that bacteria are not known to build. In 2024 a team of Chinese and American palaeontologists described something more from the same rocks: threads of a few cells to more than twenty, with what may be spores inside. And on the other side of the world, in the Northern Territory of Australia, rock of about the same age holds molecules from the skins of cells, of a kind made almost only by cells like these.

Do they belong to the family of cells alive today? Some palaeontologists think so. Others think they were relatives that died out, and that the cells alive today share an ancestor that lived much later.

Older claims are harder to believe. Coiled ribbons in rock in Michigan, about 1.87 billion years old, might be the remains of a cell like these or of a colony of bacteria. The clocks in living things' genes give dates from about 2.1 billion to about 1 billion years ago.
By about 1.05 billion years ago there is a fossil nobody argues over: a red seaweed, with a nucleus in every cell.

events.summary: About 1.05 billion years ago. A red seaweed grew in the shallows of what is now Arctic Canada. It is the oldest living thing that can be named to a group alive today, and it shows signs of sexual reproduction.

paragraphs: Somerset Island, in Nunavut, is a bare, rocky island in the Canadian Arctic where nobody lives now. In its rocks is a layer of chert, a hard stone like flint, and in the chert, too small to see without a microscope, are fossils of threads made of cells.

The threads look very like *Bangia*, a red seaweed that grows on rocks by the sea today. In 1990 Nicholas Butterfield, Andrew Knoll and Keene Swett described them as a red seaweed, and in 2000 Butterfield named them *Bangiomorpha* ("BANG-ee-oh-MOR-fuh"), "shaped like *Bangia*." Each thread was anchored to the seafloor by a holdfast, a kind of foot, made of cells different from the rest.
Most fossils this old can be called only "some kind of cell." *Bangiomorpha* is the oldest fossil that can be named to a group still alive today.

Some of the threads also carry two different kinds of cells for making new seaweed, as *Bangia* does when it reproduces sexually. So *Bangiomorpha* is the oldest fossil yet found that shows signs of sexual reproduction.

For years nobody was sure how old it was: guesses ran from about 1.2 billion years to 720 million. In 2018 Timothy Gibson and his colleagues dated black shale on Baffin Island, to the east, which holds the same fossils. The answer was about 1.05 billion years.

A red seaweed makes its food from sunlight using tiny coloured parts that were once cyanobacteria, swallowed and kept, just as mitochondria were. So the date also says that this swallowing had happened by then.

Rock at Chitrakoot, in India, about 1.6 billion years old, holds fossils that may be red seaweed too. The team that described them in 2017 named one *Rafatazmia*, after Rafat Azmi, an Indian palaeontologist who had found fossils there years before. Other scientists doubted him; the fossils turned out to be real, and far older than he had thought. Whether they are red seaweed is still argued.

placeNow.name: the Gairdner dykes, near Lake Gairdner, South Australia, Australia (31.57 S, 136.00 E, the lake)

events.summary: About 827 million years ago. Rodinia, the great continent of its time, began to crack apart. Melted rock rose into the cracks and set, and in South Australia the walls it made are still there, mostly buried under younger ground.

paragraphs: When the Earth's crust is pulled, it cracks, and melted rock rises from below and fills the cracks. The melt cools into walls of dark rock, called dykes, that cut straight down through the older rock around them. Across South Australia, from around Lake Gairdner, runs a swarm of them about a thousand kilometres long, mostly buried under younger ground.

In 1998 Michael Wingate and his colleagues dated tiny crystals from the Gairdner dykes. The dykes had set about 827 million years ago, and they were among the first cracks in a continent that held most of the land on Earth.
That continent is called Rodinia. It came together between about 1.3 billion and 900 million years ago, and in 1990 Mark and Dianna McMenamin named it from *rodina*, the Russian word for motherland.

Nobody is sure of Rodinia's shape. Some maps put Antarctica beside western North America, some put Australia there, and some put a piece of China between them. Every map has to fit the same evidence: cracks, and the lava that filled them, of the same age, on coasts that are now oceans apart.

The cracking went on for about a hundred million years. About 780 million years ago dykes filled cracks across more than 2,400 kilometres of western North America. By about 750 million years ago the land along that coast had begun to split away. About 720 million years ago lava poured out over millions of square kilometres of what is now Arctic Canada, on land that then lay near the equator.

Where Australia began to crack, a long trough opened and slowly filled with sand, mud and lime. That trough is now the rock of the Flinders Ranges and the hills around Adelaide, where the rubble of the next great ice ages was found.
A million or two years after the last of the Arctic lavas cooled, the ice began to spread.

placeNow.name: Sturt Gorge Recreation Park, Adelaide, South Australia, Australia (35.04 S, 138.58 E)

events.summary: About 717 million years ago. Ice spread from the poles to the equator and stayed for about 57 million years. Geologists call it a snowball Earth. Whether any of the sea stayed open is still argued.

paragraphs: On the southern edge of Adelaide, the Sturt River has cut a gorge through grey rock full of jumbled stones, from pebbles to boulders. More than a hundred years ago, Adelaide geologists argued that the jumble had been dropped by glaciers, and in 1950 Douglas Mawson and Reg Sprigg named this time of ice the Sturtian, after the gorge.
Rubble like it turns up on nearly every continent, of nearly the same age. That was strange enough. Stranger still, some of it seemed to have formed near the equator.

When rock forms, tiny grains of iron in it line up with the Earth's magnetism, and how steeply they point says how far from the equator the rock was. In 1964 Brian Harland, a geologist at Cambridge, argued from this that there had been ice in the tropics. In the 1960s a Soviet scientist, Mikhail Budyko, worked out that if ice ever covered the whole Earth, it would reflect so much sunlight that it could never melt, so it could never have happened. And yet the Earth is not frozen.

In 1992 Joseph Kirschvink, a geologist in California, gave the idea its name, the snowball Earth, and suggested how the ice could end. In 1998 Paul Hoffman and his colleagues published evidence from Namibia, and many more geologists began to take it seriously.

In 2010 Francis Macdonald and his colleagues dated ash among the glacial rocks of the Yukon at a little under 717 million years, and showed that the Yukon then lay within ten degrees of the equator, with ice reaching the sea.

How cold was it? Models say the equator may have been as cold as Antarctica is now. Some geologists think a strip of open water stayed near the equator. Others think the ice covered nearly everything.
The ice lasted about 57 million years, nearly as long as the time from the end of the dinosaurs to now.

events.summary: About 639 million years ago. About twenty million years after the first snowball melted, the ice came back to the equator. This time it lasted about four million years, and ash in the rubble says so.

paragraphs: In the hills of northern Namibia there is rubble that glaciers dropped, turned to stone, called the Ghaub. Here and there in it are thin layers of volcanic ash.

Volcanic ash holds tiny crystals of zircon, and a zircon starts a clock when it forms. Some of the uranium in it slowly turns into lead, at a rate that is known, so the more lead there is, the older the crystal. Ash that falls into rubble as it piles up dates the rubble.

In 2016 Anthony Prave and his colleagues dated two ash beds in the Ghaub. One, already deep in the rubble, was about 639 million years old. The other, near the top, was about 635 million, so the ice had lasted at least four million years. In 2025 Adrian Tasistro-Hart and his colleagues dated ash in the same hills that fell just before the ice arrived, also about 639 million years ago, and came to the same answer: this second snowball lasted about four million years. The first had lasted about 57 million.
Geologists call this second snowball the Marinoan, after Marino, a suburb of Adelaide. Douglas Mawson and Reg Sprigg named it in 1950, along with the Sturtian.

Was it really at the equator? In the Flinders Ranges of South Australia there is rock of the same ice age, the Elatina, laid down in a sea at the edge of the ice. In 1999 Linda Sohl, Nicholas Christie-Blick and Dennis Kent measured its magnetism and found that it formed about eight degrees from the equator. They also found that the Earth's magnetism had flipped, north for south, at least twice while it was being laid down. The magnetism flips only every so often, so the ice at the equator lasted at least hundreds of thousands of years.

About 580 million years ago ice came again, in what is now Newfoundland, near Gaskiers. That ice came and went quickly, perhaps within a few hundred thousand years, and nobody thinks it was a snowball.

events.summary: About 635 million years ago. The second snowball ended. Carbon dioxide from volcanoes, and perhaps dust darkening the ice, warmed the Earth enough to melt it, perhaps in a few thousand years. Pale limestone settled straight onto the rubble.

paragraphs: In Brachina Gorge, in the Flinders Ranges of South Australia, a creek has cut through layers of rock tilted on their sides. One layer is the rubble of the second snowball. Lying straight on top of it, with nothing in between, is a pale, fine rock, a kind of limestone, a few metres thick.
The same thing is found all over the world. Wherever there is rubble from this second snowball, there is pale limestone on top of it. Geologists call it the cap.
So how did a snowball end?

On an Earth without ice, rain takes carbon dioxide out of the air. The rain wears away rock, carries what it has dissolved to the sea, and the sea turns it into limestone. Volcanoes put the carbon dioxide back, and the two stay in rough balance.

Under the ice, there was almost no rain on bare rock, so the wearing away nearly stopped. But the volcanoes went on breathing out carbon dioxide for millions of years. It piled up in the air, perhaps to a hundred times as much as now, or more. Carbon dioxide traps the Sun's heat, and at last there was enough to start melting the ice at the equator. One recent study argues that dark volcanic dust on the ice helped, by soaking up sunlight.

Then the melting fed itself. Open sea is dark and soaks up sunlight that white ice would reflect, so the more sea opened, the warmer it got. Models say the ice could have retreated toward the poles in a few thousand years.

The air was still full of carbon dioxide. Hot, heavy rain fell on rock the ice had ground to powder, and the rivers carried what they dissolved to the sea, where it settled as the pale cap. How long that took is argued: some say thousands of years, some say hundreds of thousands.
Geologists chose the bottom of the cap at Enorama Creek as the start of a new stretch of the Earth's history, the Ediacaran, and in 2004 they marked the spot with a plaque.

events.summary: About 600 million years ago. Tiny balls of cells, each about half a millimetre across, were kept in rock in Guizhou, China. They may be the oldest animal embryos ever found, or something else entirely.

paragraphs: Near the town of Weng'an ("wung-AHN"), in Guizhou, in southern China, phosphate is mined from a layer of dark rock. Phosphate is dug for fertiliser. But geologists who break the rock and soak it in acid, the same acid that is in vinegar, find something else left at the bottom of the dish: little balls, thousands of them, each about half a millimetre across, about the size of a grain of sand.
Under a microscope, the balls are made of cells. Some hold two cells, some four, some eight, and some many hundreds, packed together like soap bubbles.
That is what an animal egg looks like as it begins to divide. In 1998 two teams, one led by Shuhai Xiao and one by Chia-Wei Li and Junyuan Chen, said these were animal embryos, the oldest ever found.
So is that what they are?

Nobody is sure. In 2007 another team said they were more likely giant bacteria, like some that live on the seafloor today. In 2011 a team led by Therese Huldtgren looked inside the balls without breaking them, using a machine that makes very bright X-rays. In some of the cells they saw what seemed to be nuclei, and in others what looked like the balls breaking open to release something. They argued that the balls were single-celled creatures, perhaps distant relatives of animals, but not animals. In 2016 a Chinese team argued back that some of the balls divide in a way only animal embryos do. Other scientists say the balls may simply have divided unevenly, which proves nothing either way.

Even the age is argued. The rock at Weng'an has never been dated in a way everyone accepts, so geologists match it with dated layers elsewhere in China. One matching says about 609 million years. Another says no older than about 587.
What would settle it is a ball that grew up: a fossil of the same creature, older and bigger, in the same rock. None has been found.

events.summary: About 580 million years ago. Ice came back, but not over the whole Earth this time. Its rubble lies on the shore of Newfoundland. A few million years later, the oldest large fossils appear.

paragraphs: On St. Mary's Bay, on the Avalon Peninsula of Newfoundland, is the small community of Gaskiers. The rock along its shore is a jumble: stones of every size, some of them scratched, set in hardened mud. In some layers single stones sit in fine, even mud, as if they had been dropped into it from above.

That is what ice leaves. A glacier grinds up rock and carries it, and scratches the stones as they scrape against each other. An iceberg drifting over the sea drops its stones one at a time into the mud below as it melts. This was an ice age, and it is named after Gaskiers.

There are thin beds of volcanic ash in the rock too, a few metres below the rubble and just above it. Ash can be dated, and in 2016 Judy Pu and her colleagues dated it. The ice came after about 580.9 million years ago and was gone by about 579.9 million. Dates from another part of Newfoundland narrowed it further, to perhaps less than 340,000 years, which is short for an ice age this old.
So was it a third snowball, like the two before it?

The team said no. Ice that covered the whole Earth would have lasted millions of years before it melted, as the snowballs did. This ice came and went too fast. Rubble that may be of about the same age is found on at least eight of the old continents, and some of it formed nearer the equator than the poles, but the ice probably did not close over the whole sea.

In 2024 another team found stones dropped by ice hundreds of metres lower in the rock, which would mean the cold began earlier and lasted between one and nearly five million years. That is still argued.

About forty kilometres away, at Mistaken Point, the rock laid down after the ice holds the oldest large fossils that most geologists accept. They appear a few million years after the ice, perhaps six, perhaps nine. Whether the ice had anything to do with them, nobody knows.

events.summary: About 574 million years ago. Fronds grew on a dark seafloor, too deep for sunlight. Ash from volcanoes buried them where they stood. They are among the oldest large living things ever found, and nobody knows what they were.

paragraphs: At Mistaken Point, at the southeastern tip of the Avalon Peninsula of Newfoundland, tilted sheets of rock slope down to the sea. On the rock are thousands of imprints: fronds like feathers, spindles, discs. Some are a few centimetres long and some nearly two metres. Visitors walk out with a guide, and before they step on the rock they put on cloth booties, so that their shoes won't wear the fossils away.
In June 1967 Shiva Balak Misra, a student from India at Memorial University in St. John's, was mapping the rocks here with his assistant, Paul Thompson, when he found them.

The creatures lived on the seafloor and were buried where they stood by ash from volcanoes, which drifted down through the water and covered them like snow. The ash can be dated. The best-known surface is about 565 million years old, and the oldest fronds at Mistaken Point are about 574 million.

The seafloor was deep. The layers above and below the fossils were laid down far below the reach of storm waves, perhaps hundreds of metres down, perhaps more. Sunlight does not reach that far. So the fronds were not plants or seaweed: there was no light for them to live on.
Look closely at a frond and each branch is made of smaller branches shaped like it, and each of those of smaller branches still. A shape built that way has a great deal of surface for its size.

None of the fronds has a mouth, a gut or a leg. Many palaeontologists think they lived by soaking up food dissolved in the water, through all that surface. What kind of living thing they were is argued: some think they were early animals, unlike any alive now; nobody has shown it for certain.
Similar fronds turn up in England, in Russia and in Australia, but the oldest are here.

events.summary: About 562 million years ago. A frond lived on a seafloor that is now Leicestershire, England. In 1956 a girl of fifteen saw its imprint and was not believed. A year later a schoolboy found it again.

paragraphs: In the summer of 1956, Tina Negus, who was fifteen, persuaded her family to go picking bilberries in Charnwood Forest, in Leicestershire, though what she was really looking for was fossils. On a rock in an old quarry, half hidden by roots, she saw the shape of a leaf, or a fern, pressed into the stone.

She had read that the rocks of Charnwood were Precambrian ("pree-KAM-bree-un"): older than the time, about 539 million years ago, when fossils of shells and bones begin to fill the rocks. Most geologists then thought there were no fossils in Precambrian rocks. She told her geography teacher, and the teacher told her the same.
So it was left there.

In the spring of 1957, Roger Mason, a schoolboy in Leicester, was climbing in an old quarry in the forest with two friends, Richard Blachford and Richard Allen, and he saw the same kind of shape. He made a rubbing of it with paper and pencil and showed it to his father, who knew a geologist at the university, Trevor Ford. Ford came to look. Quarrymen lifted out the block, and in 1958 Ford named the fossil *Charnia masoni* ("CHAR-nee-uh MAY-son-eye"), after the forest and after Roger.
*Charnia* was a frond, like a feather standing on the seafloor, with branches made of smaller branches. It had no mouth and no gut. Nobody is sure what it was.

It was not the first fossil found in Precambrian rock. Strange imprints had been found in Australia and Namibia before. But those had been taken to be younger. Charnwood's rocks were known to be Precambrian, so *Charnia* could not be explained away, and it helped convince geologists that large living things existed before the Cambrian. In 2015 the rock was dated: about 562 million years old.
The fossil itself is in Leicester Museum & Art Gallery, on New Walk.

Fifty years later, in 2007, Tina Negus and Roger Mason met at a meeting in Leicester to celebrate the find. Roger Mason said she had seen the frond before he did, and that nobody had taken her seriously.

placeNow.name: Lyamtsa, Onega Peninsula, White Sea, Arkhangelsk Oblast, Russia (64.43 N, 37.07 E, the village)

events.kindRaw: crop or animal (a living thing; the list has no better word)
events.summary: About 558 million years ago. Dickinsonia, a flat, ribbed oval, lived on the seafloor. For about seventy years nobody could say what it was. In 2018 molecules found in its fossils suggested it was an animal.

paragraphs: On the shores of the White Sea, in the far north of Russia, cliffs of sandstone sixty to a hundred metres high stand over the water. A few years before 2018, Ilya Bobrovskiy, a young geologist studying for his doctorate at the Australian National University, came here by helicopter. He hung over the edge of the cliffs on ropes, dug out great blocks of sandstone, threw them down, washed them and searched them, again and again, looking for one fossil.
The fossil was *Dickinsonia* ("dick-in-SO-nee-uh"): a flat oval with ribs across it, like a bathmat on the seafloor. The smallest are a few millimetres long and the biggest more than a metre.

Reg Sprigg named it in 1947, after Ben Dickinson, one of the leaders of the mines department of South Australia, where it had first been found. Sprigg thought it was a jellyfish. Since then it has been called a worm, a lichen, a giant single cell, and a kind of life with no living relatives.

Nobody could settle it by looking, because the shape could be read so many ways. Bobrovskiy was looking for something else. Some of the White Sea fossils still carry a thin film, all that is left of the creature's body, and in the film are molecules that last for hundreds of millions of years.

Living things make fatty molecules called sterols, and different kinds of life make different ones. Fungi make one kind, green algae another. Animals make almost only cholesterol. When Bobrovskiy and his colleagues measured the film, nearly all of it was the cholesterol kind. In 2018 they argued that *Dickinsonia* was an animal, one of the oldest yet found.

Some palaeontologists were not convinced. One pointed out that a few fungi make cholesterol too; another doubted that the film was really *Dickinsonia*'s own. Many now think it was an animal, but where it fits among animals is still argued.
*Dickinsonia* had no mouth that anyone has found. In 2025 two scientists argued that the film suggests it fed on the mats of microbes that covered the seafloor.

events.summary: About 550 million years ago. Small animals built tubes of shell, among the oldest shells yet found. In China, some tubes have tiny round holes bored through them: the oldest signs yet found of one animal hunting another.

paragraphs: In 1972 Gerard Germs, a geologist working in Namibia, described small fossils from limestone in the south of the country. Each was a tube a few millimetres across, made of little cones stacked one inside the next, like a pile of paper cups. He named them *Cloudina* ("cloud-EE-nuh"), after Preston Cloud, an American geologist who studied the oldest fossils.

The tubes were made of shell, the same stuff as a snail's shell or a seashell. The oldest yet found are in the Tsaus Mountains of southern Namibia, about 550 million years old. They are among the oldest shells anyone has found. Some living thing must have built each tube around itself, and palaeontologists generally think it was a small animal, but nobody knows what kind.
Shells are hard, so they last in rock when soft bodies do not. They also do something else. They protect what is inside.
So what were they protecting it from?

In the Dengying Formation of Shaanxi, in China, *Cloudina* tubes lie in rock of about the same age. In 2003 Hong Hua, Brian Pratt and Lu-Yi Zhang looked at nearly a hundred of them, and found that almost one in five had a small round hole bored through its wall. The holes are 15 to 85 thousandths of a millimetre wide, about as fine as a hair, or finer.
Holes like that, in shells today, are made by animals that drill through a shell to eat what is inside. So the holes in *Cloudina* are the oldest signs yet found of one animal hunting another.
The hunter has never been found. It may have had no hard parts at all, so that only its holes were kept.
There is one more clue. Another kind of shelly tube lies in the same rock, and none of those had holes. Whatever made the holes chose *Cloudina*.

placeNow.name: Fortune Head, Burin Peninsula, Newfoundland, Canada (47.08 N, 55.83 W)

events.summary: About 539 million years ago. The Cambrian began. Within about twenty million years, animals with shells, legs and eyes fill the rocks, kept because their hard parts last. But animals were probably living long before, soft and unkept.

dateLine.tail: and probably begun by 640 million years ago

paragraphs: Fortune Head is a point of land on the Burin Peninsula of Newfoundland, a short walk from the town of Fortune. From the lighthouse a path runs to the cliffs, where the layers of rock lie open to view. Taking a fossil from them is against the law.

In 1992 geologists from many countries agreed that one level in these cliffs, a little more than two metres up in one band of rock, marks the start of the Cambrian ("KAM-bree-un"), the stretch of time when fossils of animals with hard parts begin to fill the rocks.

They chose the level not by a shell but by a burrow. It is called *Treptichnus pedum* ("trep-TICK-nus PEE-dum"), and it is a tunnel in the mud that branches again and again, as if something with a front and a back pushed forward, backed up and pushed again, feeding as it went. Nobody has found the animal that made it.
In 2001 a team found the same burrow about four metres below the level. The line stays where it was agreed. It says when, not who was first.

After it, the rocks change. Within about twenty million years they hold shells, spines and armour, legs with joints and eyes, and by about 520 million years ago trilobites, armoured animals with many legs. Hard parts last, so these animals were kept.
But soft animals rot and leave little. How long were animals living before they had shells?

In rocks in Oman more than 635 million years old, there are molecules that some scientists read as made by sponges, which are animals. In 2021 another team argued that they could have come from algae, changed by time in the rock. Gene clocks, which estimate when animals split apart by counting the differences in their genes, put the first animals somewhere between about 830 and 650 million years ago. Nobody has found a fossil animal that old that everyone accepts.

events.summary: About 518 million years ago. Mud buried whole communities of sea animals in what is now Yunnan, China, and kept their soft parts too: guts, eyes, legs. About 250 kinds have been found there.

paragraphs: Maotianshan ("maow-tyen-shahn") is a hill a few kilometres east of the town of Chengjiang ("chung-jyahng"), in Yunnan, in southern China. On the afternoon of Sunday, the first of July 1984, Hou Xianguang ("ho shyen-gwahng"), a palaeontologist from Nanjing, split a slab of yellowish mudstone on the hill and saw a white half-circle in it. He thought at first it was the shell of an unknown crustacean, an animal like a shrimp.
He kept splitting. Before long it was clear that the mudstone of Maotianshan held more than shells.

Most animals leave nothing in rock but their hard parts, if they have any. At Chengjiang, fine mud buried animals so quickly, and kept them so well, that their soft parts were kept too: guts, gills, eyes, the legs of animals with no shell at all. About 250 kinds have been found since, most of them known from nowhere else.

Among them is *Haikouichthys* ("high-koo-ICK-thiss"), a small, fishlike animal described in 1999, one of the oldest relatives of fish yet found, and so of everything with a backbone. Another is *Amplectobelua*, a swimming hunter with a pair of spiny grasping arms at its head. Its biggest fossils suggest it could grow to almost a metre.

The rock is dated by tiny crystals of zircon in it. The crystals formed in older rock and were washed in with the mud, so the date is the oldest the rock can be: about 518 million years. In older books it is 525 or 530.

In 2012 Chengjiang was made a World Heritage Site. There is a museum on the shore of nearby Fuxian Lake, and the rocks around the hill where Hou Xianguang split his slab are still giving up new animals.

events.summary: About 506 million years ago. Mud on a seafloor buried sea animals, soft parts and all, in what is now the Rocky Mountains of British Columbia. Among them was Anomalocaris, a hunter that took a century to put together.

paragraphs: High on Fossil Ridge, in Yoho National Park in British Columbia, between Wapta Mountain and Mount Field, is a small quarry in dark shale. The walk there and back is about 24 kilometres, with a climb of about 900 metres, and it can be made only with a guide.

Charles Walcott, the head of the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, found the fossils near here at the end of August 1909, and opened the quarry the next year. He and his family came back for years, until 1924, and took more than 65,000 fossils away. Like the fossils at Chengjiang, about twelve million years older, they kept animals' soft parts.
The strangest story in the quarry belongs to *Anomalocaris* ("uh-NOM-uh-lo-CARE-iss").

In 1892, before Walcott came, a curved, jointed piece of fossil from these mountains was taken to be the body of a shrimp-like animal without its head, and named *Anomalocaris*, "strange shrimp." In 1911 Walcott described a ring of plates with a hole in the middle as a jellyfish, and a flat body with flaps as a kind of sea cucumber.

Between 1978 and 1985 the pieces came together. Simon Conway Morris saw that the "jellyfish" belonged to the "sea cucumber", and Derek Briggs saw that the "shrimp" was a limb. Then in 1985 Harry Whittington and Derek Briggs showed that all three were parts of one animal. The "shrimp" was a grasping arm, one of a pair at the front of the head. The "jellyfish" was a mouth. The body swam by waving its flaps. It was a hunter, one of the biggest animals of its time.

In 2012 the puzzle turned once more. Allison Daley and Jan Bergström showed that the ring-shaped mouth and the body with flaps belonged to a close cousin, *Peytoia*. *Anomalocaris* had a mouth of its own, of a different shape.
The complete fossils of *Anomalocaris* are about twenty centimetres long. Some of its loose arms are much bigger, so it may have grown to nearly twice that length.

placeNow.name: Manuels River, Conception Bay South, Newfoundland, Canada (47.52 N, 52.95 W): the best of the evidence the More opens on; the event is about the whole earth

events.summary: About 500 million years ago. Most southern land was joined in one great continent, Gondwana, reaching from near the South Pole past the equator. Fossils and the magnetism in rocks let geologists draw the map with some confidence.

paragraphs: At Manuels River, in Conception Bay South, near St. John's in Newfoundland, the river cuts through dark shale full of trilobites, armoured sea animals with many legs. One of them is *Paradoxides davidis*, which can be bigger than a man's hand. It was found first near St Davids, in Wales, and named after David Homfray, a fossil collector.
On the other side of Newfoundland, the trilobites in the old rocks of the west coast are different. They are kin to the trilobites of Greenland and of the far northwest of Scotland.
So why would the two sides of one island be so different?

In 1966 the Canadian geophysicist J. Tuzo Wilson asked a question in the title of a paper: "Did the Atlantic close and then re-open?" His answer was yes. Western Newfoundland and northwest Scotland were once on one shore of an older ocean, and eastern Newfoundland, England and Wales on the other. The old ocean closed, and the two sides were pressed together. Then the Atlantic opened, but along a different line, and it left a piece of each shore stuck to the other.

That is how a map of the world 500 million years ago is made. The magnetism locked into a rock as it formed tells how far it was from the poles, but not how far east or west. Fossils help with the rest: animals that lived along the same shore are alike, and animals on opposite shores of a wide ocean are not.

The map that comes out has the southern lands, Africa, South America, Antarctica, Australia, India and Arabia, joined in one great continent called Gondwana, which reached from near the South Pole to beyond the equator. North America sat on the equator, apart. The sea was high, and shallow seas covered much of the land.
Before this, there are too few fossils with hard parts to use this way, and the map is far less sure.

events.summary: About 470 million years ago. Plants were growing on land. The oldest widely accepted sign is their spores, specks found in rock in Jujuy, Argentina. The plants themselves have never been found; they were probably tiny, like liverworts.

dateLine.tail: and probably begun by 500 million years ago

paragraphs: Claudia Rubinstein, of a laboratory in Mendoza, in western Argentina, and her team from Argentina and Belgium dissolved pieces of rock in strong acid. The rock came from the valley of the Río Capillas, in the province of Jujuy ("hoo-HOO-ee"), and it had been laid down at the edge of the sea, where a river ran into it. What the acid could not dissolve was left at the bottom: specks far too small to see without a microscope.

Some of the specks were spores. A spore is a single cell that a plant sends out to start a new plant, and the spores of land plants have a tough outer wall. A cell that floats in water has no need of such a wall. A cell that blows through dry air would shrivel without one. So a spore with that wall is the mark of a plant that lived on land, even when it is found in rock laid down in water, where wind or rivers carried it.
In 2010 the team said that these spores, about 470 million years old, were the oldest evidence of plants on land.

The plants that made them have never been found. Spores like these are much like the spores of liverworts, small flat green plants that still grow on damp rock and soil. The oldest fossil of a whole land plant with stems, *Cooksonia* ("cook-SOH-nee-ah"), a few centimetres tall, with stems that fork, is about 432 million years old, from the Czech Republic.

In 2021 two scientists described spore-like specks about 480 million years old, from rock drilled in Western Australia in 1958. They argued that the specks were halfway between the spores of water plants and the spores of land plants, and that plants moved onto land slowly, over many millions of years. Gene clocks, which estimate when two kinds of living thing split apart by counting the differences in their genes, put the first land plants somewhere between about 515 and 474 million years ago.
The plant that made the oldest spores is still to be found.

placeNow.name: Tassili n'Ajjer, Algeria (24.92 N, 10.07 E)

events.summary: About 445 million years ago. Ice sheets spread over North Africa, which then lay near the South Pole, and the seas grew cold. Most kinds of sea animal died out, perhaps 85 kinds in every 100.

paragraphs: In the Tassili n'Ajjer ("ta-SEE-lee nah-JER"), a high plateau of sandstone in the Sahara, in southeast Algeria, there are wide floors of bare rock scored with long straight grooves, all running the same way. Grooves like these are made by ice. When a glacier slides over rock, stones frozen into its base scrape the rock beneath, the way sandpaper scratches wood.
So how did ice reach the Sahara?

It didn't, quite. The Sahara wasn't there. About 445 million years ago the land that is now North Africa lay near the South Pole, part of the great southern continent of Gondwana. An ice sheet spread over it, and the ice ran out across the land toward the sea, scraping as it went. Geologists can still follow which way it flowed.

The cold did not last long, as such things go. The coldest part may have lasted only about two hundred thousand years. But it came with one of the worst dyings in the history of life. In the seas, which held nearly all the animals then, most kinds died out: about 85 kinds in every 100, by one count. It happened in two pulses, one as the ice came and one as it melted. It is the oldest of the five great dyings that geologists count.

What killed them is argued. The old answer is the cold itself: seas cooling and the water locked up as ice, so that the sea fell and the shallow seas where most animals lived dried out. In 2012 one team suggested that the first small plants on land may have pulled enough carbon dioxide from the air to start the cooling. In 2020 another team argued that the dying came from volcanoes, which warmed the seas and took the oxygen from them, not from the ice at all.
Some of the best rocks for the argument are at Dob's Linn, a steep gorge in the south of Scotland, where the line between two stretches of geological time is drawn in dark shale.
