events.summary: About 439 million years ago. The oldest teeth of fish with jaws were kept in rock in Guizhou, China, and whole jawed fish, a little younger, in Chongqing nearby. Jaws themselves are probably older still.

dateLine.tail: and probably begun by 455 million years ago

paragraphs: In the hills of Xiushan ("shyoh-shahn") County, in Chongqing, in southern China, there is a layer of rock that kept whole fish: heads, fins, scales and all. In 2022 a team led by Zhu Min, of the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology in Beijing, described what they had found there. One of the fish, which they named *Xiushanosteus* ("shyoh-shahn-OSS-tee-us"), is about three centimetres long, with bony plates over its head and the front of its body. And it has jaws.

A jaw is a mouth that can bite. The lower part is hinged, so that it can close hard on something and hold it. For millions of years before this, there were fish without jaws, and some still live: the lamprey, which fastens itself to other fish with a round, sucking mouth, is one.

The rock at Xiushan is about 436 million years old. Before 2022, the oldest whole fish with jaws came from Yunnan, in rock about 425 million years old, so the find moved the oldest jaws back by about eleven million years.

In the same issue of the journal, a team led by Plamen Andreev described teeth from Shiqian ("shir-chyen"), in Guizhou, about 439 million years old, a little older still. Each is a little curl of teeth no more than two and a half millimetres across, a shape known from many ancient sharks and bony fish. The rows of teeth lean left or right, as teeth do on the two sides of a jaw.
So were these the first fish with jaws?

Almost certainly not. By 436 million years ago there were already several different kinds, armoured fish and early relatives of sharks among them, and kinds take time to split apart. In Colorado, in rock about 455 million years old, there are scales that some scientists think came from jawed fish. Others say scales that old are too hard to tell apart to be sure.
The oldest jaw is still to be found.

placeNow.name: Cowie, Stonehaven, Aberdeenshire, Scotland (56.97 N, 2.20 W)

events.summary: About 428 million years ago, or a little later: the date is argued. A small millipede-like animal, found at Stonehaven, Scotland, had holes in its body for breathing air, the oldest sign of an animal living on land.

dateLine.tail: and probably begun by 455 million years ago

paragraphs: On the shore at Cowie, at the north end of Stonehaven, in Aberdeenshire, layers of grey rock run down into the sea. Mike Newman, a bus driver from Aberdeen who hunted fossils in his spare time, split some of that rock and found a small piece of an animal with many legs. "The legs were very clear," he said later.

In 2004 two palaeontologists described it and named it *Pneumodesmus newmani* ("NEW-mo-DEZ-mus NEW-man-eye"), after him. On its body are tiny holes, which they read as spiracles, the openings through which millipedes and insects breathe air. An animal that breathed air lived on land, so *Pneumodesmus* became the oldest known animal to live on land.
So how old is it?

That is the argument. When it was named, its age came from fossil spores in rocks nearby: about 428 million years. In 2017 a team led by Stephanie Suarez dated crystals of zircon from volcanic ash below the fossil bed and got about 414 million years, which would make *Pneumodesmus* about fourteen million years younger. Another fossil, from the island of Kerrera, near Oban, dated by the same group at about 425 million years, would then be the oldest millipede known.

In 2024 a team led by Charles Wellman dated the rock again from its spores, looked again at zircon ages from other studies, and argued for the older age. Two of the 2017 team replied that the new samples came from a separate block of rock, cut off from the fossil bed by a fault. Nobody has settled it.

Older tracks exist. In the Lake District, in rock about 455 million years old, there are trackways of many-legged animals on volcanic ash. Most were made under water, but one trackway crosses a few centimetres of ripple tops that stood out of the water, as if the animal made a short walk on dry ground.
The first animal to live on land, whatever it was, has not been found.

placeNow.name: Culver Cliff, near Minehead, Somerset, England (51.22 N, 3.49 W)

events.summary: About 390 million years ago. The oldest forest yet found grew where Somerset, in England, is now. The largest trees were two to four metres tall, with hollow trunks and no leaves, only twigs.

paragraphs: Culver Cliff is a lone cliff of sandstone about thirty metres tall, a kilometre northwest of Minehead, on the coast of Somerset. On one surface of its rock lie at least seventeen fossil tree trunks, five to ten centimetres thick and nearly a metre and a half long. West along the coast, near Porlock Weir, there are six large hollows in the rock, each up to thirty centimetres across and filled with mud. They are where standing trees rotted away.

Geologists had not expected to find important fossil plants in these rocks. In 2024 Neil Davies, of the University of Cambridge, and Christopher Berry and William McMahon described the trunks and hollows and said they were the oldest fossil forest known. "When I first saw pictures of the tree trunks I immediately knew what they were," Berry said, "based on 30 years of studying this type of tree worldwide."

The trees are called *Calamophyton* ("KAL-am-oh-FY-ton"). The largest were two to four metres tall, with hollow trunks, and they had no leaves at all, only hundreds of twiglike branches, which they shed as they grew. There was no grass yet, and almost nothing grew beneath them, but the twigs piled up on the ground. Davies and his colleagues think the trees and their fallen twigs changed the way rivers ran, and helped hold the ground in place.
The rock was laid down by rivers, and the age comes from fossil spores in it: about 390 million years.

Before 2024, the oldest forest known was in an old quarry near Cairo, in New York State, about 386 million years old. Its trees are more like ours. Some belonged to *Archaeopteris* ("ar-kee-OP-ter-iss"), a tree with wood and leaves, whose roots reached out about eleven metres. Nearby, at Gilboa, a flood in 1869 uncovered fossil stumps standing where they grew.
Some of the cliffs along this coast of Somerset can be reached only by boat.

events.summary: About 375 million years ago. In a river in what is now Nunavut lived *Tiktaalik*, a fish with a neck and fins with bones like an arm's. Footprints in Poland suggest animals with legs were older still.

dateLine.tail: and probably begun by 395 million years ago

paragraphs: On Ellesmere Island, in Nunavut, the far north of Canada, a team led by Edward Daeschler, Neil Shubin and Farish Jenkins went looking for a particular kind of fossil. They wanted fish that lived just before animals with legs, and they knew about how old that rock should be, and what kind of rock it should be. Ellesmere Island had rock of that age and kind, bare of soil and trees. They began searching in 1999.
In the summer of 2004, Stephen Gatesy, one of the team, noticed the tip of a flat, pointed snout in the rock.

The animal it belonged to is a fish, with scales and gills. But its head is flat on top, like a crocodile's, with the eyes on top, and it has a neck, which most fish don't: it could turn its head without turning its body. Inside each front fin there are bones that match the bones of an arm: an upper arm, a forearm, and parts of a wrist that could bend. The fin still ended in fin rays, not fingers.
The team asked a council of Nunavut elders to name it. The elders chose *Tiktaalik* ("tick-TAH-lick"), an Inuktitut word for a large freshwater fish seen in the shallows.
So was *Tiktaalik* the ancestor of animals with legs?

Probably not, as it turned out. In 2010 a team from Poland and Sweden described footprints at Zachełmie ("za-HEW-myeh"), a quarry in the Holy Cross Mountains of Poland, in rock about 395 million years old. Many think they were made by animals with four legs, about twenty million years before *Tiktaalik*. Others have argued that fish made the marks. If the footprints are right, *Tiktaalik* was a late cousin, showing what the ancestor was like rather than being it.
The fossils of *Tiktaalik* are kept at the Canadian Museum of Nature, in Ottawa, until a place for them is built in Nunavut.

events.summary: About 315 million years ago. *Hylonomus*, a small lizard-like animal found in a fossil tree stump at Joggins, Nova Scotia, has long been called the oldest known reptile, an animal whose eggs could be laid on land.

dateLine.tail: and probably begun by 355 million years ago

paragraphs: At Joggins, on the Bay of Fundy, in Nova Scotia, the cliffs are layers of rock from an old swamp forest, and some of the fossil trees in them still stand upright, as they grew. They were not trees like ours. Their trunks had a soft inside, and when a tree died the inside rotted first, leaving a hollow stump standing in the swamp.

Small animals got into these stumps, perhaps by falling in, perhaps to live there, and their bones were buried inside. In 1852 the geologists Charles Lyell and William Dawson found bones inside one of them. A few years later Dawson found more bones, in other stumps, from a different animal, about twenty to twenty-five centimetres long, like a small lizard. He named it *Hylonomus* ("hy-LON-oh-mus"), which means "forest dweller."
*Hylonomus* has long been called the oldest reptile yet found, though a study in 2025 argues that it was a close cousin of the reptiles instead. It matters because of the eggs reptiles lay.

A frog's eggs are soft jelly, laid in water, and on dry land they would dry out. Reptiles, birds and mammals belong to a great group of animals whose eggs carry their own water. Inside, a thin skin wraps the growing young in its own small pond, so the egg can be laid on dry land. *Hylonomus*'s bones put it in that group, or very close to it.

But nobody has found its eggs. The oldest fossil eggs of this group yet found are dinosaur eggs about 195 million years old, more than a hundred million years younger. So the egg of *Hylonomus* is worked out from its skeleton, not seen, and whether the first such eggs had hard shells or soft, leathery ones is argued.

The group is older than *Hylonomus*. In 2025 a team described footprints with claw marks in rock about 355 million years old in Victoria, Australia, and argued that animals of the egg-laying kind made them.
At Joggins, the tides of the Bay of Fundy keep wearing the cliffs back, and new fossil trees come into view.

placeNow.short: the Riola and Vermilion Grove mines

events.summary: About 305 million years ago. Swamp forests grew across what is now Illinois, and their dead plants piled up and became coal. More coal was made in this stretch of time than in almost any other; why is argued.

paragraphs: In two coal mines near Danville, in Illinois, geologists from the Illinois State Geological Survey, among them John Nelson and Scott Elrick, looked up at the roof of the tunnels. The miners had taken out a seam of coal, and the rock left above it was full of fossil trees: stumps, fallen trunks, and leaves pressed flat in the stone. Mapped from tunnel to tunnel, the forest on the roof covered about a thousand hectares.
The coal and the forest were the same place. The coal is what the forest's swamp became.

When plants die on dry ground, they rot away. In a swamp they fall into still water with little oxygen in it, and they rot only partly, piling up as a thick brown mat called peat. Buried deep under later layers, squeezed and warmed for millions of years, peat turns into coal. Here a fault in the earth dropped the swamp, the sea came in, and mud buried the forest so quickly that the trees were kept on top of their own coal.
Between about 323 and 299 million years ago, swamps like this one covered great stretches of land near the equator, and they made more coal than almost any other stretch of time.
So why so much?

In 2012 a team that compared the genes of fungi suggested an answer. Wood is tough because of a substance called lignin, and the fungi that can break lignin down may not have evolved until the end of this stretch. Wood, they argued, was harder to rot.

In 2016 another team argued back. Many of the coal-swamp trees had little lignin, and coal kept forming wherever two things came together: a wet climate near the equator, and land that was slowly sinking, so that peat could pile up for a long time without drying out. "To form coal you need two basic conditions," one of them, Kevin Boyce, said: "wet tropics and a hole to bury organic matter in for a long period of time."

placeNow.name: Meishan, Changxing, Zhejiang, China (31.08 N, 119.71 E)

events.summary: About 252 million years ago. Within about sixty thousand years, four in five kinds of sea animal died out, and many on land. It is the most severe dying known. Volcanoes in Siberia are thought to be the cause.

paragraphs: At Meishan ("may-shahn"), in Changxing ("chahng-shing") County, in Zhejiang, in eastern China, the walls of limestone quarries show layers of rock and clay, one on top of another. Geologists have numbered the layers, and in them are the fossils of hundreds of kinds of sea animal: shellfish, corals, and tiny animals called foraminifera ("for-AM-in-IF-er-a"), each living in a shell, most no bigger than a grain of sand.
At one thin layer of white clay, numbered 25, the fossils begin to vanish, and a few layers higher most of them are gone.

Between the layers are beds of volcanic ash, and the ash holds crystals of zircon, which can be dated. In 2014 Seth Burgess, Samuel Bowring and Shen Shuzhong dated them so closely that they could say when the dying began, about 251.94 million years ago, and how long it took: about sixty thousand years, give or take nearly fifty thousand. In the life of the earth that is very fast.

How many kinds died? For years the figure was nearly 90 or even 96 kinds of sea animal in every 100. In 2016 a new count put it at about 81. Plants and animals on land suffered badly too. It is the most severe dying known.

What caused it is now argued less than it was. At the same time, in what is now Siberia, volcanoes poured out lava, layer on layer, over millions of square kilometres, for close to a million years. Melted rock also spread underground in sheets, and many think its heat baked buried rock that gave off huge amounts of carbon dioxide and other gases. The world warmed. One team, with a computer model of the oceans, worked out that the tropical seas warmed by about eleven degrees Celsius and lost much of their oxygen, and that heat and too little oxygen together could explain more than half of the dying, and where it was worst.
Geologists everywhere now draw the line between two great stretches of the earth's time at one point in the rock at Meishan, just above layer 25.

placeNow.name: Ischigualasto Provincial Park, San Juan, Argentina (30.07 S, 68.00 W)

events.summary: About 233 million years ago. The oldest dinosaurs yet found lived in what are now Brazil and Argentina. Some were small, the size of a dog, and some were six metres long, but they were few among other reptiles.

paragraphs: Ischigualasto ("ees-chee-gwah-LAHS-toh"), in the province of San Juan, in western Argentina, is a valley of bare, worn hills where little grows but bushes and cactus. People there call it the Valle de la Luna, the Valley of the Moon. Its rocks were laid down by rivers about 231 million years ago, and they hold some of the oldest dinosaurs on earth.

In 1991 Ricardo Martínez, of the National University of San Juan, was in the valley with a team that included Paul Sereno, from Chicago, when he found a skeleton almost whole. It was a little over a metre long, and it walked on its back legs. Sereno named it *Eoraptor* ("EE-oh-RAP-tor"), "dawn plunderer."

Not every early dinosaur was small. In 1959 Victorino Herrera, a goatherd, noticed bones in the same rocks, and they turned out to belong to *Herrerasaurus*, a hunter that could grow to about six metres.

But dinosaurs were few in the valley. Most of the fossils there are of other animals: rhynchosaurs ("RING-ko-sores"), reptiles with beaks that ate plants, and cynodonts ("SY-no-donts"), relatives of mammals.

Near the city of Santa Maria, in the south of Brazil, dinosaurs have been found in rock about 233 million years old, older than Ischigualasto's. And in Zimbabwe, in 2022, a team described *Mbiresaurus* ("um-BEER-eh-SORE-us"), from rock about 230 million years old.

How did so few become so many? Some scientists argue that a long spell of heavy rain, which began about 234 million years ago and lasted a million years or more, changed the plants and the climate, and that dinosaurs spread in the world that came after.

And how much older are dinosaurs than the oldest found? *Nyasasaurus*, from Tanzania, was once put at 243 million years and called perhaps the oldest dinosaur. Since then some have argued that its rock is younger, and some doubt that it was a dinosaur at all.

placeNow.name: the Palisades, along the Hudson River, New Jersey and New York, United States (40.96 N, 73.91 W)

events.summary: About 201 million years ago. Pangaea, the one great continent, began to crack, and lava poured out along the cracks across what are now four continents. Many kinds of living thing died out. The Atlantic Ocean opened later.

paragraphs: Along the west bank of the Hudson River, across from Manhattan, a wall of dark rock rises from the water, in places more than a hundred metres high. It is called the Palisades. A palisade is a fence of tall stakes, and the rock stands in tall columns, like one.

The rock of the Palisades was once melted. It pushed its way up between layers of older rock, spread out underground as a sheet about three hundred metres thick, and cooled there slowly. Melted rock from the same source, many geologists think, reached the surface nearby and poured out as lava.

At that time there was no Atlantic Ocean. Nearly all the land on earth was joined in one continent, which geologists call Pangaea ("pan-JEE-ah"), and North America, Africa and South America lay side by side. Then the land between them began to stretch and crack, and melted rock came up through the cracks.

It came up in a great many places at once. Rock of the same kind and the same age is found in Nova Scotia, in Morocco, in Brazil, in Portugal, and in West Africa, now on four continents and on both sides of an ocean. Geologists call it all one province, and it spread over perhaps eleven million square kilometres, wider than any other such outpouring known.

In 2013 a team led by Terrence Blackburn dated crystals of zircon from these rocks. The earliest lava came about 201.6 million years ago, in four pulses over about six hundred thousand years, and the first pulse came at the same time as one of the five great dyings, in the sea and on land.

The cracks went on widening, and some time later, perhaps about 190 million years ago, new ocean floor began to form between them. That floor is the floor of the Atlantic, and it is still being made, down its middle, today.
Nearly all ocean floor older than about 200 million years has since sunk back into the earth. So from here on, the floor of the sea helps geologists draw the map.

events.knownFrom: fossils that stop at one layer in the sea and in old lake beds, footprints, pollen and spores, and the breathing pores of fossil leaves

placeNow.name: St Audrie's Bay, near West Quantoxhead, Somerset, England (51.18 N, 3.28 W)

events.summary: About 201.6 million years ago. One of the five great dyings. Many kinds of animal in the sea died out, and on land the big relatives of crocodiles. The dinosaurs survived, and spread.

paragraphs: At St Audrie's Bay ("AW-dreez"), on the coast of Somerset, in the southwest of England, a stream falls over the cliff onto the beach, and the cliffs are striped. At one end they are red-brown and green, mud laid down in shallow, salty lakes on a dry plain. Then comes a band of dark grey and paler stone. Above it is the Blue Lias ("LYE-us"), stripes of dark shale and pale limestone, laid down in the sea. In the Blue Lias, higher up, are the coiled shells of an ammonite called *Psiloceras* ("sy-LOSS-er-us"). In that band, or just above it, the world changed.

In the sea, the conodonts ("KON-oh-donts"), small eel-like animals known mostly from their tiny teeth, died out for good. The ammonites, with their coiled shells, nearly vanished; *Psiloceras* probably came from one of the few lines that lived. Reefs fell apart, and most kinds of coral with them. Of the groups of closely related animals in the sea, somewhere between a quarter and three quarters died out; the estimates differ.

On land, the big relatives of the crocodiles died out: the phytosaurs ("FY-toh-sorz"), which looked much like crocodiles, and others. Only small ones were left. In 2002 Paul Olsen and his team studied footprints left in the mud of old lakes at more than seventy places in eastern North America, and found that within about thirty thousand years the biggest meat-eaters' prints were about a fifth larger than before.

What did it? In East Greenland and in Sweden, Jennifer McElwain counted the breathing pores on fossil leaves. Plants grow fewer pores when the air holds more carbon dioxide, and in 1999 she and her colleagues argued that it had risen about fourfold, and the world had warmed. In 2013 Terrence Blackburn and his team dated the dying, and found that it began at about the same time as the first lavas that poured out as Pangaea cracked. Many geologists think the carbon dioxide from those lavas warmed the world and made the sea more acid, which is hard on shells and on coral.

events.label: Archaeopteryx
events.ageText: 149 Ma · ± 1 Ma · from the ammonites in the layers (early Tithonian, which began 149.2 ± 0.7 Ma on the current chart, since 2022), not a radiometric date; the oldest specimen, from Schamhaupten, lies at the Kimmeridgian–Tithonian boundary (Rauhut 2018)

tail.reason: *Anchiornis*, in China, had feathers on its arms and legs about 160 Ma, and feather-like threads on other dinosaurs may be older still (argued)

events.knownFrom: about a dozen skeletons and one feather, kept in fine limestone

placeNow.name: Langenaltheim, near Solnhofen, Bavaria, Germany (48.89 N, 10.97 E), where the London skeleton was found

events.kindRaw: crop or animal (a living thing; the list has no better word)
events.summary: About 149 million years ago. *Archaeopteryx*, an animal with feathered wings, teeth and a long bony tail, lived on islands in a warm sea in what is now Bavaria. Dinosaurs with feathers are older still.

dateLine.tail: and probably begun by 160 million years ago

paragraphs: Around the town of Solnhofen ("ZOLN-hoe-fen"), in Bavaria, in southern Germany, the hills are full of quarries, and the stone in them is cream-coloured limestone that splits into thin, flat slabs, like the pages of a book. For more than a hundred years the best of it was used for printing pictures.

In 1861, in a quarry at Solnhofen, a slab split open on a single feather, about seven centimetres long, a dark film on the pale stone. Hermann von Meyer described it that summer, and that autumn named the animal it came from *Archaeopteryx* ("ar-kee-OP-ter-ix"), "old wing."

The same year, near the village of Langenaltheim, another slab split open on the skeleton of an animal about the size of a crow. Around its arms were the marks of feathers, laid out as in a wing. But it also had teeth in its jaws, claws on its fingers, and a long tail of bone.

Was the feather from the same kind of animal? Nobody can prove it. In 2019 Thomas Kaye and his team shone a laser on the slab and found the outline of the feather's lost quill, and argued that its shape matched none of the long flight feathers of the wing or tail of *Archaeopteryx*. In 2020 Ryan Carney and his team argued that it was one of the smaller feathers that lie over the bases of the long wing feathers.

The limestone was laid down in quiet, salty lagoons between islands. Many geologists think the water at the bottom was too salty, or had too little oxygen, for anything to live there, so whatever sank to the bottom was not eaten, and was slowly covered by fine mud.

From the 1990s, farmers and scientists in Liaoning ("lee-ow-NING"), in northeastern China, began to find small dinosaurs with feathers. One of them, *Anchiornis* ("an-kee-OR-nis"), is about 160 million years old, and it had long feathers on its arms and on its legs. Feathers are older than birds.
About a dozen skeletons have been found, all in the limestones of southern Bavaria, and only the one feather.

events.knownFrom: pollen in rock, and a few whole plants pressed flat in the mud of old lakes

placeNow.name: La Pedrera de Meià, Montsec, Lleida, Catalonia, Spain (about 42.0 N, 1.0 E)

events.kindRaw: crop or animal (a living thing; the list has no better word)
events.summary: About 125 million years ago. Among the oldest whole flowering plants yet found are some that grew in lakes in what are now Catalonia and northeastern China. They had no petals. Their pollen, found in older rock, is older still.

dateLine.tail: and probably begun by 140 million years ago

paragraphs: High in the Montsec ("mun-SEK") mountains, in Catalonia, in the northeast of Spain, is an old quarry called La Pedrera de Meià. A little more than a hundred years ago its fine, pale limestone was cut into slabs for printing, and sent to printers in Barcelona. Some slabs, split open, held fossils: fish, insects, and the stems and leaves of plants.

One of the plants was named after Lluís Marià Vidal, a Catalan mining engineer and geologist who studied the Montsec. It was named *Montsechia* ("mun-SEK-ee-a"), but for many years nobody was sure what it was: a liverwort, a horsetail, even a kind of pine.

In 2015 Bernard Gomez, David Dilcher and their team looked again, at more than a thousand specimens, and argued that it was a flowering plant, one of the oldest known. It lived under the water of a lake, like the hornwort that grows in ponds today, and it had no petals.
What makes a flowering plant is not the petals. It is that its seeds grow wrapped inside a closed case, which becomes the fruit. Each little case of *Montsechia* held a single seed.
In Liaoning, in northeastern China, another very early flowering plant, *Archaefructus* ("AR-kee-FRUK-tus"), "old fruit," grew in lakes about 125 million years ago. It had no petals either.
*Montsechia*'s rock is dated by the fossils in it, and in 2023 geologists moved the dates of that stretch of time, so the two plants now look about the same age.

Pollen is older. Flowering plants make pollen with a wall of a particular pattern, and grains like that are found in rock about 135 million years old, in Morocco, in Israel and in England. Nobody has found the plants that made them.

In 1879 Charles Darwin wrote to a friend that the rapid rise of the flowering plants, as far as anyone could judge from the rocks, was "an abominable mystery." Today the gene clocks, which count the differences in the genes of living plants, put their beginning much earlier, perhaps more than 200 million years ago. Many fossil experts doubt it.

events.label: The asteroid
events.ageText: 66.04 Ma · ± 0.04 Ma · radiometric (argon) on ash at the boundary and on glass beads from the impact, 66.043 ± 0.043 Ma (Renne 2013); a uranium–lead date in Colorado gives 66.021 ± 0.024 (Clyde 2016)
events.ageHow: radiometric (argon) on ash at the boundary and on glass beads from the impact, 66.043 ± 0.043 Ma (Renne 2013); a uranium-lead date in Colorado gives 66.021 ± 0.024 (Clyde 2016)
events.knownFrom: a thin layer of clay rich in iridium, found all round the world, and a crater buried under Yucatán

placeNow.name: Bottaccione Gorge, Gubbio, Umbria, Italy (43.365 N, 12.583 E)

events.summary: About 66 million years ago. An asteroid about ten kilometres across hit the earth where Yucatán, in Mexico, is now. About three in four kinds of living thing died out, among them every dinosaur except the birds.

paragraphs: Outside the town of Gubbio ("GOOB-bee-oh"), in Umbria, in the middle of Italy, a road runs up a narrow gorge, and beside the road is a wall of pink limestone in thin layers. The limestone was laid down on the floor of a sea, and the layers are full of the shells of tiny animals. Partway up, the shells change. Below, there are many kinds, and big ones. Above, there are only a few kinds, and small. Between the two is a layer of clay about a centimetre thick.

In the 1970s Walter Alvarez, a geologist, wanted to know how long that clay had taken to settle. His father, Luis Alvarez, a physicist, suggested measuring iridium ("ih-RID-ee-um"), a metal that is very rare in the earth's crust but falls to earth all the time in the dust of space. A little iridium would mean the clay settled fast; a lot would mean slowly.

With Frank Asaro and Helen Michel they measured it, and there was about thirty times more than they expected. They found the same in clay from the same moment in Denmark and New Zealand. In 1980 they argued that an asteroid about ten kilometres across had hit the earth, and that the dust and its effects had killed the dinosaurs.

Where was the crater? In 1978 Glen Penfield, working for Mexico's oil company with Antonio Camargo, had found a buried ring under Yucatán, and in 1981 they described it. In 1991 Alan Hildebrand, with Penfield, Camargo and others, argued that the ring, about 180 kilometres across, is the crater. It is named after a village near its middle, Chicxulub ("cheek-shoo-LOOB").

In North Dakota, in 2019, a team led by Robert DePalma, then a graduate student, described a site called Tanis. Fish there were buried with tiny beads of glass from the impact in their gills, in a layer that the team argued was laid down by a surge of water within an hour of the strike, three thousand kilometres away. Some geologists doubt parts of that reading. If it is right, Tanis records the first hour.

events.label: Hot spike
events.ageText: 56.01 Ma · ± 0.05 Ma · astronomical: the layers' rhythm in seafloor mud, tuned to the earth's orbit, not a radiometric date (Zeebe and Lourens 2019); it lasted about 170,000 years
events.ageHow: astronomical: the layers' rhythm in seafloor mud, tuned to the earth's orbit, not a radiometric date (Zeebe and Lourens 2019); it lasted about 170,000 years
events.knownFrom: a sudden change in the carbon of seafloor mud and soils, and the teeth of small horses

placeNow.name: Cabin Fork, Bighorn Basin, Wyoming, United States (43.91 N, 107.69 W)

events.summary: About 56 million years ago. A great deal of carbon reached the air and the sea over a few thousand years, and the world warmed by about five or six degrees. Some animals grew smaller.

paragraphs: In the Bighorn Basin, in northern Wyoming, the bare hills are striped red, purple and grey. Each stripe is an old soil, laid down on the flood plain of rivers and buried, one on top of another. Teeth and jaws of small mammals weather out of the hillsides.
Some of the teeth belong to *Sifrhippus* ("SIF-er-HIP-us"), one of the oldest horses. It had several toes on each foot, each with a little hoof of its own, and it lived among trees.

In 2012 Ross Secord and his team measured the teeth layer by layer at Cabin Fork. The size of a tooth tells you the size of the animal. Before a certain layer the horses weighed about five and a half kilograms. Over the next 130,000 years or so, they shrank to about four, the size of a small house cat. Then they grew again, to about seven.

What happened at that layer happened all over the world. The carbon in soils and in seafloor mud changes suddenly, in a way that means a huge amount of carbon reached the air and the sea over a few thousand years. The earth warmed by about five or six degrees on average. The warm spell, from its start until the earth began to cool again, lasted about 170,000 years.
Why the horses shrank is argued. Many think warm-blooded animals tend to be smaller where it is hotter; some think the plants had become poorer food.
The carbon's source is argued too. Many now think most of it came from volcanoes, at the time the North Atlantic was opening. Others argue for gas from the sea floor, or thawing frozen soils.

The warming was found first in the sea. In 1991 James Kennett and Lowell Stott studied a core of mud drilled from the seafloor off Antarctica, and found that many kinds of tiny animal living on the deep sea floor had died out at once, while those near the surface lived on.
The carbon came fast, but at least ten times more slowly than people are putting carbon into the air today.

events.label: Antarctica freezes
events.ageText: 33.9 Ma · ± 0.1 Ma · the base of the Oligocene, tuned to the earth's orbit and checked against dated ash; the biggest step of ice, about 33.7 Ma (Hutchinson 2021)
events.ageHow: the base of the Oligocene, tuned to the earth's orbit and checked against dated ash; the biggest step of ice, about 33.7 Ma (Hutchinson 2021)

tail.reason: the start of the change, as the review of 2021 counts it; mountain glaciers may have grown on high ground in East Antarctica earlier still (argued)

events.knownFrom: the shells of tiny single-celled creatures in seafloor mud, and stones dropped by ice

placeNow.name: ODP Site 1218, the floor of the equatorial Pacific (8.89 N, 135.37 W)

events.summary: About 34 million years ago. Over a few hundred thousand years, an ice sheet grew across East Antarctica, the sea fell by about seventy metres, and the world grew cooler. There has been ice there ever since.

dateLine.tail: and probably begun by 34.4 million years ago

paragraphs: In 2001 a drilling ship in the Pacific, north of the equator, lowered a pipe through nearly five kilometres of water and drilled into the mud of the sea floor. The mud came up in long tubes, called cores, and in it were the shells of tiny creatures, each a single cell, that had lived on the floor of the deep sea. Each shell was about the size of a grain of fine sand.
The shells hold a record of ice on another continent.

Oxygen comes in kinds that weigh slightly different amounts, and seawater holds both. When water evaporates from the sea, the lighter oxygen goes up more easily than the heavy. If that water falls as snow on land and stays there as ice, the sea is left with a little more of the heavy oxygen. The tiny creatures build their shells from the sea, so their shells keep its mix. Cold water also adds heavy oxygen to a shell, so the shells record cold and ice together, and geologists use other clues to tell them apart.

In 2005 Helen Coxall and her colleagues, working on that core, showed that the heavy oxygen jumped in two steps, a few hundred thousand years apart, about 34 million years ago. The first came mostly from the deep sea cooling. The second, bigger one marks an ice sheet growing across Antarctica, most likely East Antarctica. As water was locked up in the ice, the sea fell by about seventy metres.

Why then? For a long time the favourite answer was that Antarctica drifted away from Australia and South America, and that a current began to run round it, keeping warm water away. Many now think the bigger cause was that the air held less and less carbon dioxide, until it crossed a line where snow on Antarctica no longer melted in summer.
West Antarctica, the smaller part, seems to have stayed free of ice for a while, at least near its Pacific coast, with forests of southern beech on it.
There has been ice on Antarctica ever since.

events.label: Grasslands
events.ageText: 22 Ma · at least 21.9 Ma, possibly as old as about 23 to 27 Ma (Strömberg 2005: 7 to 11 million years after 34) · the oldest grass-dominated habitats yet shown in the North American interior, from the age of the layers (Strömberg 2005, 2006); estimated, not a radiometric date on the samples
events.ageHow: at least 21.9 Ma, possibly as old as about 23 to 27 Ma (Strömberg 2005: 7 to 11 million years after 34) · the oldest grass-dominated habitats yet shown in the North American interior, from the age of the layers (Strömberg 2005, 2006); estimated, not a radiometric date on the samples

tail.reason: grasses of open country had become many kinds by then, though they did not yet cover the land; grasses themselves are much older, from the time of the dinosaurs

events.knownFrom: tiny pieces of glass that grass leaves make, kept in old soils, and the teeth of grazing animals

placeNow.name: the Great Plains, in Nebraska, Wyoming and nearby states, United States (no single site; for a point, Agate Fossil Beds, Nebraska, 42.42 N, 103.75 W)

events.kindRaw: crop or animal (a living thing; the list has no better word)
events.summary: About 22 million years ago. In the middle of North America, grass came to cover open country. Grasses are much older than that, and they spread at different times on different continents.

dateLine.tail: and probably begun by 34 million years ago

paragraphs: Run a finger along the edge of some blades of grass, the wrong way, and they can cut you. Grass leaves are stiff with tiny pieces of glass, made from silica that the roots draw up from the soil. The pieces are called phytoliths ("FY-toe-liths"), "plant stones," and each kind of grass makes them in its own shapes: some like dumbbells, some like saddles, some like little crosses.
When a leaf rots, its phytoliths stay behind in the soil. So an old soil, buried and turned to rock, can say what grew on it, long after every leaf is gone.

Caroline Strömberg spent years dissolving away samples of old soils from the Great Plains of North America, in Nebraska, Wyoming and the states around them, to free the phytoliths, and counting them under a microscope. Grasses of open, sunny country were already there by about 34 million years ago, as many kinds, but they were only a small part of the plants. Trees still ruled. Places where grass outnumbered everything else came later, by about 22 million years ago.
The horses of the Great Plains grew tall teeth, which wear down slowly, at least four million years after that. Grass is hard on teeth, and so is the grit that comes with it.

In South America it went the other way round. Animals in Patagonia had tall teeth long before grass took over there, and some argue the cause was volcanic ash on the leaves. In East Africa, a team found in 2023 that grasses of a hot-country kind were common in places about twenty million years ago, earlier than had been thought.
Grass itself is older than any of this. In 2005 Vandana Prasad and her team found phytoliths of grass in the fossil dung of dinosaurs in central India, about 66 million years old.
Grasslands of a new kind, the ones that grow best where it is hot and dry, spread over the warmer parts of the world later still, between about eight and six million years ago.

events.label: Hot-country grasses
events.ageText: 8 Ma to 6 Ma · a span, not the same everywhere: in East Africa about 8 to 7 Ma; in northern Pakistan from about 7.4 to 7.0 Ma in the soils (Quade 1989), mostly C4 by about 5 Ma; in South America by about 7.6 Ma; in southern North America 6.8 to 5.7; later in the north (Cerling 1997); dated by the layers, by their magnetism and by ash beds, not on the teeth themselves; the dot is at the start of the span

events.knownFrom: the mix of carbon in the tooth enamel of grazing animals, and in lumps of lime in old soils

placeNow.name: the Potwar Plateau, northern Punjab, Pakistan; for a point, Rohtas Fort, near Jhelum (32.97 N, 73.58 E)

events.kindRaw: crop or animal (a living thing; the list has no better word)
events.summary: About 8 to 6 million years ago. Grasses that grow best in hot, bright, dry places spread over much of the warmer part of the world. The teeth of the animals that ate them show when.

dateLine.tail: and probably begun by 32 million years ago

paragraphs: On the Potwar Plateau, in northern Pakistan, between the Indus and the Jhelum, dry stream beds cut through layers of red, orange and yellow-brown rock. Many of the layers are old soils, built up by rivers from the young Himalaya. In them are lumps of lime that formed in the soil, and the teeth of animals that lived on it.
Carbon comes in two kinds that last: ordinary carbon, and a slightly heavier kind, carbon-13. Plants take in both, but not in the same mix.

Most plants make food with a substance that, in heat, often grabs oxygen by mistake. Some grasses add an extra step. They catch carbon dioxide in the outer cells of the leaf and pump it to the cells around each vein, so the work is done where carbon dioxide is plentiful. The pump costs energy, so it pays best where it is hot and bright, and helps where water is short. These are called C4 plants, and they keep more of the heavy carbon than other plants do. The mix passes into the soil and into the teeth of animals that eat them, and enamel keeps it for millions of years.

In 1989 Jay Quade, Thure Cerling and John Bowman measured the lime in the Potwar soils, and found that between about 7.4 and 7.0 million years ago, the plants of the river plains changed from mostly trees and shrubs to mostly C4 grasses.

In 1997 Cerling's team measured more than five hundred teeth of horses, rhinoceroses and other plant-eaters, from five continents. Across the warmer part of the world, between about eight and six million years ago, the grazers began eating C4 grasses. Farther north it came later, or not at all.

Why then? Cerling's team argued that the carbon dioxide in the air had fallen too low for ordinary plants where it was hot. Others found little sign of a fall, and argue for fire and long dry seasons.
Today C4 plants do about a quarter of all the food-making on land. Maize, sugarcane and millet are among them.

events.label: Walking upright
events.ageText: 7 Ma · ± 0.2 Ma · from beryllium in the sand and clay at the find site, 7.2 to 6.8 Ma (Lebatard 2008), not from the bones, which lay on the surface
events.ageHow: from beryllium in the sand and clay at the find site, 7.2 to 6.8 Ma (Lebatard 2008), not from the bones, which lay on the surface
events.knownFrom: a skull, a thigh bone and two forearm bones, all argued over

placeNow.name: Toros-Ménalla, Djourab, northern Chad (16.25 N, 17.48 E)

events.kindRaw: crop or animal (a living thing; the list has no better word)
events.summary: About 7 million years ago. An ape that may have walked upright lived beside a lake in what is now the desert of northern Chad. Whether it walked upright has been argued for more than twenty years, and still is.

paragraphs: The Djourab ("joo-RAHB"), in the north of Chad, is a desert of dunes and flat, wind-scoured ground. It drives the sand along the ground, and the sand wears the rock down, a little every year, and uncovers whatever bones the rock holds.

On 19 July 2001 four men working for a team from Chad and France, Ahounta Djimdoumalbaye ("ah-OON-ta jim-doo-mal-BYE"), Fanoné Gongdibé, Mahamat Adoum and Alain Beauvilain, found a skull lying on the sand at a place called Toros-Ménalla. It was crushed and twisted, with small canine teeth and a heavy ridge over the eyes. The President of Chad, Idriss Déby, gave it the name Toumaï ("too-MY"), a Daza word.

In 2002 Michel Brunet and the team named the species *Sahelanthropus tchadensis* ("sa-HEL-an-THRO-pus chad-EN-sis"). They argued that it was on our side of the split from the chimpanzees, and that the hole where the spinal cord leaves the skull sat far enough forward to mean it walked upright.
A thigh bone had been found at the same place. It was put away with the bones of other animals, and in 2004 a student, Aude Bergeret, noticed it in a laboratory in Poitiers, in France.

That bone has been argued over ever since. In 2020 one team said it was not the thigh bone of an animal that walked upright. In 2022 another team, with the bone and two from the forearm, said it was, though the animal climbed too. In 2024 a third team said the evidence did not support it. In January 2026 a fourth found three features in the bone that they read as signs of walking upright. And nobody can show that the thigh bone and the skull came from the same animal.
Seven million years ago this desert was the shore of a lake, with fish, crocodiles and hippos. The sand and clay around the bones were dated by the beryllium they had taken from the air.
In Kenya, a thigh bone about six million years old, of an ape called *Orrorin* ("or-ROAR-in"), makes what many think is a stronger case.

events.label: Stone tools
events.ageText: 3.3 Ma · between 3.33 and 3.11 Ma · from the volcanic ash layers above and below and from the rock's magnetism, not from the tools themselves (Harmand 2015); a critique argues the tools' place in the layers is not secure
events.ageHow: between 3.33 and 3.11 Ma · from the volcanic ash layers above and below and from the rock's magnetism, not from the tools themselves (Harmand 2015); a critique argues the tools' place in the layers is not secure
events.knownFrom: about a hundred and fifty pieces of struck stone, some dug from the layer, many picked up from the surface

placeNow.name: Lomekwi 3, West Turkana, Turkana County, Kenya (3.87 N, 35.75 E)

events.summary: About 3.3 million years ago. Someone struck flakes off stones beside what is now Lake Turkana, in Kenya. These are the oldest stone tools yet found, and nobody knows who made them.

paragraphs: West of Lake Turkana, in northern Kenya, the land is hot and dry and cut by gullies. On the morning of 9 July 2011, Sonia Harmand and Jason Lewis, of a team working in Kenya, took a wrong turn on their way to a fossil site. By the afternoon Sammy Lokorodi, a Turkana man working with the team, had spotted pieces of struck stone lying on the ground.
They named the place Lomekwi 3 ("lo-MEK-wee"), and they came back to dig.

A tool of this kind is made by hitting one stone with another, so that a sharp flake breaks off. The flake can cut. The stone it came off, called a core, keeps the scars of every blow. The team found cores, flakes, stones used as hammers, and stones that may have been used as anvils, about a hundred and fifty pieces in all. Some were big and heavy, struck while resting on another stone.

The tools could not be dated. The layers could. Above and below the tools were layers of volcanic ash, and the rock between them had been laid down when the earth's magnetism pointed one way. In 2015 the team put the tools at about 3.3 million years old, seven hundred thousand years older than any tools known before.

Who made them is a mystery. No toolmakers' bones were found with them. A skull of an ape-like human relative, *Kenyanthropus* ("ken-YAN-thro-pus"), of about the same age, had been found about a kilometre away, but that proves nothing.

Some archaeologists doubt the date. In 2016 Manuel Domínguez-Rodrigo and Luis Alcalá argued that many of the pieces were picked up from the surface, that those dug from the layer might have worked their way down from the surface into the sand, and that the dated ash might not belong to the same layer. The team says the tools came from the dated layer.
Younger tools of a more practised kind, made the same way for hundreds of thousands of years, are found in Kenya from about 2.9 million years ago, and in Ethiopia from about 2.6 million.

events.label: Panama closes
events.ageText: 2.8 Ma · ± 0.2 Ma (our figure; the paper gives none) · estimate from three kinds of evidence: the sea animals on the two sides, the chemistry of the two seas, and the land animals that crossed (O'Dea 2016); a minority argues for about 13 to 15 Ma (Montes 2015)

placeNow.name: Corte Culebra, the Panama Canal, Panama (9.07 N, 79.67 W)

events.summary: About 2.8 million years ago. The last sea passage between North and South America closed, at what is now Panama. Animals walked across both ways, and the Pacific and the Caribbean went their separate ways.

paragraphs: In the middle of the Isthmus of Panama, the Panama Canal runs through a deep cut in the hills, called Corte Culebra. Ships pass through it every day, from the Atlantic side to the Pacific. From 2007 to 2016 the canal was enlarged, with new locks and a new channel on the Pacific side, and the digging opened fresh slopes of rock, up to fifty metres high, along some twenty kilometres.

Geologists have searched the rock of the cut ever since it was first dug. In it they found the bones of land animals, among them horses, between about fifteen and nineteen million years old, of kinds known from North America. So Panama was already land, joined to North America, long ago. The question was when the last gap of sea between Panama and South America closed.

Before it closed, sea water ran between the Pacific and the Caribbean, and sea animals lived on both sides as one. When it closed, each was cut in two. Nancy Knowlton studied snapping shrimp, which live on both coasts in pairs that look nearly alike. Put together in a dish, a shrimp from one side and its partner from the other mostly snapped at each other, and almost never bred.

In 2016 a large team led by Aaron O'Dea brought the evidence together: the sea animals, the chemistry of the two seas, which grew apart, and the land animals that crossed. Their answer was that the last passage closed about 2.8 million years ago.

Not everyone agrees. In 2015 Camilo Montes and his team argued, from tiny crystals carried by rivers into Colombia, that the gap had closed between 13 and 15 million years ago. Others think the land closed and opened again more than once.

When the way was open, animals walked it. Armadillos, opossums and porcupines went north; cats, bears, horses and camels went south. A study published this year argues that North American animals had gathered in Mexico for millions of years before, waiting.
Today the Canal joins the two oceans again, with locks that lift ships over the land.

events.label: Ice by turns
events.ageText: 2.58 Ma · ± 0.01 Ma · the base of the Quaternary at Monte San Nicola, tuned to the earth's orbit by the rhythm of its layers, with a magnetic reversal about a metre below (Rio 1998, 2.588; the point fixed in 1996 as the base of the Gelasian, ratified as the base of the Quaternary in 2009)

events.knownFrom: stones dropped by ice into seafloor mud, and the shells of tiny single-celled creatures in it

placeNow.name: Monte San Nicola, near Gela, Sicily, Italy (37.147 N, 14.204 E)

events.summary: About 2.6 million years ago. Ice sheets began to grow over the north of the world and melt away again, over and over. There have been about fifty cold spells since. We live in a warm one.

dateLine.tail: and probably begun by 2.75 million years ago

paragraphs: On the side of Monte San Nicola, a hill about ten kilometres inland from the town of Gela ("JEH-la"), near the south coast of Sicily, the ground is striped. Pale bands of limestone and limy clay alternate with thin dark ones.

The rock was laid down on the deep floor of the Mediterranean. The dark bands formed at times when the deep water ran short of oxygen and more food fell from above than could be eaten, so it piled up on the bottom. That happened at a rhythm, set by the slow wobble of the earth as it moves round the sun, and by counting the bands geologists can tell their age.

Geologists had already marked a point in this hillside, at the foot of one pale band. In 2009 they agreed that it marks the start of the stretch of time we live in, called the Quaternary ("KWA-ter-nary"). Its age is about 2.58 million years.

They chose that time because of ice. In mud drilled from the floor of the North Pacific, small stones turn up from about 2.75 million years ago, far more than before. Only ice can carry stones that far out to sea. From about then, ice sheets grew over the far north of Europe and Asia, then Alaska, then the rest of North America.

And then melt. Then grow again. The shells of tiny single-celled creatures in seafloor mud keep the record, in their heavy and light oxygen, the same record that shows Antarctica freezing. For more than a million years the ice came and went about every 41,000 years. In the last million years it has come and gone about every 100,000 years, and the ice grew bigger than it had before.

In 1976 James Hays, John Imbrie and Nicholas Shackleton found those rhythms in mud from the southern Indian Ocean, and matched them to slow changes in the earth's tilt and orbit, which Milutin Milanković, a Serbian engineer and mathematician, had worked out decades before.
Since then there have been about fifty cold spells. The last ended about twelve thousand years ago.

events.label: Homo sapiens
events.ageText: 0.315 Ma · ± 0.034 Ma · thermoluminescence on burnt flints in the same layers as the bones; a tooth gives 0.286 ± 0.032 Ma by another method (Richter 2017)

placeNow.name: Jebel Irhoud, Morocco (31.86 N, 8.87 W)

events.kindRaw: crop or animal (a living thing; the list has no better word)
events.summary: About 315,000 years ago. People with faces like ours lived in what is now Morocco. Their bones, from Jebel Irhoud, are the oldest yet found of our own species, though some argue they were not quite us.

dateLine.tail: and probably begun by 350,000 years ago

paragraphs: Jebel Irhoud ("jbel ee-GHOOD," the *gh* soft, like a French *r*) is a hill in Morocco, about fifty kilometres inland, southeast of the port of Safi. In 1961 miners digging there for barite, a heavy white mineral, broke into a cave that had long ago filled up with earth and stones. In the earth that filled it was a human skull.
Over the next few years more bones were found. The people they came from were at first thought to be a kind of Neanderthal, and perhaps 40,000 years old. Later dating made them about 160,000.

In 2004 a team from Morocco and Germany, led by Abdelouahed Ben-Ncer and Jean-Jacques Hublin, began to dig again in what was left of the cave. They found more bones: pieces of skulls, a jaw, teeth. They also found flints that had been dropped in fires.

Heat makes a flint into a clock. A stone soaks up energy, very slowly, from the faint radioactivity of the ground around it and of the stone itself, and stores it. A fire empties the store. In a laboratory, heating the flint again makes it glow, a little, by the amount stored since the fire. In 2017 Daniel Richter and his team dated the burnt flints to about 315,000 years ago, give or take 34,000.

Before then, the oldest bones of our species were from Omo, in Ethiopia, thought to be about 195,000 years old. In 2022 the ash above them was traced to the volcano it came from, Shala, and those bones are now at least about 230,000.

The faces of the Irhoud people were much like ours. Their skulls were not. Ours are round at the back, and theirs were long and low. Some say that makes them early members of our species, with the round skull coming later; some say they were close cousins, not quite us.
Hublin's team has argued that our species did not begin in one place. People across much of Africa may all have been part of it. Irhoud is where the oldest bones happen to have survived.

events.ageText: 0.142 Ma · + 0.029 / − 0.022 Ma · uranium-series on a lump of cave stone that formed within the bead layer, above most of the beads, so a minimum (Sehasseh 2021: 142,290 + 29,300 / − 22,060); luminescence dates on the sand of the same layer are younger, about 109,000 to 54,000, and the authors say the two disagree

placeNow.name: Bizmoune Cave, near Essaouira, Morocco (coordinates to confirm: the paper's printed figure, 31°39′96″ N, cannot be right)

events.summary: Perhaps 142,000 years ago. People in what is now Morocco pierced small sea-snail shells and, it seems, wore them on strings. If the date holds, they are the oldest beads yet found.

paragraphs: Bizmoune ("biz-MOON") Cave is in the hills of western Morocco, about twelve kilometres from the Atlantic coast, near the town of Essaouira ("ess-a-WEER-a"). Between 2014 and 2018 a team that included Abdeljalil Bouzouggar, of Morocco's national institute of archaeology in Rabat, Steven Kuhn and Philippe Fernandez dug into its floor. In one layer they found thirty-three small sea-snail shells, each a little over a centimetre long. Every one had a hole in it.

A hole alone proves nothing, because the sea, and other animals, can hole a shell. So the team, with El Mehdi Sehasseh leading the study of the shells, looked closely. The edges of many holes were chipped, as if worked with a stone tool. Three in four were polished and scratched around the shell's open mouth, where a string would rub. Some were stained with red ochre, a coloured earth. And the snails lived in the sea, but someone had carried their shells up to the cave from a coast that was then thirty to fifty kilometres away. From all this the team argued that people had strung the shells and worn them.

How old are they? In the same layer, water dripping in the cave had built a small lump of stone, and most of the beads lay deeper down than it. Stone like that holds a little uranium, which turns into thorium at a steady rate, so a laboratory can tell how long ago it began to grow. This lump began about 142,000 years ago, so the beads below it are probably older still.

But the team also dated the sand of the same layer another way, by the light stored in its grains, and got younger ages, between about 109,000 and 54,000 years. They said so plainly, and said that the difference needs more work.

So the oldest beads yet found may be these, or they may not. Pierced shells from Skhul ("SKOOL"), a cave in Israel, are between about 100,000 and 135,000 years old, and shells from the Grotte des Pigeons, at Taforalt, in northeastern Morocco, are about 82,000.

placeNow.name: Blombos Cave, near Still Bay (Stilbaai), Western Cape, South Africa (34.41 S, 21.22 E)

events.summary: About 77,000 years ago. People living in a cave above the sea in what is now South Africa cut crossed lines into lumps of red ochre, wore shell beads, and later drew with ochre on stone.

paragraphs: Blombos ("BLOM-boss") Cave is in a cliff above the sea near Still Bay, in the Western Cape, about three hundred kilometres east of Cape Town. Christopher Henshilwood spent holidays near there as a boy, and in 1991, as an archaeologist looking for a place to dig, he came back and found the cave.

Under the layers left by people in the last two thousand years are far older ones, and in them the team found lumps of ochre, a soft red stone that people have long ground up for paint. Two of the lumps, reported in 2002, had been scraped and ground flat, and then cut with a band of lines that cross one another. Burnt stone tools from the same layer were dated by the light they give off when heated again, to about 77,000 years ago.

In 2004 the team reported shells of a small snail that lives where rivers meet the sea, each pierced with a hole, some with traces of ochre, about 75,000 years old. They are worn in just the places a string would wear them.

In 2011 the team dug up a flake of silcrete ("SIL-kreet"), a hard stone, about four centimetres long. Later, in a laboratory in Cape Town, Luca Pollarolo was sorting flakes when he noticed red lines on this one: six lines crossed by three others. The team tried drawing on stone with ochre themselves, and argued that the lines had been drawn with a sharpened piece of ochre, like a crayon, about 73,000 years ago. The lines stop at the broken edges of the flake, so the drawing was once bigger.

Did the crossed lines mean something to the people who made them? The team argues that they did, because the same pattern turns up again and again, on ochre and on stone, over thousands of years. Nobody can be sure.

events.label: Sulawesi
events.ageText: 0.0678 Ma · minimum · uranium-series on a crust grown over the stencil, 71,600 ± 3,800; the authors take 67,800 as the least the stencil can be (Oktaviana 2026)
events.ageHow: minimum · uranium-series on a crust grown over the stencil, 71,600 ± 3,800; the authors take 67,800 as the least the stencil can be (Oktaviana 2026)
events.knownFrom: thin crusts of mineral grown over paint on cave walls, dated by their uranium

placeNow.name: Liang Metanduno, Muna Island, Southeast Sulawesi, Indonesia (coordinates to confirm)

events.summary: At least 67,800 years ago. Someone pressed a hand to the rock of a cave on Muna, an island off Sulawesi, in Indonesia, and blew red paint around it. It may be the oldest cave painting yet dated.

paragraphs: On Muna ("MOO-na"), an island off the southeast of Sulawesi, in Indonesia, is a cave called Liang Metanduno ("LEE-ang meh-tan-DOO-no"). It is a wide room open to the daylight, and its walls are covered with paintings in red: horses, boats, people.

In 2015 Adhi Agus Oktaviana, an Indonesian archaeologist, found something fainter among them: hand stencils. A stencil is made by holding a hand flat against the rock and blowing paint around it, so that its shape is left behind, bare rock in a cloud of red.

How do you date paint? Water seeping down a cave wall can leave a thin crust of mineral, and a crust that grew over a painting must be younger than the painting. The crust holds a little uranium, which turns into thorium at a steady rate, so a laboratory can tell when the crust began to grow: the least the painting can be.

In January 2026 Oktaviana, Maxime Aubert, Adam Brumm and their team reported that the crust over one stencil had begun to grow about 71,600 years ago, give or take 3,800, so the stencil is at least 67,800 years old. The tip of one finger looks narrowed, as if paint was added or the hand was moved. It may be the oldest cave painting yet dated anywhere.

In the limestone hills of Maros and Pangkep, near Makassar, the same team has dated paintings of other kinds. In 2017 Basran Burhan found a painting of a warty pig more than a metre long in a cave called Leang Tedongnge ("LEH-ang teh-DONG-ngeh"); it is at least 45,500 years old. In Leang Karampuang a pig stands among three figures that look like people, at least 51,200 years ago.

Not everyone trusts these crusts. Water can wash uranium out of one, and that makes it look older than it is. In May 2026 Georges Sauvet, a French specialist in cave art, argued that, in a race for the oldest date, very old ages are being accepted too easily; the team answers that it sampled with care.

events.label: Lebombo bone
events.ageText: 0.043 Ma · ± 0.001 Ma · calibrated radiocarbon on the layers and on things of plant and bone in them, about 44,000 to 42,000 (d'Errico 2012, Villa 2012), not on the bone itself; once given as about 35,000 (Beaumont, 1970s)

placeNow.name: Border Cave, Lebombo Mountains, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, on the border with Eswatini (27.02 S, 31.99 E)

events.summary: About 43,000 years ago. Someone in a cave in the Lebombo Mountains, on what is now the border of South Africa and Eswatini, cut twenty-nine notches across a baboon's leg bone. Nobody knows why.

paragraphs: Border Cave is a rock shelter in a cliff of the Lebombo ("leh-BOM-bo") Mountains, where KwaZulu-Natal, in South Africa, meets Eswatini, about twelve kilometres from Ingwavuma ("ing-gwa-VOO-ma"). People lived in it, on and off, for more than two hundred thousand years, and what they left is still in its floor: grass they slept on, beads of ostrich eggshell, bone points like the arrowheads the San made much later, a lump of beeswax.

The archaeologist Peter Beaumont dug there in the 1970s and found many of the things the cave is known for. Among his finds was a small bone, about eight centimetres long, from the leg of a baboon. Twenty-nine notches had been cut across it, one below another.

How old is it? Charcoal, wood, beeswax and an eggshell bead from the same layers have been dated by their carbon, and they put the bone at about 44,000 to 42,000 years old. It was once thought to be about 35,000, and some books still say so.
What were the notches for? A notch is easy to make and hard to read. Some have called the bone a calendar of the moon, and some the oldest piece of mathematics, but both are guesses.

Francesco d'Errico looked at its notches under a microscope, and argued that they were cut with four different tools, on four separate occasions, as if someone came back to add to them. That would make the bone a record of something: a tally, a count of things or days. Others point out that in Australia, Aboriginal message sticks carry rows of notches that helped a messenger remember a message, and counted nothing at all.
So the twenty-nine notches may count something, or they may not. What they count, if anything, nobody knows.

events.label: Flutes
events.ageText: 0.042 Ma · ± 0.001 Ma · the start of the layers the Geißenklösterle flutes lie in, about 43,000 to 42,000, by radiocarbon on cleaned bone (Higham 2012); the Hohle Fels vulture-bone flute, in another cave nearby, is about 40,000 (Conard 2009)

placeNow.name: Geißenklösterle, near Blaubeuren, Swabian Jura, Baden-Württemberg, Germany (48.40 N, 9.77 E)

events.summary: About 42,000 years ago. People in what is now southern Germany made flutes from the wing bones of birds and from mammoth ivory. They are the oldest musical instruments yet found that nobody disputes.

paragraphs: In the Swabian Jura, in the southwest of Germany, deep valleys run through the limestone, and there are caves high in their walls. Geißenklösterle ("GUY-sen-KLER-ster-leh") is one of them, in the valley of the Ach, near Blaubeuren ("blow-BOY-ren"). Archaeologists dug in it, on and off, from the 1970s to 2002.

Among what they found were pieces of the wing bones of swans, made into flutes. And there were thirty-one small pieces of mammoth ivory which, fitted back together, made another flute, about nineteen centimetres long, with at least three finger holes. It was reported in 2004.

A bird's wing bone is already a tube. A mammoth's tusk is solid, and curved. To make a flute of it, the maker must have split a length of tusk down the middle, hollowed out each half, and then fitted the two halves back together so closely that the seam would not leak air.

How old are they? In 2012 Tom Higham, Nicholas Conard and their colleagues dated bones from the layers, cleaned with great care so that no modern carbon remained, and found that the layers the flutes lie in began about 43,000 to 42,000 years ago, older than had been thought.

In 2008, in Hohle Fels ("HOH-leh FELS"), another cave a few kilometres away, Conard's team from the University of Tübingen found twelve pieces of a flute made from the wing bone of a griffon vulture. Put together, it is almost twenty-two centimetres long and has five finger holes, with two notches cut into one end, probably where the player blew. It is about 40,000 years old.

Is there anything older? In 1995, in Divje babe ("DEEV-yeh BAH-beh"), a cave in Slovenia, Ivan Turk's team found the thigh bone of a young cave bear with holes in it, from a time when Neanderthals lived there, about 50,000 to 60,000 years ago. His team argues that it is a flute. Others argue that the holes were bitten by hyenas. The argument has gone on for more than thirty years.

events.label: El Castillo
events.ageText: 0.0408 Ma · minimum · uranium-series on a crust over a red disc, measured at 41,400 ± 570, given as at least 40,800 (Pike 2012)
events.ageHow: minimum · uranium-series on a crust over a red disc, measured at 41,400 ± 570, given as at least 40,800 (Pike 2012)

placeNow.name: Cueva de El Castillo, Puente Viesgo, Cantabria, Spain (43.29 N, 3.97 W); open to visitors on guided tours

events.summary: At least 40,800 years ago. Someone painted a red disc on the wall of El Castillo, a cave in Cantabria, in northern Spain. Who painted it, our kind of people or Neanderthals, is argued.

paragraphs: Above the village of Puente Viesgo ("PWEN-teh VYES-go"), in Cantabria, in the north of Spain, is a cone-shaped hill called Monte Castillo, and inside it are caves. In 1903 Hermilio Alcalde del Río ("er-MEE-lyo al-KAL-deh del REE-o"), who ran the school of arts and crafts in Torrelavega and searched the caves of Cantabria, found paintings in one of them, El Castillo ("el kas-TEE-yo"). People have counted more than two thousand images there since, among them more than eighty hands, outlined in red on the rock.
On one wall, now called the Panel of Hands, the hand stencils are mixed with red discs.

In 2012 Alistair Pike and his team dated the paintings in eleven caves in Spain. They used the thin crusts of mineral that water had laid over the paint. A crust holds a little uranium, which turns into thorium at a steady rate, so its date is the least the painting under it can be. At El Castillo, the crust over one red disc was at least 40,800 years old, and the crust over a hand stencil at least 37,300.
Who painted the disc? People of our own kind were arriving in Europe about then, and Neanderthals were living in Spain. Pike said either might have done it; others thought our kind far more likely.

In 2018 Dirk Hoffmann and his team dated crusts in three other caves, and found one over a sign shaped like a ladder in La Pasiega ("la pa-SYEH-ga"), on the same hill, that was at least 64,800 years old. That is before our kind is known to have reached Europe, so they argued that Neanderthals had painted it.

Other specialists replied that water can wash uranium out of a crust and make it look older than it is. In 2019 forty-four of them wrote that there was "still no archaeological evidence" that Neanderthals made Iberian cave art. Hoffmann's team replied. The argument is open.
El Castillo is open to visitors, with a guide.

events.label: Hohle Fels Venus
events.ageText: 0.040 Ma · ± 0.003 Ma · from the layer: radiocarbon on bones in it gives at least 35,000 calendar years (Conard 2009), now usually given as about 40,000; not dated on the ivory

placeNow.name: Hohle Fels, near Schelklingen, Ach valley, Baden-Württemberg, Germany (48.38 N, 9.76 E); kept at the Urgeschichtliches Museum Blaubeuren

events.summary: About 40,000 years ago. Someone in a cave in what is now southern Germany carved a woman from mammoth ivory, small enough to close a hand around. It is the oldest carving of a person that nobody disputes.

paragraphs: Hohle Fels ("HOH-leh FELS") means "hollow rock." It is a cave near the small town of Schelklingen ("SHELK-ling-en"), in the valley of the Ach, in the Swabian Jura, in the southwest of Germany.

In September 2008 a team led by Nicholas Conard, of the University of Tübingen, was digging about three metres below the cave floor and about twenty metres in from the entrance, deep in the layers that people had left. Over ten days they found six small pieces of carved mammoth ivory, all within a patch about the size of a doormat. The biggest piece came out on the ninth of September.

Fitted together, the pieces make a woman about six centimetres tall, small enough to close a hand around. She is nearly whole: only her left arm and shoulder are missing. Her breasts are large, her hips are wide, and her arms are short, with the hands on her belly. Where her head should be there is a small ring, pierced through, so she may have hung from a cord.
That same month, about seventy centimetres away and in the same layer, the team found the pieces of a flute made from a vulture's wing bone.
How old is she? The ivory has not been dated, but bones from the layer she lay in have, by their carbon, and she is at least 35,000 years old and probably about 40,000.

She is the oldest carving of a person that nobody disputes. In another cave not far away, Hohlenstein-Stadel, people of about the same time carved a figure in ivory that stands like a person but has the head of a lion; it is kept in Ulm. Paintings of figures that look like people are older: on Sulawesi, in Indonesia, they are at least 51,200 years old.
Archaeologists call small carved women like this one *Venus* figures, after the Roman goddess of love. What she meant to the people who carved her, nobody knows.

events.label: Chauvet
events.ageText: 0.037 Ma · the first of two times people used the cave, 37,000 to 33,500, from a model built on more than 350 dates, most by radiocarbon on charcoal and bone (Quiles 2016); the second, 31,000 to 28,000; most of the black drawings belong to the first

placeNow.name: Grotte Chauvet-Pont d'Arc, Vallon-Pont-d'Arc, Ardèche, France (44.39 N, 4.41 E); closed; the replica, Grotte Chauvet 2 – Ardèche, nearby (44.41 N, 4.43 E)

events.summary: About 37,000 years ago. People began to draw on the walls of a cave in the Ardèche, in southern France: lions, mammoths, rhinoceroses and horses. A fall of rock sealed the cave, and nobody entered it again until 1994.

paragraphs: On a Sunday afternoon in December 1994, three cavers, Jean-Marie Chauvet ("show-VAY"), Éliette Brunel and Christian Hillaire, were walking along the cliffs near the Pont d'Arc, a great natural arch of rock over the river Ardèche ("ar-DESH"), in the south of France. At a small opening in the rock they felt a faint draught of air, and a draught means a cave behind. They cleared away the stones and climbed down a ladder into the dark.
In the beam of her lamp Éliette Brunel saw two small lines of red ochre on the rock. "Ils sont venus!" she called: "They came!"

They had found a long cave, painted and drawn on for much of its length. On Christmas Eve they went back and laid strips of plastic along a single path, so that nobody would step on the floor, where the bones of animals lay, and the hollows where cave bears had slept.
There are hundreds of animals on its walls, and many of them are dangerous ones: lions, mammoths, rhinoceroses, bears. In a painted cave that is unusual.

How old are they? Many are drawn in charcoal, and charcoal can be dated by its carbon. In 2016 Anita Quiles, Hélène Valladas and their team put together more than 350 dates from the cave, and found that people used it at two times: between about 37,000 and 33,500 years ago, and again between about 31,000 and 28,000. The charcoal drawings that have been dated belong to the first.
Then rock fell from the cliff above the entrance, and sealed the cave.
It has been kept closed since 1994, to protect it. A copy of it opened nearby in 2015, and anyone can visit that.

events.label: Lady of Brassempouy
events.ageText: 0.030 Ma · ± 0.002 Ma · from the layer and the kind of tools in it (Middle Gravettian), about 26,000 to 24,000 radiocarbon years, which calibrates to about 30,000 to 28,000 years ago (IntCal20, run by the checker); the museum's own date is about 30,000 years ago; not dated on the ivory, and the 1890s digging makes the layer itself uncertain (White 2006)

placeNow.name: Grotte du Pape, Brassempouy, Landes, France (43.63 N, 0.70 W); kept at the Musée d'Archéologie nationale, Saint-Germain-en-Laye

events.summary: About 30,000 years ago. Someone in what is now southwestern France carved a woman's head from mammoth ivory, smaller than a thumb, with a pattern of squares over her hair. It is one of the oldest carved faces yet found.

paragraphs: Brassempouy ("brah-sahn-poo-EE") is a village in the Landes, in the southwest of France, and in a wood near it, beside a small stream, is a small cave called the Grotte du Pape, the Pope's Cave.

In 1892 a crowd of visitors on a scientific outing dug into it, each for himself, and the floor was badly torn up. Two years later Édouard Piette ("pee-ET"), who studied the people of the ice age, came to dig with J. de Laporterie, who had been digging there since 1890. Among their finds, in 1894, was a woman's head, carved from mammoth ivory. It is a little more than three and a half centimetres tall, smaller than a thumb.

The face is a narrow triangle, with a forehead, eyebrows and a long nose. There is no mouth. Over the head, and falling to each side of the neck, is a pattern of lines cut at right angles, like a grid of little squares.

What is the pattern? Some say a hood, some say braided hair, some say a wig. In French she is called *la Dame à la capuche*, the Lady with the Hood, but that is a nickname, not a finding. Nobody knows.

How old is she? The digging of the 1890s was rough, and workers were said to be paid for each object they found. In 2006 Randall White, an archaeologist, looked again at the old records and at the tools found with the figures, and placed them in layers left by people who lived there about 30,000 years ago.
At least eight other carvings of people came out of the same cave, most of them bodies, without heads. The Lady is the only face.

She is kept at the national archaeology museum, in a château at Saint-Germain-en-Laye, near Paris. She is kept in a room that opens only by appointment, because ivory is easily damaged. In Brassempouy, at the Maison de la Dame, visitors can see a copy.

events.ageText: 0.0265 Ma to 0.019 Ma · a span: nearly all ice sheets stood at their largest between about 26,500 and 19,000 to 20,000 years ago, from more than 5,700 radiocarbon and other dates on their edges (Clark 2009); the ice that covered Chicago reached farthest south, into central Illinois, about 24,000 years ago; the dot is at the start of the span
