placeNow.name: Chicago, Illinois, United States (41.88 N, 87.63 W)

events.summary: About 26,500 to 19,000 years ago. The ice of the last cold spell was at its largest. Chicago lay under about half a mile of ice, and the sea was about 120 to 130 metres lower than today.

paragraphs: Twenty-four thousand years ago, the place where Chicago stands was under ice more than half a mile thick, more than eight hundred metres. The top of it was higher than the tallest building in Chicago is now.

The ice had come from the north. It grew over Canada until it was as much as three kilometres thick, and it spread south and pushed down the basin where Lake Michigan is now, like a great tongue. It reached northeastern Illinois about 30,000 years ago. By about 24,000 years ago it had reached farthest south, into the middle of Illinois, and it covered all of the Chicago region.

Ice was spread over much of the north of the world at once: over almost all of Canada, much of Britain and Ireland, and Scandinavia. Nearly all of these ice sheets were at their largest between about 26,500 and 19,000 years ago. Geologists call that time the Last Glacial Maximum.

So much water was locked up in the ice that the sea was about 120 to 130 metres lower than it is now. Coral shows it. The kind called elkhorn coral grows only just under the surface of the sea. Richard Fairbanks and his team drilled into the sea floor off Barbados, and in 1989 reported elkhorn coral from the time of the ice about 120 metres down, where it could never have grown.
Where the sea had been shallow, it was now dry land. Siberia and Alaska were joined by a broad plain, where the Bering Strait is now.
The world as a whole was about five or six degrees colder than it is today. Some scientists put it closer to four and a half.

Then the ice began to melt back. As it shrank, it left long, low ridges of rubble around the south end of Lake Michigan. Chicago was free of ice by about 17,000 years ago. The melting ice filled the basin with a lake higher than Lake Michigan is now, called Lake Chicago, and much of the city stands on that lake's flat old floor.

events.picturesWanted: a map of the ice at its largest, with Chicago and the shoreline marked (to be drawn for CW from the Time Machine's own globe and sea-level layer); elkhorn coral (Commons; licence to check).

events.label: Lascaux
events.ageText: 0.021 Ma · ± 0.0005 Ma · radiocarbon on reindeer bone from the floor, about 21,500 to 21,000 calendar years ago (Ducasse and Langlais 2019); these date people's visits, not the paint; the figures in older books, about 17,000 and 18,600, were radiocarbon years
events.ageHow: radiocarbon on reindeer bone from the floor, about 21,500 to 21,000 calendar years ago (Ducasse and Langlais 2019); these date people's visits, not the paint; the figures in older books, about 17,000 and 18,600, were radiocarbon years
events.knownFrom: bone, antler and charcoal left on the cave floor; the black paint, mostly manganese, cannot itself be dated by its carbon (to confirm)

placeNow.name: Grotte de Lascaux, Montignac-Lascaux, Dordogne, France (45.05 N, 1.17 E); closed since 1963; Lascaux IV, the International Centre for Cave Art, in Montignac

events.summary: About 21,000 years ago. People painted bulls, horses and deer on the walls of a cave in the Dordogne, in southwestern France. Four young people found the cave in September 1940. The largest bull is five metres long.

paragraphs: On 8 September 1940, on a hill above the town of Montignac ("mon-tee-NYAK"), in the Dordogne, in the southwest of France, Marcel Ravidat ("rah-vee-DAH"), a young apprentice mechanic, found a hole where a tree had fallen. Four days later he came back with three others, Jacques Marsal, Georges Agniel ("ahn-YEL") and Simon Coencas. Simon was thirteen. His family had come to Montignac from near Paris that June, to take refuge from the war.

Ravidat went down first. At the bottom was a hall seventeen metres long, and on its walls and ceiling were animals: horses, deer, and bulls, painted in black and red and yellow. The largest bull is more than five metres long. It is said to be the largest animal painted in any cave yet found.
The four told their teacher, Léon Laval, and he came down on the eighteenth. Within days the Abbé Henri Breuil, a priest who studied painted caves, was there too.

The cave opened to the public in 1948. Many thousands came, and the warmth and breath of so many visitors, with the light, brought green growths on the walls. In 1963 André Malraux, France's minister of culture, closed it. A copy of the hall and its paintings was made nearby, and opened in 1983. A fuller copy opened in 2016, in Montignac.

How old are the paintings? The black paint is made mostly from manganese minerals, with no charcoal in it, so it has never been dated directly. But the people who painted left things on the floor: bits of bone and antler, and charcoal. In 2019 Sylvain Ducasse and Mathieu Langlais dated pieces of reindeer bone from the floor, and put the people's visits at about 21,500 to 21,000 years ago. Older books say about 17,000. That figure was in radiocarbon years, which run short of ordinary years this far back.
Simon Coencas, the last of the four, died in 2020, at ninety-three.

events.picturesWanted: the Hall of the Bulls ("Lascaux-salle-des-taureaux.jpg", Commons, tagged public domain: licence to check, the tag is doubtful); the Ministry of Culture's photographs (archeologie.culture.gouv.fr/lascaux): licence to ask.
references: Sylvain Ducasse and Mathieu Langlais, "Twenty years on, a new date with Lascaux. Reassessing the chronology of the cave's Paleolithic occupations through new 14C AMS dating," *PALEO*, 2019.
Ministère de la Culture, "Lascaux: dating the figures" and "The discovery" (archeologie.culture.gouv.fr/lascaux).
Norbert Aujoulat, *Lascaux: Movement, Space and Time* (Abrams, 2005).
Gregory Curtis, *The Cave Painters* (Knopf, 2006). For a parent.

events.label: Ishango bone
events.ageText: 0.020 Ma · + 0.005 / − 0.002 Ma · the age of the layers it lay in, about 25,000 to 20,000, by radiocarbon and (to confirm) amino-acid dating (Brooks and Smith 1987); the museum calls the bone "nearly 20,000 years old"; volcanoes nearby upset the carbon, so the dates are less certain than usual; first thought to be about 8,500 to 11,000

events.knownFrom: one notched bone with a chip of quartz in its end, a second notched bone never published, and the layers of a camp beside a lake

placeNow.name: Ishango, where the Semliki River leaves Lake Edward, Virunga National Park, North Kivu, Democratic Republic of the Congo (0.13 S, 29.60 E); kept at the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences, Brussels

events.summary: About 20,000 years ago. Someone at Ishango, beside a lake in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo, cut rows of notches into a bone. The numbers of notches have puzzled people ever since.

paragraphs: Ishango ("ee-SHAHNG-go") is on the shore of Lake Edward, near where the Semliki River ("sem-LEE-kee") flows out of it, in Virunga ("vee-ROONG-ga") National Park, in the east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. In 1950, when the Congo was ruled by Belgium, Jean de Heinzelin, a Belgian geologist, dug there and found the layers of a camp where people had lived long ago. Among what they left was a bone about ten centimetres long, now dark brown. A small chip of quartz is set into one end, so it may have been a tool for engraving.
Along the bone are three rows of notches, cut in groups. De Heinzelin counted them like this.
Add up the first row and you get 60. The third also comes to 60. The middle one comes to 48.

The numbers 11, 13, 17 and 19 are the only prime numbers between 10 and 20: numbers that can't be divided evenly except by 1 and by themselves. In the middle row, 3 is followed by its double, 6, and 4 by its double, 8; then 10 comes before its half, 5.

What does it mean? De Heinzelin wondered, in 1962, whether the people of Ishango knew about primes. Alexander Marshack argued that the notches kept track of the moon over six months. Vladimir Pletser and Dirk Huylebrouck have argued that they show counting in twelves. In 2026 a team asked grown-ups to work with notches as small as these, and found they could not count them exactly enough to do sums.
At first the layers were thought to be about 8,500 to 11,000 years old. In 1987 Alison Brooks and Catherine Smith dated them again, and the bone is now thought to be about 20,000 years old.
A second notched bone was found at Ishango in 1959. It is in Brussels too, and it has hardly been studied.

events.picturesWanted: the Ishango bone, both faces (Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences: licence to ask; Commons "Category:Ishango bone": licence to check); the shore of Lake Edward at Ishango (Commons; licence to check). A drawing of the three rows of notches, to be made for CW.
references: Jean de Heinzelin, "Ishango," *Scientific American*, June 1962.
Alison Brooks and Catherine Smith, "Ishango revisited: new age determinations and cultural interpretations," *The African Archaeological Review*, 1987.
Vladimir Pletser and Dirk Huylebrouck, "The Ishango artefact: the missing base 12 link," *Forma*, 1999.
Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences, "The Ishango bone" (naturalsciences.be) and "Ishango" (ishango.naturalsciences.be).
Alexander Marshack, *The Roots of Civilization* (McGraw-Hill, 1972). For a parent; read as one man's argument.

events.ageText: 0.017 Ma · ± 0.001 Ma · radiocarbon on charcoal in the paint of the bison, 14,000 ± 400 radiocarbon years (Valladas 1992), which calibrates to about 17,000 years ago (IntCal20, 15,900 to 18,100, run by the checker); a sign in the same cave has a uranium-series minimum age of at least 35,600 (Pike 2012; 36,160 ± 610), argued

placeNow.name: Cueva de Altamira, Santillana del Mar, Cantabria, Spain (43.38 N, 4.12 W); closed except to five visitors a week; the Neocueva, a copy, at the Museo Nacional y Centro de Investigación de Altamira

events.summary: About 17,000 years ago. People painted bison in red and black on the low ceiling of a cave in Cantabria, in northern Spain. When the paintings were found, in 1879, the experts refused to believe they were old.

paragraphs: Altamira ("al-ta-MEE-ra") is a cave near the town of Santillana del Mar ("san-tee-YA-na del MAR"), in Cantabria, in the north of Spain. A local man, Modesto Cubillas, found its entrance in about 1868. In 1875 Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola ("sow-TWOH-la"), a man of the district who was curious about the distant past, first visited the cave.
In 1879 he came back to dig in its floor, with his daughter, María, who was eight. While he dug, she looked up, and on the ceiling she saw bison.

There are more than twenty great animals on the ceiling: bison, two horses and a female deer, painted in red, yellow and black. The largest are well over a metre long. The painters chose places where the rock bulges, so the bodies seem to swell out of the ceiling.

In 1880 Sautuola published a short book about the cave, and said the paintings were very old. The experts, among them Émile Cartailhac ("kar-tie-YAK"), in France, would not believe it. Paintings so fine and so fresh, they thought, could not be the work of people of the ice age, and some said they were fakes. Juan Vilanova y Piera, a Spanish geologist, stood by him, but it did not help.

Then, in France, other caves were found with paintings on their walls, at La Mouthe in 1895 and at Font-de-Gaume in 1901. In 1902 Cartailhac published an article that he called "Mea culpa d'un sceptique": a sceptic's "my fault."

In 1992 Hélène Valladas and her team dated charcoal from the paint of the bison, and it was about 17,000 years old. A red sign in the same cave, dated another way in 2012, is at least 35,600, but that way of dating is argued.
The cave was closed in 2002 to protect it. A copy of the ceiling was made inside the museum nearby.
Sautuola died in 1888, fourteen years before Cartailhac's article.

events.picturesWanted: the bison ceiling ("Altamira-plafond.jpg", Commons, tagged public domain as a faithful copy of a 2-D work: licence to check, the tag is risky for a curved ceiling; or the museum's photographs, licence to ask); the Neocueva (Commons; licence to check).
references: Hélène Valladas and others, "Direct radiocarbon dates for prehistoric paintings at the Altamira, El Castillo and Niaux caves," *Nature*, 1992.
Alistair Pike and others, "U-Series Dating of Paleolithic Art in 11 Caves in Spain," *Science*, 2012.
Émile Cartailhac, "Les cavernes ornées de dessins. La grotte d'Altamira, Espagne. 'Mea culpa' d'un sceptique," *L'Anthropologie*, 1902 (title to confirm).
Gregory Curtis, *The Cave Painters* (Knopf, 2006). For a parent.

events.label: Ice lets go

place.name: the NorthGRIP drill site, central Greenland (75.10 N, 42.32 W), where the ice that records the change was drilled

events.summary: About 10,000 BCE. After a hundred thousand years of cold, the world warmed for good, and it happened fast. Ice drilled from Greenland shows the warming took only a few decades. This line starts there.

paragraphs: In a freezer near Copenhagen there are long sticks of ice, a little thicker than your arm. They were drilled out of the ice that covers Greenland, piece after piece, from the top all the way down to the rock, more than three kilometres below.
The ice is made of snow.

Every year, snow falls on the middle of Greenland and does not melt. The next year's snow falls on top of it and presses it down. Over thousands of years the old snow turns to ice, in layers, one for each year, like the rings of a tree. Count the layers and you know how old the ice is. The ice also keeps signs of how cold it was when the snow fell.
So what does the ice say?

For most of the last hundred thousand years, the world was colder than it is now. Ice sheets covered much of North America and northern Europe. At the coldest, so much water was locked up in ice that the sea was about 130 metres lower than it is today, and people could walk from Asia to America.

Then, 1,492 metres down in one of the Greenland ice cores, something changes. In the layers below that point, the snow fell in bitter cold. In the layers above it, Greenland is about ten degrees warmer. Some of the signs in the ice change from one year to the next. The whole warming took a few decades.
The ice at that depth is about 11,700 years old. This line starts near there, at a round number.
Why did the cold end so suddenly? Scientists are still working on it.
The great ice sheets took thousands of years more to melt, and the sea took thousands of years to rise. But the cold had broken, and it has not come back.
Farms, cities, writing and everything else on this line happened in the warm.

events.picturesWanted: an ice core with visible yearly layers (Commons, `GISP2 1855m ice core layers.png`; licence to check); a graph of Greenland temperature over the last 20,000 years, showing the jump (to be drawn for CW from published data).
references: J. P. Steffensen and others, "High-resolution Greenland ice core data show abrupt climate change happens in few years," *Science*, 2008. How fast the signals changed.

Mike Walker and others, "Formal definition and dating of the GSSP (Global Stratotype Section and Point) for the base of the Holocene using the Greenland NGRIP ice core, and selected auxiliary records," *Journal of Quaternary Science*, 2009. The depth (1,492.45 m) and the date (11,700 years before 2000).

Alexi Grachev and Jeffrey Severinghaus, "A revised +10±4 °C magnitude of the abrupt change in Greenland temperature at the Younger Dryas termination using published GISP2 gas isotope data and air thermal diffusion constants," *Quaternary Science Reviews*, 2005. About ten degrees.
Kurt Lambeck and others, "Sea level and global ice volumes from the Last Glacial Maximum to the Holocene," *PNAS*, 2014. The sea about 130 metres lower.

events.label: Jōmon pots, already old

place.name: Ōdai Yamamoto

events.summary: About 10000 BCE. The Jōmon people of Japan made pottery long before the ice let go, some of the oldest pots anywhere. History does not begin at the left edge of this line. The line is just where the world got warm enough for everything else to start happening quickly.
events.legacy: September 2026: a blurb from general knowledge, unsourced; no More

events.label: Göbekli Tepe

place.name: Göbekli Tepe, near Şanlıurfa, southeast Turkey (37.22 N, 38.92 E)

events.summary: About 9500 BCE. On a hill in what is now southeast Turkey, people who hunted and gathered their food carved stone pillars as tall as a house and stood them in rings. Nobody knows why.

paragraphs: A stone pillar stands in a ring of other pillars. It is shaped like a capital T, is as tall as a two-storey house, and weighs about as much as seven cars. Down its sides, someone carved two long arms. The hands meet at the front, above a belt. Other pillars nearby are covered with carved foxes, boars, snakes, vultures and scorpions.
The hill is called Göbekli Tepe, which means "Potbelly Hill" in Turkish. Say "guh-bek-LEE TEP-eh." It is in southeast Turkey.
The pillars were cut from the limestone of the hill itself with flint tools.
One pillar was never finished. It still lies where it was being cut, seven metres long. Standing, it would have weighed about fifty tonnes.
What makes the pillars strange is that no one knows much about the people who made them. At that time, nobody in the world farmed. Nobody kept sheep.
Still, moving one of these stones could have taken hundreds of people pulling together. It must have taken months or years to build. All of those people had to be fed while they worked.
So what did the builders eat?

They hunted gazelle and gathered wild plants, including wild wheat. Within about a thousand years, and not far away, people were farming wheat. But so far as we know, there were no farms when this was being built.

Nobody knows what the rings were for, either. Klaus Schmidt thought the rings were a temple, a place people travelled to but did not live. He was the archaeologist who began digging at the site in 1995 and realised its importance.

Newer digging has found tanks cut into the rock to hold rainwater, and a great many stones for grinding seeds. Those suggest people lived there too. Even now, most of the hill has not been explored. There is much more to be discovered.
For now, we know the pillars with arms have no faces. Maybe someday we'll know why.

events.picturesWanted: the pillar with arms and hands (Enclosure D, pillar 18); a carved fox or vulture. Source and licence to be found.
references: Klaus Schmidt, *Göbekli Tepe: A Stone Age Sanctuary in South-Eastern Anatolia* (ex oriente, 2012). The excavator's own account, and his view that nobody lived there.

Lee Clare and others, "How did they do it? Making and moving monoliths at Göbekli Tepe," *The Tepe Telegrams*, German Archaeological Institute, 2016. Pillar sizes and weights, the unfinished pillar, flint tools.
Andrew Curry, "Last Stand of the Hunter-Gatherers?", *Archaeology*, May/June 2021. The newer finds: the rainwater cistern, thousands of grinding tools, houses with hearths.

Andrew Curry, "Göbekli Tepe: The World's First Temple?", *Smithsonian Magazine*, 2008. The 1963 survey and the graveyard mistake.

events.label: Figs

place.name: Gilgal I, Lower Jordan Valley, about 13 km north of Jericho, West Bank (32.03 N, 35.48 E)

events.summary: About 9400 BCE. In a village near Jericho, people stored figs of a kind that cannot grow from seed. Someone may have planted the trees, which would make figs one of the first crops.

paragraphs: Nine small figs, burnt black, lie in the remains of a house. With them are hundreds of tiny fig seeds.

The house is at a place called Gilgal, in the Jordan Valley, not far from the town of Jericho. Say "GIL-gahl." The people who lived there about 11,400 years ago hunted and gathered their food. They also stored wild barley, wild oats and acorns.
In 2006, three scientists, Mordechai Kislev, Anat Hartmann and Ofer Bar-Yosef, looked closely at the figs, and found something odd about the seeds.
A wild fig tree needs help to make good seeds. A tiny wasp crawls inside the young fig and carries pollen in. Without the wasp, most wild figs fall off before they ripen.
Some fig trees are different. Their figs ripen without the wasp. They stay on the tree and turn soft and sweet. But their seeds are empty, and cannot grow into new trees.
The figs at Gilgal were that kind.
So how did those trees spread?

A fig tree has a second way to make more of itself. Cut off a branch, push it into the ground, and it grows roots. Kislev, Hartmann and Bar-Yosef thought that is what the people at Gilgal did. They chose trees whose figs stayed on the branch and turned sweet, and they planted cuttings. If so, people were growing figs on purpose about a thousand years before they grew wheat or barley.
Not everyone agrees.

Other scientists answered the same year. Fig trees of this kind, they said, also make some figs with good seeds, so they can spread on their own. The people at Gilgal may simply have picked figs from wild trees that happened to be sweet.
Planted, or picked? Nobody can be sure.
Either way, someone stored the figs, and perhaps dried them first. They are still the shape of figs.

events.picturesWanted: a fresh fig cut in half, to show the seeds (Commons; licence to check). No free image of the Gilgal figs is known.
references: Mordechai Kislev, Anat Hartmann and Ofer Bar-Yosef, "Early domesticated fig in the Jordan Valley," *Science*, 2006. The figs and the planting idea.
Simcha Lev-Yadun, Gidi Ne'eman, Shahal Abbo and Moshe Flaishman, "Comment on 'Early domesticated fig in the Jordan Valley'," *Science*, 2006. The answer.
Tim Denham, "Early fig domestication, or gathering of wild parthenocarpic figs?", *Antiquity*, 2007. The question restated.
Harvard Gazette, "Figs likely first domesticated crop," 2006. The count of 313 seed-like drupelets.

events.label: Jericho tower

place.name: Tell es-Sultan, Jericho, West Bank (31.87 N, 35.44 E)

events.summary: About 8300 BCE. At Jericho, near the Jordan River, people built a round stone tower about eight metres tall, with a staircase inside. Nobody knows what it was for. It is still standing.

paragraphs: A round tower of rough stones stands in a deep trench. It is about eight metres tall, as high as a house of three storeys. At its foot is a small doorway. Inside, a narrow staircase of twenty-two stone steps climbs through the tower to the top.

The tower is at Jericho, beside a spring that never runs dry, near the Jordan River in what is now the West Bank. It was built about 10,300 years ago. At that time nobody in this part of the world made pottery, and the people of Jericho were only beginning to grow some of their food. Yet they gathered and stacked enough stone to build this, and a long wall beside it.
The archaeologist Kathleen Kenyon dug the tower out in the 1950s.
What was it for?
Kenyon thought it was for defence: a lookout beside a town wall. But nobody has found signs of an enemy at that time.
In 1986 another archaeologist, Ofer Bar-Yosef, suggested that the wall was built to hold back floods and mud washing down from the hills, and that the tower was used for ceremonies.

Later, two other archaeologists, Roy Liran and Ran Barkai, pointed to the sky. West of Jericho rises a mountain called Quruntul. Say "koo-roon-TOOL." On the longest day of the year, the Sun sets behind that mountain, and as it sets, the mountain's shadow stretches out across the plain and reaches the tower. The staircase inside points toward the same mountain. Liran and Barkai suggested the tower helped persuade people to live together as one community.
A lookout, a place for ceremonies, or something to do with the Sun? Each idea still has supporters. Nobody knows.
It is one of the oldest stone towers anyone has found.
A metal grate now covers the top of the stairs.

events.picturesWanted: the tower in its trench (Commons, `Tower of Jericho.jpg`; licence to check); a photograph down the staircase if one exists with a clear licence.
references: Kathleen Kenyon, *Digging Up Jericho* (1957). Her excavation and her reading of the tower.
Ofer Bar-Yosef, "The walls of Jericho: an alternative interpretation," *Current Anthropology*, 1986. The flood wall.
Roy Liran and Ran Barkai, "Casting a shadow on Neolithic Jericho," *Antiquity* Project Gallery, 2011. The midsummer shadow and the alignment.
UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Ancient Jericho/Tell es-Sultan" (inscribed 2023). The site.

events.label: Squash

place.name: Guilá Naquitz cave, near Mitla, Oaxaca, Mexico (16.98 N, 96.31 W)

events.summary: About 8000 BCE. In a cave in the hills of southern Mexico, people left squash seeds bigger than wild squash makes. Someone was growing squash. Farming had begun in the Americas, separately from anywhere else.

paragraphs: A squash seed, about as long as your thumbnail, was dug from the floor of a cave in southern Mexico. It is pale and flat, like a pumpkin seed. It is about 10,000 years old.

The cave is called Guilá Naquitz. Say "gee-LAH nah-KEETS." It is high in the dry hills of Oaxaca. Small groups of people camped there from time to time. They left behind scraps of what they ate: acorns, nuts, cactus fruit, agave, and bits of squash.
The archaeologist Kent Flannery dug the cave in the 1960s. His team kept everything, down to the seeds.

Thirty years later, another archaeologist, Bruce Smith, looked at the squash again. By then it was possible to find the age of a single seed, using a speck of the seed itself. The oldest was about 10,000 years old.
But was it wild squash, or grown?

Smith compared the seeds and stems from the cave with those of wild squash. Wild squash is small and hard, with small seeds and a thin stem. The squash from the cave had bigger seeds and thicker stems.

When people save seeds from the plants they like best, and plant them, year after year, the plants change. Their fruits and seeds get bigger. Someone at Guilá Naquitz was choosing and planting squash.

At about the same time, people in the Middle East were beginning to farm wheat and barley. Nobody in Mexico knew that. Nobody in the Middle East knew there was a Mexico. Farming was invented at least twice, by people who never met.
Maize came later. In this same cave, the oldest cobs of maize are about four thousand years younger than the oldest squash seed.
Many pumpkins, courgettes and acorn squash belong to the same kind of plant as the seeds in the cave.

events.picturesWanted: the cave mouth (Commons, `Guila Naquitz cave.jpg`, CC BY-SA 2.5, JerryFriedman); wild squash beside a garden squash, at the same scale (licence to check).
references: Bruce D. Smith, "The initial domestication of *Cucurbita pepo* in the Americas 10,000 years ago," *Science*, 1997. The dates and the seeds and stems.
Kent V. Flannery, ed., *Guilá Naquitz: Archaic Foraging and Early Agriculture in Oaxaca, Mexico* (Academic Press, 1986). The cave and what was eaten there.
Dolores Piperno and Kent Flannery, "The earliest archaeological maize (*Zea mays* L.) from highland Mexico: new accelerator dates and their implications," *PNAS*, 2001. The maize cobs.

events.label: Rice

place.name: Shangshan, Pujiang County, Zhejiang, China (29.46 N, 119.97 E)

events.summary: About 7500 BCE. Along the Yangtze River in southern China, people gathered wild rice and began to plant it. Over thousands of years it became the rice that now feeds more than half the world.

paragraphs: Look at a grain of rice under a microscope, at the very bottom, where it was joined to the plant. There is a little scar.
On some grains the scar is smooth and round, like a clean break. On others it is rough and torn.
The difference tells you whether people were growing the rice.

Wild rice drops its grains as soon as they are ripe. Each grain breaks off cleanly by itself and falls to the ground, where it can grow. That leaves the smooth scar. Dropping its grain is good for the rice, and bad for anyone who wants to eat it, because by the time the rice is ripe, much of it is already on the ground.

Now and then, a wild rice plant holds on to its grains. If people cut the stalks to gather rice, those are the plants whose grain they carry home. If they plant some of that grain the next year, more of the next crop holds on. To get the grain off, people have to beat the stalks, and that leaves the rough, torn scar.
So archaeologists count scars.

At Tianluoshan, a village near the coast of China about 7,000 years ago, Dorian Fuller and his colleagues looked at the bottoms of 2,641 rice grains. Say "tyen-lwoh-shahn." Over about three hundred years, the share with torn scars rose from about a quarter to nearly four in ten.

Rice-growing in that part of China had begun long before. At Shangshan, about 9,500 years ago, potters mixed rice husks into their clay. Some husks are still inside the broken pots. Say "shahng-shahn."
How long did it take to turn wild rice into a crop that keeps its grain?

That is still argued. Fuller and others think it took thousands of years. Other scientists study tiny specks of glassy stone that form inside rice leaves. They think the change had already begun about 10,000 years ago. The two sides are measuring different things, and nobody has settled it.
Today rice is the main food of more than half the people in the world.

events.picturesWanted: spikelet bases under the microscope, wild and domesticated side by side (from Fuller 2009 or Zheng 2016; licence to check; a drawing for CW may be needed); the Shangshan site (Commons, `Shangshan Relic Site(West site) 2013.JPG`; licence to check).
references: Dorian Fuller and others, "The domestication process and domestication rate in rice: spikelet bases from the Lower Yangtze," *Science*, 2009. The 2,641 grains at Tianluoshan.

Yunfei Zheng, Gary Crawford, Leping Jiang and Xugao Chen, "Rice domestication revealed by reduced shattering of archaeological rice from the Lower Yangtze valley," *Scientific Reports*, 2016. The scars, and the slow change across several sites.
Xinxin Zuo, Houyuan Lu and others, "Dating rice remains through phytolith carbon-14 study reveals domestication at the beginning of the Holocene," *PNAS*, 2017. The earlier start.
Li Liu, Gyoung-Ah Lee, Leping Jiang and Juzhong Zhang, "The earliest rice domestication in China," *Antiquity* Project Gallery, 2007. Husks in the Shangshan pots.

events.label: Çatalhöyük

place.name: Çatalhöyük, Konya Plain, central Turkey (37.67 N, 32.83 E)

events.summary: About 7100 BCE. On a plain in central Turkey, people built a town of mud-brick houses packed so tightly that it had no streets. They walked across the roofs and climbed down ladders into their homes.

paragraphs: A low hill rises about twenty metres above a flat plain in central Turkey. It is not a natural hill. It is made of houses, built one on top of another for more than a thousand years.
The place is now called Çatalhöyük. Say "chah-TAHL-huh-yook."

The houses were built of mud brick, wall against wall, like the cells of a honeycomb. There were no streets between them, and no doors in their outside walls. To visit a neighbour, you walked across the flat roofs. To go home, you climbed down a wooden ladder through a hole in your roof. The same hole let out the smoke from the oven.

Inside, people plastered their walls white, and plastered them again, many times. Some painted the walls with red patterns, with wild cattle, and with vultures. Some set the horns of wild cattle into the walls and covered them in plaster.
And under the floors, people buried their dead. They slept and cooked and worked above the graves of those who had lived there before.
How many people lived there?

When James Mellaart first dug at Çatalhöyük, in the 1960s, he guessed five to seven thousand. Later guesses went as high as ten thousand. Later, from 1993, a team led by Ian Hodder dug much more slowly, sometimes spending a whole season on a single house. They found that not every house was lived in at the same time.

In 2024 two archaeologists, Ian Kuijt and Arkadiusz Marciniak, went through the evidence again. In a typical year, they think, about 600 to 800 people lived there. On their count, Çatalhöyük was less like a city than a large, crowded village that lasted a very long time.
Nobody knows why its people chose to live packed so close together, with open land all around.
Most of the hill has still not been dug.

events.picturesWanted: the model of the packed rooftops (Commons, `MUFT - Catal Höyük Modell.jpg`; licence to check); a wall painting held in a museum (Konya or Ankara; Commons; licence to check). Use only paintings that were photographed or are in museums, not Mellaart's drawings.
references: Ian Hodder, *The Leopard's Tale: Revealing the Mysteries of Çatalhöyük* (Thames & Hudson, 2006). The houses, roofs, burials and paintings.

Ian Kuijt and Arkadiusz Marciniak, "How many people lived in the world's earliest villages? Reconsidering community size and population pressure at Neolithic Çatalhöyük," *Journal of Anthropological Archaeology*, 2024. The 600 to 800.
Alex Bayliss and others, "Getting to the bottom of it all: a Bayesian approach to dating the start of Çatalhöyük," *Journal of World Prehistory*, 2015. The dates.
UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Neolithic Site of Çatalhöyük" (inscribed 2012). The site.

events.label: Maize

place.name: the Balsas River valley, Guerrero, southwest Mexico (18.3 N, 99.8 W). The exact spot is unknown.

events.summary: About 7000 BCE. In the hills of southwest Mexico, people began choosing seeds from a wild grass called teosinte. Over thousands of years it became maize, the corn that now feeds much of the world.

paragraphs: A wild grass grows on the hillsides of southwest Mexico. Its name is teosinte. Say "tay-oh-SIN-tay." Its ear is about as long as your little finger, and it holds only five to twelve seeds. Each seed is locked inside a case so hard that you could break a tooth on it.
This grass is the ancestor of corn.
How do you get from one to the other?

Someone had to choose. Every year, the people who gathered teosinte kept some seeds to plant. If they kept seeds from the plants they liked best, with bigger ears or softer cases, the next year's plants were a little more like that. Nobody planned corn. It happened a little at a time, over thousands of years, because people kept choosing.

We know roughly where it started because of the plant's own genes. Every kind of maize in the world is most closely related to the teosinte that grows in the Balsas River valley. In a rock shelter there, archaeologists found grinding stones with tiny grains of maize starch still stuck to them. The grains are about 8,700 years old.
The earliest maize cobs that survive, from a dry cave in Oaxaca, are about 6,250 years old. They are about as long as the top joint of your thumb.
A scientist named George Beadle once heated teosinte seeds in a pan. They popped. So one of the first things people could have done with teosinte, even before it changed, was make popcorn.
Today more maize is grown than any other grain.
Teosinte still grows wild in those hills. It still has its hard little seeds.

events.picturesWanted: a teosinte ear beside a modern corn cob, at the same scale (widely photographed; a public-domain or CC version is needed).
references: Dolores Piperno and others, "Starch grain and phytolith evidence for early ninth millennium B.P. maize from the Central Balsas River Valley, Mexico," *PNAS*, 2009. The grinding stones and the 8,700-year date.
Dolores Piperno and Kent Flannery, "The earliest archaeological maize from highland Mexico," *PNAS*, 2001. The Guilá Naquitz cobs.
Yoshihiro Matsuoka and others, "A single domestication for maize shown by multilocus microsatellite genotyping," *PNAS*, 2002. All maize descends from Balsas teosinte.
John Doebley, "The genetics of maize evolution," *Annual Review of Genetics*, 2004. Teosinte's ear and hard case.

source.section: 7. A lake drains, the world cools

events.label: Lake Agassiz

place.name: Hudson Bay, Canada, the lake's way out to the sea (58 N, 85 W, approximate). The lake itself lay over Manitoba, Ontario and Minnesota.

events.summary: About 6200 BCE. In Canada, a huge lake left by the melting ice broke through the ice that held it back and poured into the Atlantic. For about 150 years, the lands around the North Atlantic turned colder.

paragraphs: Around the city of Winnipeg, in Canada, the land is flat as a table for hundreds of kilometres. It is flat because it was once the bottom of a lake.
The lake is called Lake Agassiz. Say "AG-uh-see."

As the great ice sheet over North America melted, its water had nowhere to go. The rivers there run north, and the ice was in the way. So the meltwater piled up along the edge of the ice, in a lake that at times was bigger than any lake on Earth today.
Then the ice holding the lake back gave way.

A little more than 8,200 years ago, the lake drained out through Hudson Bay into the Atlantic Ocean. It held more than enough water to cover the whole of the United States ten metres deep. Nobody knows exactly how fast it emptied.
What happened next shows up in the ice of Greenland.

The layers of ice from just after the flood show a sudden cold. For about a century and a half, Greenland was colder, by several degrees at the worst. Mud from lakes and the sea floor shows the cold too, in many places around the North Atlantic.
Why would a lake make the world colder?

Fresh water is lighter than salt water, so it floats on top. Many scientists think a great sheet of fresh water spread over the North Atlantic and slowed an ocean current that carries warm water north.
What did the cold mean for people?

By then people in the Middle East had been farming for about three thousand years. Some archaeologists once thought the cold drove them out of their villages. When others checked thousands of dates from those villages, they found no sign of that. People changed instead. In one village in what is now Syria, they changed the way they built their houses, kept their animals and made their pots, all at about this time.
They stayed.
The land around Winnipeg is still flat.

events.picturesWanted: a map of Lake Agassiz at its largest beside the ice sheet (USGS, `USGS map of Lake Agassiz.jpg`, probably public domain; to confirm); the flat Red River valley from the air.
references: D. C. Barber and others, "Forcing of the cold event of 8,200 years ago by catastrophic drainage of Laurentide lakes," *Nature*, 1999. The drainage and its date.
Richard Alley and others, "Holocene climatic instability: a prominent, widespread event 8200 yr ago," *Geology*, 1997. The cold in the Greenland ice.
Elizabeth Thomas and others, "The 8.2 ka event from Greenland ice cores," *Quaternary Science Reviews*, 2007. The 160 years.

Pascal Flohr, Dominik Fleitmann and others, "Evidence of resilience to past climate change in Southwest Asia: early farming communities and the 9.2 and 8.2 ka events," *Quaternary Science Reviews*, 2016. No collapse.
Peter Akkermans and others, "Weathering climate change in the Near East: dating and Neolithic adaptations 8200 years ago," *Antiquity* Project Gallery, 2010. Tell Sabi Abyad.

events.label: Storegga slide

place.name: the Storegga, on the edge of the sea floor off western Norway (64.5 N, 5.5 E)

events.summary: About 6150 BCE. Under the sea off Norway, a piece of the sea floor almost as big as Iceland slid into deep water. The tsunami it made swept across the North Sea to Scotland and beyond.

paragraphs: In the Shetland Islands, north of Scotland, there is a layer of sand in the peat. The peat was made by plants, slowly, in quiet water. The sand does not belong there. It was thrown in by the sea, and in some places it lies about twenty metres above where the sea was at the time.
Something threw the sea that high.

Off the coast of Norway, the sea floor ends at a steep edge. Beyond it the water is thousands of metres deep. About 8,200 years ago, a piece of that edge broke loose and slid down into the deep. It covered an area almost as big as Iceland. The mud and sand that moved would bury the whole of Scotland about forty metres deep.

When that much sea floor moves at once, the water above it moves too. That is a tsunami: a wave caused not by wind but by the ground under the sea. The wave spread across the North Sea in a few hours. Its sand is found in Norway, Scotland, the Faroe Islands and Shetland.
Where the North Sea is now, there was land.

The ice had melted, and the sea was rising, but slowly. Between Britain and the rest of Europe lay low hills, marshes and rivers, where people hunted and fished. Archaeologists call it Doggerland. By the time of the slide much of it was already underwater, and what was left may have been islands.
Did the wave finish Doggerland? Some scientists think it did. Others think the islands lasted a while longer. Nobody knows how many people lived there, or how many were lost.
Fishing boats still pull up bones and stone tools from the bottom of the North Sea.

events.picturesWanted: a map of the North Sea with Doggerland's coast about 8,000 years ago (several published reconstructions; licence to check); the Colinda harpoon point, trawled up in 1931 (British Museum or Norwich Castle).
references: Petter Bryn and others, "Explaining the Storegga Slide," *Marine and Petroleum Geology*, 2005. Size and cause of the slide.
Stein Bondevik and others, "Record-breaking height for 8000-year-old tsunami in the North Atlantic," *Eos*, 2003. The Shetland deposits.
Vincent Gaffney, Simon Fitch and David Smith, *Europe's Lost World: The Rediscovery of Doggerland* (Council for British Archaeology, 2009). Doggerland.
James Walker and others, "A great wave: the Storegga tsunami and the end of Doggerland?", *Antiquity*, 2020. The argument about whether the wave ended it.

events.label: Crater Lake

place.name: Crater Lake, Oregon, USA (42.94 N, 122.10 W)

events.summary: About 5700 BCE. In what is now Oregon, a volcano called Mount Mazama erupted and its top fell in. Rain and snow filled the hole, and made Crater Lake, the deepest lake in the United States.

paragraphs: In 1938, in a cave in the desert of Oregon, an archaeologist named Luther Cressman dug up dozens of sandals. They were woven from the shredded bark of sagebrush, a grey bush of the desert. Each had a flap to fold over the toes.
The sandals lay under a layer of volcanic ash.

So the sandals were older than the ash. Years later, when it became possible to measure the age of old plant material, some of the sandals were tested. They were more than 9,000 years old. They are among the oldest shoes ever found.
Where did the ash come from?
About a hundred kilometres to the southwest there had been a mountain about 3,700 metres high. It is called Mount Mazama. Say "muh-ZAH-muh."

About 7,700 years ago, Mount Mazama erupted. It threw out about fifty cubic kilometres of melted rock, as ash and pumice. With so much gone from inside it, the top half of the mountain fell in. Where the peak had been, there was a hole about ten kilometres across.
Ash fell over eight of today's states and into Canada, as far as Alberta and Saskatchewan. Geologists still use the ash to date what lies above and below it, just as at the cave.
Over the next few hundred years, rain and snow filled the hole. It became Crater Lake. It is 592 metres deep, the deepest lake in the United States.
Were people there to see it?

The sandals show that people had lived in that country for a thousand years and more before the eruption. The Klamath people live there still. Their name for the lake is giiwas. Say "GEE-wahs." They tell of a fight between Llao, the chief of the world below, and Skell, the chief of the world above, which ends with Llao's mountain falling in.
The Klamath Tribes say the story is their ancestors' memory of the eruption. Nobody can prove how old a spoken story is.
But someone was almost certainly there.

events.picturesWanted: Crater Lake from the air (Commons, `Aerial Crater Lake (cropped).jpg`; licence to check); a Fort Rock sandal (University of Oregon Museum of Natural and Cultural History; permission needed).
references: Charles Bacon and Marvin Lanphere, "Eruptive history and geochronology of Mount Mazama and the Crater Lake region, Oregon," *GSA Bulletin*, 2006. The mountain and the eruption.
Jonathan Egan, Richard Staff and Jeff Blackford, "A high-precision age estimate of the Holocene Plinian eruption of Mount Mazama, Oregon, USA," *The Holocene*, 2015. The date.
US Geological Survey, "Geology and history summary for Mount Mazama and Crater Lake" (usgs.gov). Height, collapse, depth.
Thomas Connolly, "Fort Rock sandals," *Oregon Encyclopedia* (oregonencyclopedia.org). The sandals and their dates.
Klamath Tribes News, "Crater Lake under federal management for 124 years," 4 May 2026. The Tribes' own account of giiwas and the story.

events.label: Green Sahara

place.name: Tassili n'Ajjer, southeast Algeria (25.50 N, 9.00 E); the milk was found at Takarkori, in the Acacus Mountains just across the border in Libya

events.summary: About 5000 BCE. The Sahara was grassland, with lakes and rivers. People there herded cattle, milked them, and painted them on the rocks. Over the next two thousand years the rains failed and the desert came.

paragraphs: On the walls of rock shelters in the Sahara Desert, there are paintings of cattle. Whole herds of them, with long curving horns. People walk among them.
The paintings are in Tassili n'Ajjer, a range of sandstone mountains in Algeria. Say "tah-SEE-lee nah-ZHAIR." Today it hardly ever rains there. Cattle could not live there.
So why are there cattle on the walls?

Because the Sahara was not always a desert. From about 15,000 years ago until about 5,500 years ago, the summer rains reached much farther north than they do now. The Sahara was grassland, with lakes, rivers and trees.

People herded cattle there, and painted them. But a painting on a rock is hard to date, so nobody knows exactly how old the cattle paintings are. Most are thought to be between about 7,000 and 3,000 years old.
A cooking pot is easier. And a pot remembers what was in it.

When food is cooked in a clay pot, a little of its fat soaks into the clay and stays there, for thousands of years. At Takarkori, a rock shelter in the next range of mountains, across the border in Libya, archaeologists found broken pots about 7,000 years old. Say "tah-kar-KOR-ee." In 2012 a team of chemists, led by Julie Dunne and Richard Evershed, tested the fat in those pots. Of the pots that still held animal fat from that time, about half had held milk.
So the people of the green Sahara did not keep cattle only for meat. About 7,000 years ago, they were milking them.

Then the rains moved south again. Some scientists think the change came quickly, over a few hundred years. Others think it came at different times in different places, later the farther south you go. Either way, the lakes dried up and the grass died, and the herders and their cattle moved away.
The paintings stayed where they were.

events.picturesWanted: a Tassili cattle painting (Commons, `Cave painting from the Tassili n'Ajjer mountains.jpg`; licence to check; avoid copies made in the 1950s, some of which are unreliable).
references: Julie Dunne, Richard Evershed and others, "First dairying in green Saharan Africa in the fifth millennium BC," *Nature*, 2012. The milk in the Takarkori pots.

Peter deMenocal and others, "Abrupt onset and termination of the African Humid Period: rapid climate responses to gradual insolation forcing," *Quaternary Science Reviews*, 2000. The green Sahara and its quick end.
Timothy Shanahan and others, "The time-transgressive termination of the African Humid Period," *Nature Geoscience*, 2015. The end coming later farther south.
David Coulson and Alec Campbell, *African Rock Art: Paintings and Engravings on Stone* (Abrams, 2001). The Tassili paintings and their uncertain dates.
UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Tassili n'Ajjer" (inscribed 1982).

events.label: Copper

place.name: Belovode, near Veliko Laole, eastern Serbia (44.32 N, 21.43 E, approximate)

events.summary: About 5000 BCE. At Belovode, in what is now Serbia, people heated green and black rocks in a fire until copper ran out of them. It is the oldest sure sign anyone has found of metal made from stone.

paragraphs: In the ground of a village called Belovode, in Serbia, archaeologists found small lumps of black, glassy stuff, none bigger than a grape. Say "BEH-loh-voh-deh."
The lumps are slag. Slag is what is left of a rock after metal has been melted out of it. These lumps are about 7,000 years old.
How do you get metal out of a rock?

Now and then, copper is found in the ground as metal, in lumps. People had been hammering lumps like that into beads for thousands of years. But most copper is not lying about as metal. It is locked inside rocks, often green or blue or black ones, mixed with other things.
To get it out, you heat the rock in a fire far hotter than a cooking fire, about 1,100 degrees. The copper runs out as tiny shining drops. What is left of the rock becomes slag.
But could the people of Belovode simply have melted down copper lumps they had found?

No. Miljana Radivojević and her colleagues looked at the slag under a microscope and tested what was in it. It held crystals that form only when rock is heated in this way. It also held other metals, such as manganese, that a lump of pure copper would not have. The people of Belovode had been getting copper out of stone.
Was this the first place anyone did it?

Nobody knows. When the results were published, in 2010, the Belovode slag was the oldest certain evidence of it anywhere. Some archaeologists think the idea was invented only once, in the Middle East, and that older evidence there will turn up. Others think people worked it out in several places, on their own.
One older claim, at Çatalhöyük in Turkey, was checked again in 2017. The "slag" there turned out to be green paint, made from a copper rock, that had melted by accident when a house burned down.
At Belovode, the fire was lit on purpose.

events.picturesWanted: malachite, the green copper ore, raw and polished (Commons, `Category:Malachite`; licence to check). No free image of the Belovode slag is known.
references: Miljana Radivojević, Thilo Rehren, Ernst Pernicka, Dušan Šljivar, Michael Brauns and Dušan Borić, "On the origins of extractive metallurgy: new evidence from Europe," *Journal of Archaeological Science*, 2010. The slag, the heat, and why it was smelting.
Benjamin Roberts, Christopher Thornton and Vincent Pigott, "Development of metallurgy in Eurasia," *Antiquity*, 2009. The case for a single invention.
Miljana Radivojević and others, "Repealing the Çatalhöyük extractive metallurgy: the green, the fire and the 'slag'," *Journal of Archaeological Science*, 2017. The burned house.
Bruce Bower, "Serbian site may have hosted first copper makers," *Science News*, 2010. The argument, in plain words.

events.label: Silk

place.name: Qingtai, Xingyang, Henan, China (34.8 N, 113.4 E, approximate)

events.summary: About 3500 BCE. In central China, people buried babies with cloth woven of silk. Burnt scraps of it are the oldest silk cloth yet found. Silk is a single thread, unwound from a caterpillar's cocoon.

paragraphs: In 1926, at a village called Xiyincun, in northern China, an archaeologist named Li Ji found half of a silkworm's cocoon. Say "shee-yin-TSWUN." Someone had cut it in half, cleanly, with a sharp edge, about 6,000 years before.
Nobody knows why.

A cocoon is made by a caterpillar called a silkworm. Before it turns into a moth, the caterpillar wraps itself in a thread that it makes inside its own body. The thread is finer than a hair, and it goes round and round. It is all one thread. Unwound, it can be several hundred metres long. A sticky gum holds the cocoon together.
To unwind it, you drop the cocoon into hot water. The gum softens, and the thread comes away in one long strand. Twist several strands together and you have thread strong enough to weave.
Who first did it, and when?

The oldest silk cloth anyone has found comes from Qingtai, in central China, from about 5,500 years ago. Say "ching-TIE." Babies who had died were buried there in large clay jars, and two scraps of silk cloth were found with them. The cloth is burnt black, but it is still woven cloth.

There are older traces. At Jiahu, also in central China, scientists tested soil from under the bodies in graves about 8,500 years old. Say "jyah-HOO." In two of the graves they found tiny traces of silk. There is no cloth left, only the stuff that silk is made of. Nobody can tell whether it came from wild silkworms or ones that people raised.

Wild silkworms still live in China. The silkworm that people raise is a different kind, bred from the wild one over thousands of years. Its moths cannot fly. Like the wild ones, they do not eat, and they live only long enough to lay eggs.
An old Chinese story says that silk was discovered by an empress named Leizu, when a cocoon fell into her cup of hot tea. It is a story.
Every silkworm moth that people raise depends on them. Not one of them can fly away.

events.picturesWanted: a silkworm cocoon, and silk being reeled from cocoons in hot water (Commons; licence to check).
references: Yuxuan Gong, Li Li, Decai Gong, Hao Yin and Juzhong Zhang, "Biomolecular evidence of silk from 8,500 years ago," *PLoS ONE*, 2016. Jiahu.
Xiyao Zhang and Xiaoming Yang, "Silk and silkworm: (re)discussion on the origin and early history of using silk fibres," *Asian Social Science*, 2024. Qingtai, Xiyincun, and what each shows.
Shelagh Vainker, *Chinese Silk: A Cultural History* (Rutgers University Press, 2004). Silk in China.
Food and Agriculture Organization, *Silk Reeling and Testing Manual*. Thread length and reeling.

events.label: Wheel

place.name: Bronocice, near Kraków, southern Poland (50.33 N, 20.33 E, approximate)

events.summary: About 3500 BCE. In what is now southern Poland, someone drew a wagon on a clay pot: a box, four wheels, and a pole to pull it by. It is one of the oldest pictures of a wheel anywhere.

paragraphs: A clay pot, found in southern Poland, has pictures scratched into its side. One of them is tiny and very simple: a box with a small circle at each corner, and a long line out in front.
It is a wagon, seen from above, with four wheels and a pole to hitch an animal to.
The pot was dug up at Bronocice, near the city of Kraków, in the 1970s. Say "bro-no-CHEE-tseh." It is about 5,500 years old. It is one of the oldest pictures of a wheel anywhere.
Where was the wheel invented?

Nobody knows. It seems to turn up in several places at once. Within a few hundred years of the Bronocice pot, there are signs for wagons on clay tablets from Uruk, in what is now Iraq. There are wheel ruts, two tracks side by side pressed into the ground, under an old grave mound in northern Germany. And in a marsh in Slovenia there is a real wheel.

The wheel from the marsh is made of two planks of ash wood, held together by cross-pieces. It is 72 centimetres across, about as tall as a table. Its axle, made of oak, was found too. The wheel was fixed tight to the axle, so wheel and axle turned together.
People had been making round things for thousands of years. So why did the wheel take so long?

Because the wheel is the easy part. The axle is hard. The archaeologist David Anthony points out that the axle, and the hole it turns in, have to be almost perfectly round and smooth, or they grind and stick. A thick axle rubs too much. A thin one breaks under the load. Getting it right takes careful woodwork.

So which came first: the drawing in Poland, the signs in Iraq, or the ruts in Germany? Archaeologists still argue. Some think the idea spread fast from one place. Others think more than one people worked it out.
The wheel from the marsh is in a museum in Ljubljana. It is more than 5,000 years old, and it still has its axle.

events.picturesWanted: the Bronocice pot and its wagon drawing (Commons, `Category:Bronocice pot`; licence to check); the Ljubljana Marshes wheel and axle (Commons, `Ljubljana Marshes Wheel with axle (oldest wooden wheel yet discovered).jpg`; licence to check).
references: J. A. Bakker, J. Kruk, A. E. Lanting and S. Milisauskas, "The earliest evidence of wheeled vehicles in Europe and the Near East," *Antiquity*, 1999. Bronocice, Uruk, and the wheel appearing in several places.
David W. Anthony, *The Horse, the Wheel, and Language* (Princeton University Press, 2007). Why the axle is the hard part.
Richard W. Bulliet, *The Wheel: Inventions and Reinventions* (Columbia University Press, 2016). The argument over where it began.
Kiel University, "3400 BC: The oldest evidence for the use of the wheel and wagon originates from Northern Germany" (news release, 2022). The Flintbek ruts.

events.label: Writing at Uruk

place.name: Uruk (now Warka), southern Iraq (31.32 N, 45.64 E)

events.summary: About 3300 BCE. In Uruk, in what is now Iraq, people began pressing signs into wet clay to keep track of barley, beer and sheep. It is one of the two oldest kinds of writing we know of.

paragraphs: A piece of clay about the size of a bar of soap has marks pressed into it. Some of the marks are round holes. Some are little wedges. One looks like a jar with a pointed bottom.
The round holes and wedges are numbers. The jar means beer.

This is some of the oldest writing in the world. It was found in the ruins of Uruk, a city in what is now southern Iraq, which about 5,300 years ago was one of the largest cities anywhere. Archaeologists have dug up about five thousand tablets like it there.
What did the first writers write about?

Mostly, things to count. How much barley came in. How much went out. How many sheep, how much beer, how many workers and how much each was paid. Almost every early tablet is a record of this kind. A few are lists of words, which may have been how the writers learned the signs.

The writer held a sharpened reed and pressed it into clay while the clay was still soft. Then the tablet dried hard. A dried tablet lasts a very long time, and if a building burns down around it, it bakes and lasts even longer.

Some tablets end with a sign that may be a person's name: Kushim. It appears on several records of barley. If it is a name, Kushim is one of the first people in history whose name we can read, and what we know about Kushim is that he or she was keeping accounts. But the sign may be a title instead of a name. Nobody is sure.
Over the next thousand years, the signs became wedge-shaped marks called cuneiform. Say "kyoo-NAY-i-form." People used them to write laws, letters, stories and poems.
It started with beer and barley.

events.picturesWanted: a proto-cuneiform tablet from Uruk showing number signs and the beer sign (British Museum, Metropolitan Museum, or the Schøyen Collection's Kushim tablet; licences to check).
references: Hans Nissen, Peter Damerow and Robert Englund, *Archaic Bookkeeping: Early Writing and Techniques of Economic Administration in the Ancient Near East* (University of Chicago Press, 1993). What the early tablets record.
Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (cdli.earth). Images and readings of Uruk tablets, including those naming Kushim.
Irving Finkel and Jonathan Taylor, *Cuneiform* (British Museum Press, 2015). How cuneiform grew from these signs.

events.label: Ötzi

place.name: the Tisenjoch pass, Ötztal Alps, on the border of Italy and Austria (46.78 N, 10.84 E)

events.summary: About 3300 BCE. A man died high in the Alps between what are now Italy and Austria. The ice kept his body, clothes and tools until two hikers found him in 1991.

paragraphs: In September 1991, two hikers crossing a pass high in the Alps saw a brown shape sticking out of melting ice. It was a man's head and shoulders. They thought he was a climber who had died a few years before.
He had died about 5,300 years before.
He is called Ötzi, after the Ötztal, the valley below. Say "UHT-see." The ice had kept not only his body but everything he carried. Nothing else like it has ever been found from that time.
What did a man carry, 5,300 years ago, on a walk through the mountains?

An axe with a blade of almost pure copper. A bow of yew wood, taller than he was, not yet finished. A quiver holding fourteen arrows, only two of them ready to shoot. A flint knife. A fur hat. Shoes with bearskin soles, stuffed with grass to keep his feet warm. A pouch with a fire-making kit.
Scientists could even tell what he last ate. His stomach held ibex meat and bread made from an early kind of wheat.
He was about forty-five years old. His skin carries sixty-one tattoos, made of short lines rubbed with charcoal. Most are on his back and legs, over places where his joints would have ached.

For ten years, everyone thought he had died of cold. Then, in 2001, an X-ray showed a stone arrowhead in his left shoulder. Someone had shot him from behind. He probably died soon after. Nobody knows who shot him, or why.
Ötzi is now in a museum in Bolzano, Italy. He is kept in a cold room, as cold as the glacier was, and visitors can look at him through a small window.

events.picturesWanted: the copper axe; the reconstructed shoe (South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology, which licenses images).
references: South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology, "Ötzi – the Iceman" (iceman.it). Finds, the cold room, the museum's own summary.

events.label: Caral

place.name: Caral, Supe Valley, Peru (10.89 S, 77.52 W)

events.summary: About 2600 BCE. In a desert valley in Peru, people built a city of stepped stone mounds and sunken plazas, about as old as Egypt's great pyramids. They made no pottery and left no writing. They left flutes.

paragraphs: More than thirty flutes, made from the bones of pelicans and condors, were found at Caral, in Peru. They are more than 4,000 years old.

Caral stands in the valley of the Supe River, about twenty-three kilometres inland from the Pacific coast. Say "kah-RAHL." Almost no rain falls there. The river comes down from the Andes mountains, and along its banks the valley is green.

The city had six great mounds, built in steps like pyramids, with flat tops and stairways. The biggest has a base longer than a football field. There were sunken round plazas, houses and workshops. Perhaps three thousand people lived there.
How do we know how old it is?

The builders filled the insides of their mounds with stones, carried in bags woven from reeds, and they left the bags in place. Reeds can be dated. In 2001 the archaeologist Ruth Shady, who began digging at Caral in 1994, published the dates with two colleagues, Jonathan Haas and Winifred Creamer. The oldest bags were about 4,600 years old. Caral was being built at about the same time as the great pyramids of Egypt, on the other side of the world.
Who were the people of Caral?

They grew cotton, squash and beans. Down on the coast, other people fished for anchovies and sardines. Shady thinks the two traded: the farmers gave cotton for fishing nets, and the fishers gave dried fish.

They made no pottery. No writing has been found. Shady has said she found a quipu, a bundle of knotted strings like those that people in the Andes used much later to keep records. She has not yet published it, so nobody else can judge.
No signs of war have been found at Caral, so far.
Someone carved the flutes and played them. Nobody knows what music they made.

events.picturesWanted: the main mound, the Pirámide Mayor (Commons, `Pirámide mayor de Caral.jpg`; licence to check); one of the flutes, if a free image exists.
references: Ruth Shady Solís, Jonathan Haas and Winifred Creamer, "Dating Caral, a preceramic site in the Supe Valley on the central coast of Peru," *Science*, 2001. The reed-bag dates.
Jonathan Haas, Winifred Creamer and Alvaro Ruiz, "Dating the Late Archaic occupation of the Norte Chico region in Peru," *Nature*, 2004. Many more dates across the valley.
UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Sacred City of Caral-Supe" (inscribed 2009). The six mounds and the site.
Guy Gugliotta, "The first city in the New World?", *Smithsonian Magazine*, August 2002. The flutes, the cotton and the fish.

events.label: Great Pyramid

place.name: Giza, near Cairo, Egypt (29.98 N, 31.13 E)

events.summary: About 2560 BCE. In Egypt, the Great Pyramid was finished as a tomb for King Khufu. It was the tallest thing people had built for almost 3,800 years. Some of the workers' own records survive.

paragraphs: On a sheet of papyrus, a kind of paper made from reeds, someone kept a diary. Day by day, it records a crew of about forty men loading blocks of white limestone onto a boat, carrying them along the Nile, and delivering them to a building site called the Horizon of Khufu.

The man who kept the diary was named Merer. Say "MEH-rer." He was the inspector in charge of the crew. His diary was found in 2013 by the archaeologist Pierre Tallet and his team, in caves near the Red Sea, where boats had once been stored. It is the oldest papyrus with writing on it that anyone has found.
The building site was the Great Pyramid.

It was built as a tomb for Khufu, a king of Egypt. Say "KOO-foo." It was made of about two million three hundred thousand blocks of stone, and it stood 146 metres high. For nearly 3,800 years, nothing people built anywhere was taller.
Who built it?

A Greek writer, Herodotus, who visited Egypt about two thousand years later, said that a hundred thousand men worked on it. Others have said they were slaves. What has been found since tells a different story.

In 1990 a tourist's horse stumbled on a buried mud-brick wall near the pyramids. Behind it was a cemetery for the workers, with hundreds of graves. Their bones show hard lives, and also care: broken arms and legs that had been set, and had healed.
Nearby, archaeologists have dug up a town where pyramid workers lived, with bakeries and the bones of the cattle, sheep and goats they ate.

How many workers were there? Estimates run from about ten thousand to forty thousand. Nobody knows exactly. Most archaeologists now think they were not slaves, but people working for the king for a time, in gangs with names like "Friends of Khufu".
Pieces of Merer's diary are now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.

references: Pierre Tallet and Mark Lehner, *The Red Sea Scrolls: How Ancient Papyri Reveal the Secrets of the Pyramids* (Thames & Hudson, 2021). Merer's diary.
Mark Lehner and Zahi Hawass, *Giza and the Pyramids: The Definitive Story* (Thames & Hudson, 2017). The pyramid, the workers' town and the cemetery.
Zahi Hawass, "The discovery of the tombs of the pyramid builders at Giza" (guardians.net/hawass, 1997). The 1990 discovery and the healed bones.
NOVA, "Who built the pyramids?" (pbs.org). The estimates of the workforce.

events.label: Mohenjo-daro

place.name: Mohenjo-daro, Sindh, Pakistan (27.33 N, 68.14 E)

events.summary: About 2500 BCE. In the valley of the Indus River, in what is now Pakistan, people built a city of brick with covered drains under its streets. Their writing has never been read.

paragraphs: Along a street of baked brick runs a drain. It is covered with more bricks, so the dirty water flows out of sight. Smaller drains come into it from the houses on each side. Many of the houses had a room with a brick floor for washing, and some had a toilet.
This was about 4,500 years ago.

The city is called Mohenjo-daro. Say "mo-HEN-jo DAH-ro." It stands beside the Indus River in what is now Pakistan. Tens of thousands of people may have lived there. Its streets were laid out in straight lines, and its bricks were made to the same proportions, as if everyone followed the same rules.
It was one of many cities along the Indus. They traded with cities as far away as Iraq.
So why don't we know more about them?
Because nobody can read what they wrote.

The people of the Indus carved signs on small square stones called seals, often above a picture of an animal. Thousands of seals have been found. There are about four hundred different signs. But most inscriptions are only four or five signs long, nobody knows what language they wrote, and no stone has been found with the same words in the Indus script and in a script we can read. Many people have claimed to read it. None has convinced the others.
So we can walk the streets of Mohenjo-daro and see how carefully it was built. We cannot read a single word its people left.
By about 1900 BCE, the city had been left empty, and nobody knows exactly why.
The seals are small enough to hold in your hand.

events.picturesWanted: a covered street drain at Mohenjo-daro; an Indus seal with a bull or "unicorn" and signs (National Museum of Pakistan, or Commons).
references: Jonathan Mark Kenoyer, *Ancient Cities of the Indus Valley Civilization* (Oxford University Press, 1998). The city, drains and seals.
Iravatham Mahadevan, *The Indus Script: Texts, Concordance and Tables* (Archaeological Survey of India, 1977). The count of signs and the length of inscriptions.
Andrew Robinson, *The Indus: Lost Civilizations* (Reaktion, 2015). Attempts at decipherment.
UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Archaeological Ruins at Moenjodaro." Site facts.

events.label: Campo del Cielo

place.name: Campo del Cielo, Chaco and Santiago del Estero provinces, Argentina (27.47 S, 60.58 W)

events.summary: About 2500 BCE. A mass of iron from space broke apart over what is now Argentina. Its pieces made a line of craters and left tonnes of iron in the ground.

paragraphs: In a field in northern Argentina lies a lump of metal as heavy as five elephants. It is dark and pitted, with smooth hollows like thumbprints. It is made of iron and nickel.
It came from space.

About 4,500 years ago, a mass of iron came down through the air over this plain. It broke apart as it fell. The pieces hit the ground along a line almost twenty kilometres long and made more than twenty craters. The biggest crater is more than a hundred metres across.
A piece of rock or metal from space that reaches the ground is called a meteorite. Iron meteorites are rare. Most meteorites that fall are stone.

The people who lived on the plain knew about the iron long before anyone wrote it down. In 1576, Spanish soldiers went looking for a great mass of iron that the local people used for their weapons. They found it. The Moqoit people, who still live there, call the place Piguen N'onaxa. The Spanish name, Campo del Cielo, means field of the sky.
How do we know when it fell?
Trees were burned when the pieces hit, and the charcoal has been dated. The dates cluster around 4,000 to 4,700 years ago. That is as close as anyone can get.

More than a hundred tonnes of the iron have been found, in pieces from the size of a pea to the size of a car. The largest, called Gancedo, weighs about thirty tonnes. It is the third-heaviest meteorite ever found.
The great irons still lie on the plain, and people can touch them.

events.picturesWanted: the El Chaco or Gancedo meteorite with people beside it for scale (Commons; licence to check).
references: William Cassidy, L. M. Villar, T. E. Bunch, T. P. Kohman and D. J. Milton, "Meteorites and craters of Campo del Cielo, Argentina," *Science*, 1965. The craters and the line they make.

events.label: Stonehenge

place.name: Stonehenge, Wiltshire, England (51.18 N, 1.83 W)

events.summary: About 2500 BCE. On a plain in southern England, people raised a ring of giant stones. The stones came from three places: a wood nearby, hills in Wales, and probably the far northeast of Scotland.

paragraphs: On a grassy plain in the south of England, a ring of huge grey stones stands against the sky. The tallest are higher than a two-storey house, and some pairs carry a third stone laid across their tops. This is Stonehenge. Its biggest stones were raised about 4,500 years ago.

Those big stones are called sarsens ("SAR-senz"). A typical one weighs about twenty tonnes, as much as three big elephants. In 2020 a team led by the geographer David Nash compared the chemistry of the stones with sarsen boulders from all over southern England, and found that most of the big stones match a single place, West Woods, about 25 kilometres to the north.
The smaller stones inside the ring, called bluestones, came much farther. They were brought from the Preseli Hills in Wales, about 230 kilometres away.

Then, in 2024, came a surprise. Deep inside the ring lies a flat stone of about six tonnes, called the Altar Stone. When scientists dated tiny mineral grains in chips of the stone, the grains matched rock in the far northeast of Scotland, more than 750 kilometres away. Some scientists have since questioned that, and the argument is not over.

How do you move a six-tonne stone 750 kilometres? Nobody knows. The people who built Stonehenge had no writing and left no record. Some think the Altar Stone came around the coast by boat; others think it was dragged over land on wooden sledges. Nobody knows, either, why anyone would bring stones so far when there was stone close at hand.

The builders did leave one clue to what they had in mind, because the stones are lined up with the Sun. On the longest day of the year, the Sun rises just to the left of a big stone outside the ring, called the Heel Stone. On the shortest day, the Sun once set between the two uprights of the tallest pair.
The Altar Stone from Scotland still lies in the middle of the ring, under two stones that fell from the tallest pair.

events.picturesWanted: Stonehenge from the air, showing the ring and the horseshoe (English Heritage or Commons; licence to check); the Altar Stone under the fallen stones (Commons; licence to check).
references: David Nash and others, "Origins of the sarsen megaliths at Stonehenge," *Science Advances*, 2020. West Woods; 50 of the 52 sarsens; their weights.
Mike Parker Pearson and others, "Megalith quarries for Stonehenge's bluestones," *Antiquity*, 2019. The Preseli outcrops and the distance.
Anthony Clarke and others, "A Scottish provenance for the Altar Stone of Stonehenge," *Nature*, 2024. The Altar Stone from northeast Scotland.

events.label: Enheduanna

place.name: Ur (Tell el-Muqayyar), southern Iraq (30.96 N, 46.10 E)

events.summary: About 2300 BCE. At Ur, in what is now Iraq, a king's daughter named Enheduanna was high priestess of the moon god. Poems copied centuries later carry her name. She may be the first author whose name we know.

paragraphs: A round stone about as wide as a dinner plate was dug up in pieces at Ur, in what is now southern Iraq. On one side, a row of people are carved making an offering. On the other side is writing that names Enheduanna ("en-hed-oo-AH-na"), daughter of King Sargon, and scholars think she is one of the people in the row.
Sargon had conquered all of southern Iraq and more, and he made his daughter high priestess of the moon god at Ur. She is remembered, though, for something else.
A collection of forty-two short hymns, one for each of the great temples of the land, ends with these lines:

paragraphs.quote: The compiler of the tablets was Enheduanna. My king, something has been created that no one has created before.

paragraphs: A longer poem is spoken in her own voice. In it, a man named Lugal-Ane has driven her out of her temple. "He made me fly like a swallow from the window," she says. By the end of the poem, the goddess Inanna is on her side again.

Did she write these poems? Nobody can be sure. Every copy we have was made about five hundred years after her lifetime, most of them by students practising their writing. Some scholars, such as William Hallo, take her name on the poems as a sign that she wrote them. Others think later writers put a famous name on the poems to make them grander.
If she did write them, she is the first author anywhere whose name we know. Older poems exist, but none of them carries an author's name.
The round stone has been put back together, and it is in a museum in Philadelphia, in the United States. Her name is still on it.

events.picturesWanted: the Disc of Enheduanna, both faces (Penn Museum, B16665; licence to check).
references: Penn Museum, "Disc of Enheduanna," object B16665 (collections.penn.museum). The disc, its size, its inscription.

Sophus Helle, *Enheduana: The Complete Poems of the World's First Author* (Yale University Press, 2023). The poems and the argument about authorship.

events.label: First alphabet

place.name: Serabit el-Khadim, Sinai, Egypt (29.04 N, 33.46 E)

events.summary: About 1850 BCE. At turquoise mines in Egypt's Sinai desert, people who did not write Egyptian borrowed a few Egyptian pictures and used each one for a single sound. Most alphabets used today come from their idea.

paragraphs: A little stone sphinx, a bit longer than a pencil, is kept at the British Museum in London. On its right shoulder is a line of Egyptian writing, made of tiny pictures, saying that the sphinx is "beloved of Hathor, mistress of turquoise." Hathor was an Egyptian goddess. On its left shoulder and its base are other marks. Some of them look like Egyptian pictures, but they are not Egyptian writing.
The sphinx was found at Serabit el-Khadim ("seh-RAH-beet el-KHAH-dim"), in the Sinai desert, where the kings of Egypt sent workers to dig turquoise, a blue-green stone.

In 1916 an Egyptologist named Alan Gardiner studied the strange marks and found a word in them. It was written with four signs, the first of them a house, and when he read the signs as sounds, they spelled the name of a goddess, Baalat, "the Lady."
How had pictures turned into sounds?

Egyptian writing used hundreds of signs. Some stood for whole words and some for sounds, and it took years to learn them all. The new writing kept only a couple of dozen pictures and used each one for the first sound of its name in the writers' own language. Their word for house began with the sound b, so a house stood for b. Their word for water began with m, so wavy water stood for m. With so few signs to learn, almost anyone could learn to write.

Who had the idea? The Egyptologist Orly Goldwasser thinks it was the workers at the mines, who could not read Egyptian. Others think the writers were people from Canaan, the land to the northeast, who worked alongside the Egyptians and knew something of their writing. Marks of the same kind, found beside a desert road in Egypt called Wadi el-Hol, may be just as old, and nobody knows for sure where it began.
Over many hundreds of years the signs changed shape again and again, as traders passed them along from one people to another. The house became the letter B on this page, and the water became M.

references: British Museum collection record, EA 41748 (britishmuseum.org). The sphinx, its size, its two inscriptions and its date.

Orly Goldwasser, "How the Alphabet Was Born from Hieroglyphs," *Biblical Archaeology Review*, 2010. The miners' idea.
