events.label: Thera

place.name: Thera (Santorini), in the Aegean Sea, Greece (36.40 N, 25.40 E)

events.summary: About 1600 BCE. The volcanic island of Thera, in the Aegean Sea, blew apart in one of the largest eruptions of the last ten thousand years. Its ash and waves reached Crete.

paragraphs: Today, big ships sail into a bay on the Greek island of Santorini and anchor in water hundreds of metres deep. Cliffs rise all around them, striped red, black and white.
The bay is the inside of a volcano.

About 3,600 years ago, the island, then called Thera, erupted. It threw out enough ash and rock to bury a large city many times over. When the eruption was over, the middle of the island had fallen in, and the sea poured into the hole.

People lived on Thera. Their town, now called Akrotiri, was buried in ash, and the ash kept it: houses two and three storeys high, with pictures painted on the walls of swallows, boys fishing and blue monkeys. Archaeologists have found almost no bodies there, and few valuable things. The people seem to have left in time. Where they went, nobody knows.
What happened to Crete?

Crete is a large island about 110 kilometres to the south. A people now called the Minoans lived there, in towns with great palaces. Ash from Thera fell on Crete. At Palaikastro, on Crete's eastern end, scientists have found a layer of sea sand, broken pottery and shells thrown far inland by a tsunami.

In 1939, a Greek archaeologist named Spyridon Marinatos suggested that the eruption destroyed the Minoans. It is a good story, and for a long time many people believed it. But digging since then shows that the Minoan palaces carried on for several generations after the eruption. They were hurt, but not destroyed. What finally ended them is still argued about.
Even the date is argued about. Some methods give about 1600 BCE. Others give about 1500. Scientists have been arguing for fifty years.
The ships anchor where the middle of the island used to be.

references: Sturt Manning, "Eruption of Thera/Santorini," in Eric Cline, ed., *The Oxford Handbook of the Bronze Age Aegean* (2010). The eruption and its date.

Hendrik Bruins and others, "Geoarchaeological tsunami deposits at Palaikastro (Crete) and the Late Minoan IA eruption of Santorini," *Journal of Archaeological Science*, 2008. The tsunami layer on Crete.
Spyridon Marinatos, "The volcanic destruction of Minoan Crete," *Antiquity*, 1939. The original theory.

events.label: Rhind papyrus

place.name: Thebes (Luxor), Egypt (25.70 N, 32.64 E)

events.summary: About 1550 BCE. In Egypt, a scribe named Ahmes copied out a scroll of arithmetic problems and their answers. It shows how Egyptians multiplied using nothing but doubling and adding.

paragraphs: A scroll of papyrus, a kind of paper made from reeds, is about five metres long. It begins with a promise: it will give "accurate reckoning for inquiring into things, and the knowledge of all things."
Then come more than eighty problems, with their answers.

The scribe who copied it wrote his name at the start: Ahmes. He says he copied it from an older scroll, written more than two hundred years before. That makes it one of the oldest books of mathematics in the world, and Ahmes one of the first people we know by name to have written mathematics down.
The problems are practical. How to share loaves of bread among ten men. How much grain fits in a round store. How steep to make the side of a pyramid.
How did an Egyptian scribe multiply?
By doubling. Suppose you want 13 times 12. Write 1 and 12. Double both: 2 and 24. Double again: 4 and 48. Again: 8 and 96. Stop there, because the next double, 16, is more than 13.
Now look down the left side for numbers that add up to 13. 1 and 4 and 8 make 13. Add the numbers beside them: 12 and 48 and 96. That makes 156, which is 13 times 12.

That is all there is to it. Nothing but doubling and adding, and no table of times to learn. It works for any two whole numbers, because every whole number can be made by adding some of 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and so on.
In 1858 a Scottish lawyer named Alexander Henry Rhind bought the scroll in Luxor. That is why it carries his name instead of the scribe's.
It is in the British Museum. At the very start of the scroll, the scribe's name is still there: Ahmes.

events.picturesWanted: a section of the papyrus (British Museum, EA 10057; licence to check).
references: Gay Robins and Charles Shute, *The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus: An Ancient Egyptian Text* (British Museum Press, 1987). The scroll, its problems and its methods.

Annette Imhausen, *Mathematics in Ancient Egypt: A Contextual History* (Princeton, 2016). Egyptian multiplication and who the scribes were.

events.label: Oldest song

place.name: Ugarit (Ras Shamra), on the coast of Syria (35.60 N, 35.78 E)

events.summary: About 1400 BCE. In the city of Ugarit, in what is now Syria, someone wrote a song on a clay tablet, with instructions for playing it. It is the oldest nearly complete written music we have.

paragraphs: A broken clay tablet has two parts, separated by a line. Above the line are the words of a song. Below the line are names and numbers.
The names and numbers are the music.

The tablet was found in the 1950s in the ruins of Ugarit, a port on the coast of what is now Syria. Say "OO-ga-rit." About 3,400 years ago, merchants there spoke and wrote in many languages. This song is in Hurrian, a language that is only partly understood today. It is a song to Nikkal, a goddess of orchards.

The instructions below the line are for a lyre. A lyre is a small stringed instrument, held in the arms. Its strings run from a sound box up to a crossbar. The instructions name pairs of strings, and each name is followed by a number. The names of the pairs are known from other tablets. So the tablet tells a player which strings to play, and something about how many times.
So what does it sound like?
That is the trouble. Nobody agrees.

We don't know how the lyre was tuned. We don't know whether each pair of strings was played together or one after the other. We don't know whether the numbers mean how many times to play, or something else. We don't know how the words fit the notes, or how fast it went.

Since the 1970s, several people have worked it out, each carefully, each in a different way. Their versions sound nothing alike. Some play the notes one after another, as a tune. Others play them two at a time.
Every recording you can find is someone's best guess.

references: Emmanuel Laroche, "Documents hourrites," in *Ugaritica V* (1968). First publication of the Hurrian songs.
Anne Draffkorn Kilmer, "The Cult Song with Music from Ancient Ugarit: Another Interpretation," *Revue d'Assyriologie*, 1974. One reconstruction.
Richard Dumbrill, *The Archaeomusicology of the Ancient Near East* (Trafford, 2005). Another reconstruction and a survey of the disagreements.
Martin West, "The Babylonian Musical Notation and the Hurrian Melodic Texts," *Music & Letters*, 1994. Why the readings differ.

events.label: Uluburun ship

place.name: Uluburun, near Kaş, southern Turkey (36.13 N, 29.68 E)

events.summary: About 1320 BCE. A ship sank off the south coast of Turkey carrying ten tonnes of copper and one tonne of tin. Melted together, they would have made eleven tonnes of bronze.

paragraphs: In 1982 a sponge diver named Mehmed Çakır came up from the sea floor off the south coast of Turkey. He said he had seen "metal biscuits with ears."
They were slabs of copper.

Archaeologists dived on the spot for eleven summers. The wreck lay more than forty metres down, so each dive was short, and they made more than twenty-two thousand of them. The ship had sunk about 3,300 years ago. It is called the Uluburun ship, after the cape where it lies. Say "oo-loo-boo-ROON."
It was carrying about ten tonnes of copper, in flat slabs with a stubby handle at each of the four corners. Those were the ears. And it was carrying about one tonne of tin.
Ten to one. That is the recipe for bronze.

Copper alone is soft. A copper blade bends and soon loses its edge. Melt about one part tin with ten parts copper and you get bronze, which is about twice as hard. It can be poured into a mould to make an axe, a sword, a pot or a statue. By the time this ship sailed, people had been making bronze for well over a thousand years.
So why carry the two metals separately?

Because they came from different places. Copper is found in many places. Tin is found in only a few. In 2022 scientists traced the ship's tin. About a third of it came from mines in what is now Uzbekistan, thousands of kilometres to the east. The rest came from Kestel, in Turkey.
The ship carried other things too: glass, ebony, ivory, amber from the shores of the Baltic Sea, and a small gold beetle with the name of Nefertiti, a queen of Egypt.
Nobody knows for certain where it was going, or who owned it.
The copper and the tin are in a museum in Bodrum, farther west along the same coast.

events.picturesWanted: an oxhide copper ingot from the wreck (Bodrum Museum of Underwater Archaeology or Institute of Nautical Archaeology; licence to check); a diver on the wreck (INA; permission needed).

events.label: Oracle bones

place.name: Yinxu, Anyang, Henan, China (36.13 N, 114.31 E)

events.summary: About 1200 BCE. At Anyang, in China, the kings of the Shang carved their questions to their ancestors on bones and turtle shells. The writing is already fully grown. Today's Chinese characters come straight down from it.

paragraphs: On the inside of a turtle's flat undershell, someone has cut neat rows of small hollows and scorched each one. On the outside, a crack runs from each scorched spot, and next to the cracks someone has carved a question: Will it rain? Will the harvest be good? Is one of the king's ancestors causing his toothache?

This is how the kings of the Shang asked their dead ancestors for advice, about 3,200 years ago, at Anyang ("AHN-yahng") in northern China. The king's diviners pressed something red-hot into the hollows until the shell or bone cracked, and read the answer in the cracks. Then the question was carved beside the cracks. The Chinese character for this kind of divining, 卜, still looks like one of those cracks.

Well over a hundred thousand pieces of these bones and shells have been found. Their writing uses four to five thousand different characters, of which scholars can read about a quarter with certainty. The characters used in China today come straight down from the ones on the bones.

Was this the beginning of Chinese writing? Almost certainly not. The writing on the bones is a full writing system, with thousands of signs used with ease, and writing like that takes a long time to grow.

So where is the earlier writing? One of the characters on the bones gives a clue. The character for a book, 册 ("tsuh"), is a picture of strips of bamboo or wood tied together with cord, and people wrote on such strips with a brush. In Iraq, people pressed their writing into clay, which lasts for thousands of years. Bamboo rots, so if the Shang wrote a great deal on it, we may never know.
Specialists agree that the Chinese invented their writing themselves. It was not borrowed from anywhere else.

For years, farmers near Anyang dug up the bones and sold them as "dragon bones," to be ground into medicine. In 1899 a scholar named Wang Yirong recognised the marks on them as ancient Chinese writing. How many questions were ground into medicine before then, nobody knows.

references: David N. Keightley, *Sources of Shang History: The Oracle-Bone Inscriptions of Bronze Age China* (University of California Press, 1978). How divination worked; 册 in the inscriptions.
William G. Boltz, "The invention of writing in China," *Oriens Extremus*, 2000/01. A fully developed system, invented in China.

Robert Bagley, "Anyang writing and the origin of the Chinese writing system," in Stephen Houston, ed., *The First Writing* (Cambridge University Press, 2004). Writing invented in China, before Anyang.
UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Yin Xu" (inscribed 2006). The site and its dates.

events.label: Olmec heads

place.name: San Lorenzo, Veracruz, Mexico (17.75 N, 94.76 W, approximate)

events.summary: Before 900 BCE. Near the Gulf coast of Mexico, a people we call the Olmec carved giant stone heads, each a different face in a different helmet. Nobody knows whose faces they are.

paragraphs: A stone face almost three metres tall looks out from a museum in Xalapa ("hah-LAH-pah"), in Mexico. It weighs about twenty-five tonnes. It has full cheeks, a broad, flat nose and thick lips, and it wears a close-fitting helmet.

Sixteen more heads like it have been found, seventeen in all, at four places near the Gulf of Mexico. Each has a different face, and each wears a different helmet with its own pattern. The smallest weighs about six tonnes and the biggest about forty.

They were made by a people we call the Olmec ("OHL-mek"), though that is not their own name. "Olmec" is a word from Nahuatl, the Aztecs' language, meaning "rubber people," which the Aztecs, more than two thousand years later, used for the people living near that coast in their own time. Nobody knows what the people who carved the heads called themselves.
The heads at San Lorenzo, the oldest of the four places, had been buried by about 900 BCE, so they were carved before then.

How were they moved? Most of the heads were carved from single boulders of basalt, a hard, dark volcanic rock, and the boulders came from the Tuxtla Mountains, a long way from where the heads were found. The Olmec had no horses or oxen to pull loads, and no wagons. Many archaeologists think they dragged the boulders to the rivers and floated them on rafts, but nobody knows for sure.

Whose faces are they? Most archaeologists think they are rulers. Some of the heads seem to have been carved from older stones, huge carved blocks that may have been thrones, and an archaeologist named James Porter has suggested that when a ruler died, his throne was carved into his face. That is a guess.
Seventeen faces, and not one name.

events.picturesWanted: San Lorenzo Head 1 (Museo de Antropología de Xalapa; Commons; licence to check); two heads side by side to show the different helmets.
references: Richard A. Diehl, *The Olmecs: America's First Civilization* (Thames & Hudson, 2004). The heads, the sites, the dates.
Christopher A. Pool, *Olmec Archaeology and Early Mesoamerica* (Cambridge University Press, 2007). The heads and the stone they came from.
James B. Porter, "Olmec colossal heads as recarved thrones: 'mutilation,' revolution, and recarving," *RES: Anthropology and Aesthetics*, 1989. The throne idea.
Norman Hammond, "The Cobata colossal head: an unfinished Olmec monument?", *Antiquity*, 2001. The largest head.

events.label: Nok heads

place.name: the Nok region, Kaduna State, central Nigeria (9.50 N, 8.00 E)

events.summary: From about 900 BCE. In what is now central Nigeria, people made life-size clay heads with carefully shaped eyes and hair. They are among the oldest large sculptures from Africa south of the Sahara.

paragraphs: A clay head, about as big as a real one, looks straight ahead. Its eyes are shaped like triangles, with a hole in the middle of each for the pupil. Its hair is piled up in neat rolls and buns. Someone spent a long time on it.
It is between two and three thousand years old.

In 1943, men digging for tin near the village of Nok, in central Nigeria, found a clay head in the gravel. A clerk at the mine took it home and used it as a scarecrow in a yam field for a year. Then a young archaeologist named Bernard Fagg saw it. Since then, hundreds of heads and parts of figures have been found across the region.
Nok is the name of the village. It is not the name of the people who made the heads.
What do we know about them?

They farmed pearl millet and cowpeas. They were among the first people in West Africa to make iron, heating rock in clay furnaces until the metal ran out. Their figures were hollow, built up from coils of clay and then carved, with walls thin enough to fire without cracking. Almost none has been found whole.

Most of what we don't know was lost more recently. For fifty years, Nok figures have been dug up and sold to collectors. When a figure is pulled out of the ground in a hurry, nobody writes down where it was, what lay beside it, or how deep it was buried. The figure survives. The answers to how it was used do not.
Were the heads portraits? Were they made for the dead? Nobody knows.
Nobody knows what the people who made them called themselves.

events.picturesWanted: a Nok head with the triangular eyes (National Commission for Museums and Monuments, Nigeria; Commons; check that any image shown is of a documented piece).
references: Bernard Fagg, *Nok Terracottas* (Ethnographica, 1977). The first finds and the scarecrow.
Peter Breunig and Nicole Rupp, "An outline of recent studies on the Nigerian Nok Culture," *Journal of African Archaeology*, 2016. Dates, farming and iron.
Peter Breunig, ed., *Nok: African Sculpture in Archaeological Context* (Africa Magna Verlag, 2014). How the figures were made.
Gabriele Franke, "A chronology of the Central Nigerian Nok Culture," *Journal of African Archaeology*, 2016. The dates.

events.label: Iron

place.name: Tell Hammeh, Jordan Valley, Jordan (32.2 N, 35.6 E, approximate), where early iron-making waste has been dated

events.summary: About 900 BCE. Around the eastern Mediterranean, making iron became common. Copper and tin, the metals of bronze, are rare. Iron is in rock almost everywhere. Metal no longer had to come from far away.

paragraphs: In the tomb of Tutankhamun ("toot-ahnk-AH-mun"), a young king of Egypt who died about 3,350 years ago, lay a dagger with a gold handle and a blade of iron. The iron came from the sky. In 2016 scientists found nickel and cobalt in the blade, mixed with the iron the way they are mixed in meteorites, which are pieces of rock or metal from space that have reached the ground. In the young king's time iron was a treasure, and kings sent gifts of it to other kings.
About four hundred years later, at a place called Tell Hammeh in the Jordan Valley, people were making iron so often that they left heaps of waste behind. What had changed?

Not the iron. Iron is one of the most common things in the ground. About one twentieth of the Earth's rocky crust is iron, and it is what makes many rocks and soils red or brown. Copper is about a thousand times rarer, and tin more than twenty thousand times rarer.

That mattered, because for many centuries the best tools had been made of bronze, which is copper with a little tin. Tin is found in only a few places, so bronze-makers depended on traders who brought it from far away.

What changed was that people learned how to get iron out of rock. They heated the rock with charcoal in a small clay furnace. The iron did not melt. Instead it gathered into a glowing, spongy lump full of glassy waste, and the smith beat the lump with a hammer, again and again, to drive the waste out. Once people knew how to do it, a village could make its own metal from rock nearby, without waiting for tin from the far end of a trade route.
Was iron better than bronze? Not at first. Plain iron is no harder than good bronze, and smiths had to learn to turn it into steel and harden it before it was.
Tutankhamun's dagger is in the Grand Egyptian Museum, near Cairo. Its blade has hardly rusted.

events.picturesWanted: Tutankhamun's iron dagger (Egyptian Museum, Cairo or Grand Egyptian Museum; licence to check); a lump of iron ore beside a bloom (Commons; licence to check).
references: Nathaniel Erb-Satullo, "The innovation and adoption of iron in the ancient Near East," *Journal of Archaeological Research*, 2019. When iron became common, why, how hard it was, and the Hittite myth.
Daniela Comelli and others, "The meteoritic origin of Tutankhamun's iron dagger blade," *Meteoritics & Planetary Science*, 2016. Nickel and cobalt in the blade.

Harald Alexander Veldhuijzen and Thilo Rehren, "Slags and the city: early iron production at Tell Hammeh, Jordan, and Tel Beth-Shemesh, Israel," in Susan La Niece, Duncan Hook and Paul Craddock, eds., *Metals and Mines: Studies in Archaeometallurgy* (Archetype and the British Museum, 2007), pp. 189–201. The waste at Tell Hammeh and its date.
Historical Metallurgy Society, "Bloomery" (historicalmetallurgy.org). How the furnace worked.

events.label: Lapita voyagers

place.name: Nukuleka, Tongatapu, Tonga (21.13 S, 175.15 W)

events.summary: About 850 BCE. Sailors from the islands near New Guinea, whose pottery is called Lapita, reached Tonga, in the middle of the Pacific. No human had ever set foot there before.

paragraphs: A piece of broken pottery lies on a beach in Tonga. Its surface is covered with fine patterns: rows of tiny dots, pressed into the wet clay with a toothed stamp before it was fired.
Pottery with these patterns has been found on islands across more than four thousand kilometres of the Pacific.

It is called Lapita pottery, after a beach in New Caledonia where it was dug up in 1952. The people who made it lived at first on the islands near New Guinea. Then, a little more than three thousand years ago, they began to sail east.

East of the Solomon Islands, the islands get farther apart. Before then, people had crossed plenty of sea, but usually with the next island in sight or nearly so. The Lapita sailors went where no land could be seen, and kept going. From Vanuatu to Fiji is about 850 kilometres of open water.
How do you find an island you have never seen?

Nobody knows exactly how the Lapita sailors did it. Later Pacific navigators found their way by the stars, the shape of the waves, the clouds that gather over land, and birds that fly out to fish and back to land at night. The Lapita sailors probably knew some of the same things.
They did not travel light. They brought pigs, dogs and chickens, and plants to grow: taro, yams, breadfruit. Everywhere they landed, they were the first people ever to live there.
About 2,850 years ago they reached Tonga. At a place called Nukuleka, archaeologists have found some of the oldest Lapita pottery in Tonga, dated by the coral tools buried with it.
Their descendants kept sailing. Over the next two thousand years, they reached Hawaii, New Zealand and Easter Island.

events.picturesWanted: a Lapita pot or sherd with dentate stamping (Commons; museum sources in Fiji, Vanuatu or New Caledonia).
references: Patrick Kirch, *On the Road of the Winds: An Archaeological History of the Pacific Islands* (University of California Press, 2nd ed., 2017). The Lapita spread.
David Burley and others, "High precision U/Th dating of first Polynesian settlement," *PLoS ONE*, 2012. Nukuleka and its date.
Geoffrey Irwin, *The Prehistoric Exploration and Colonisation of the Pacific* (Cambridge, 1992). Navigation and why the sailors went east.

events.label: Greek alphabet

place.name: Eretria, Euboea, Greece (38.39 N, 23.79 E), where some of the oldest Greek letters have been found. The wine jug in the More is from Athens.

events.summary: About 775 BCE. Greeks borrowed the alphabet of the Phoenicians, traders from what is now Lebanon. Phoenician letters had none for vowels, so the Greeks made some. Within fifty years, Greeks were scratching verses onto cups and jugs.

paragraphs: Around the shoulder of a wine jug found in a graveyard in Athens, someone has scratched a line of writing. It runs from right to left, the letters face backwards, and it says:

paragraphs.quote: Whoever of all these dancers now dances most gracefully…

paragraphs: Then it breaks off. The jug was probably a prize. It was made about 2,760 years ago, and its line is one of the oldest pieces of writing in the Greek alphabet.

The Greeks got their letters from the Phoenicians ("fuh-NEE-shunz"), traders and sailors from the coast of what is now Lebanon, whose letters had come down from the alphabet of the turquoise mines in Egypt. Greek writers, such as the historian Herodotus, called their letters "Phoenician letters."

But the Greeks had a problem. Phoenician letters were all consonants, sounds like b, d, k and m, with no letters for vowels like a, e and o. A Phoenician reader filled in the vowels from knowing the language, and a Greek reader could not do that so easily. Phoenician, though, also had some sounds that Greek did not use, so the Greeks had letters to spare, and they used the spare letters for vowels.

The first Phoenician letter, aleph, stood for a catch in the throat, like the stop in the middle of "uh-oh." The Greeks used it for the sound a and called it alpha, and in the same way other spare letters became e, i, o and u.

Who did this, and where? Nobody knows exactly. Many scholars think it happened on the island of Euboea ("yoo-BEE-uh"), at towns like Eretria ("eh-RET-ree-uh"), where some of the oldest Greek letters have been found. Some scholars think the vowels were invented only once, and copied everywhere from there.
Within fifty years, Greeks were scratching their names, boasts and jokes onto cups.
Alpha and beta, the first two Greek letters, gave us the word alphabet, and alpha became the A on this page.

events.picturesWanted: the Dipylon jug and its inscription (National Archaeological Museum, Athens, inv. 192; Commons; licence to check); a chart of aleph to alpha to A (to be drawn for CW).
references: John K. Papadopoulos, "The early history of the Greek alphabet: new evidence from Eretria and Methone," *Antiquity*, 2016. The date, Eretria, and vowels invented once.
Herodotus, *Histories*, Book 5, section 58. The Greeks calling their letters "Phoenician letters."
Barry B. Powell, *Homer and the Origin of the Greek Alphabet* (Cambridge University Press, 1991). Early Greek inscriptions, including the Dipylon jug.
National Archaeological Museum, Athens, the Dipylon oinochoe, inv. 192. The jug.

events.label: Assyrian eclipse

place.name: northern Assyria; Nineveh marks it (36.36 N, 43.15 E). The revolt in the same line was at Ashur (35.46 N, 43.26 E).

events.summary: 15 June 763 BCE. In Assyria, in what is now northern Iraq, the Moon covered the Sun. Scribes wrote it in their list of years. That one line puts dates on about three hundred years of Assyrian history.

paragraphs: A clay tablet holds a list of years. In Assyria, a year did not have a number; it had a name. Each year was named after an important official, and scribes kept long lists of the names, in order, with a few words about what happened in each year. One line reads:

paragraphs.quote: Bur-Sagale, governor of Guzana: revolt in the city of Ashur. In the month of Simanu, an eclipse of the Sun.

paragraphs: Bur-Sagale ("boor-sah-GAH-lay") was the official. Ashur was a city of Assyria, in what is now northern Iraq, and Simanu was a month in late spring and early summer.

An eclipse of the Sun happens when the Moon moves in front of it, and the Moon and the Earth move so regularly that astronomers can work out every eclipse there has ever been, and where its shadow fell. In 1867 a British scholar named Henry Rawlinson, who had helped work out how to read Assyrian writing, looked for an eclipse that would fit, and found one. On 15 June 763 BCE, late in the morning, the shadow of the Moon crossed northern Assyria, and along its path the day went dark.

Why does one line matter so much? Because the list is a chain, and once one link is fixed, the rest follow. If Bur-Sagale's year was 763 BCE, then the next year on the list was 762 BCE, the one after that 761, and so on, name after name, forwards and backwards. The list covers about three hundred years, and the eclipse gives a date to almost every one of them. Without it, the names would still be in order, but nobody could say when any of them was.
There is a check. A completely different list, of the kings of Babylon, kept much later by a Greek astronomer named Ptolemy, gives the same years for the kings who appear on both lists.
The eclipse that stopped a battle beside the Halys River, 178 years later, was dated the same way, by working backwards from the sky.

events.picturesWanted: a tablet of the eponym list (British Museum; licence to check); a map of the eclipse's path over northern Iraq (from the NASA eclipse catalogue, public domain, redrawn for CW).
references: Henry Rawlinson, "The Assyrian canon verified by the record of a solar eclipse, B.C. 763," *The Athenaeum*, no. 2064, 18 May 1867, pp. 660–661. The identification.
Alan Millard, *The Eponyms of the Assyrian Empire 910–612 BC* (State Archives of Assyria Studies 2, Helsinki, 1994; online at oracc.museum.upenn.edu). The list and the line quoted.
NASA Eclipse Web Site, "Total solar eclipse of −762 June 15" (eclipse.gsfc.nasa.gov). The path and the time.
F. Richard Stephenson, *Historical Eclipses and Earth's Rotation* (Cambridge University Press, 1997). How ancient eclipses are dated.

events.label: Homer written down

place.name: Greece; the exact place is unknown (38.0 N, 23.7 E marks Athens, where a written version is later reported)
place.note: marks Athens, where a written version is later reported

events.summary: 700s or 600s BCE. Homer is thought to have been a travelling poet who recited stories about the Trojan War. Around this time, his stories were first written down.

paragraphs: A long poem called the Iliad tells about a few weeks near the end of a war at a city called Troy. It is more than fifteen thousand lines long. Another, the Odyssey, tells about a soldier's ten-year journey home from that war. It is about twelve thousand lines.
For a long time, nobody wrote them down.

The Greeks said both poems were made by a poet called Homer. Nobody knows who Homer was, when he lived, or whether he was one person. What seems likely is that poems like these were sung by travelling poets, who performed them from memory to anyone who would listen.
How could anyone remember fifteen thousand lines?

In the 1930s, an American scholar named Milman Parry went to the mountains of what was then Yugoslavia. There he met singers who could not read or write, and who sang long poems about old wars, some as long as the Odyssey. They did not memorise the words exactly. They knew thousands of ready-made phrases and scenes, and they rebuilt the poem each time they sang it. The Iliad is full of the same kind of phrases: "rosy-fingered dawn," "swift-footed Achilles."
The Greeks had begun writing with an alphabet not long before, around 800 BCE. At some point in the next two hundred years, someone wrote the poems down. Nobody knows who, or exactly when.

That first written copy is lost. The oldest pieces we have were found in Egypt, on scraps of papyrus about four hundred years younger. The oldest complete copy of the Iliad was made about 1,200 years after that, in the 900s.
It is in a library in Venice.

events.picturesWanted: a page of the Venetus A manuscript (Biblioteca Marciana, Venice; Homer Multitext images are CC BY-NC-SA, non-commercial only).
references: Milman Parry, *The Making of Homeric Verse: The Collected Papers of Milman Parry*, ed. Adam Parry (Oxford, 1971). The singers and the phrases.
Albert Lord, *The Singer of Tales* (Harvard, 1960). Parry's work with the singers, written up by his assistant.
Barry Powell, *Homer and the Origin of the Greek Alphabet* (Cambridge, 1991). The alphabet and when the poems could have been written.
The Homer Multitext project (homermultitext.org). The Venetus A manuscript.

events.label: Jerwan aqueduct

place.name: Jerwan, Duhok province, Kurdistan Region of Iraq (36.67 N, 43.38 E, approximate)

events.summary: About 690 BCE. In what is now northern Iraq, the Assyrian king Sennacherib built a stone bridge to carry a canal of water across a valley, on its way to his capital city, Nineveh.

paragraphs: In a valley in the hills of northern Iraq, a long, broken wall of cut stone runs across the fields. It is about 280 metres long and 22 metres wide, and where it crossed a stream it once stood about nine metres high, with the stream running under it through pointed arches. On top of the wall ran water.

It is a bridge built to carry a canal, at a place called Jerwan ("jer-WAHN"). A channel built to carry water a long way is called an aqueduct. Most of this one ran along the ground, but at Jerwan, where it had to cross a valley, it ran on top of the bridge.

Who built it? His name is on it. Some of the blocks are carved with his words: "I had an aqueduct of white stone blocks made." The king was Sennacherib ("seh-NAK-er-ib"), who ruled Assyria about 2,700 years ago from his capital, Nineveh, a city beside the Tigris River. He wanted more water for the fields and meadows around Nineveh, so he had canals dug from the hills to the north to bring the water of mountain streams to the city. One of them ran about 95 kilometres, from a gorge called Khinis to Nineveh, and the bridge at Jerwan carried it across the valley.

How much stone did it take? In 1933 two archaeologists working for the Oriental Institute in Chicago, Thorkild Jacobsen and Seton Lloyd, dug the bridge out and guessed that it was built of more than two million blocks. In 2014 two other scholars worked it out again, more carefully, and arrived at about 440,000. Each block weighed about as much as three grown men, and someone had to cut every one of them, carry it, and set it in place.
It is one of the oldest bridges for water known anywhere. Parts of it still stand, and some of the blocks still carry the king's words.

events.picturesWanted: the Jerwan aqueduct today (Commons or the Land of Nineveh Archaeological Project; licence to check); an inscribed block.
references: Thorkild Jacobsen and Seton Lloyd, *Sennacherib's Aqueduct at Jerwan* (Oriental Institute Publications 24, University of Chicago Press, 1935; free at isac.uchicago.edu). The 1933 dig and the first estimate.

Frederick Mario Fales and Roswitha Del Fabbro, "Back to Sennacherib's aqueduct at Jerwan: a reassessment of the textual evidence," *Iraq* 76, 2014, pp. 65–98. The size, the new count, the inscription.
John MacGinnis, Daniele Morandi Bonacossi and Jason Ur, "Divine channels: rediscovering the canal networks of the Assyrian Empire," *ANE Today*, October 2021 (anetoday.org). The length of the canal.

events.label: Nineveh's library

place.name: Nineveh (Kuyunjik), Mosul, Iraq (36.36 N, 43.15 E)

events.summary: About 650 BCE. At Nineveh, in what is now Iraq, King Ashurbanipal, who could read, gathered tens of thousands of clay tablets: stories, medicine, omens and word lists. Thousands survived the city's destruction, broken into pieces.

paragraphs: In 1872, at the British Museum in London, a broken clay tablet lay half hidden under a thick, hard crust. When the crust was cleaned away, the writing underneath told of a great flood: a man builds a boat, fills it with animals and rides out the storm, then sends out birds to look for dry land. The first person in more than two thousand years to read it was George Smith, an assistant at the museum who had trained as a banknote engraver and taught himself to read the old writing. The tablet was part of a long poem now called the Epic of Gilgamesh.
A story told years later says Smith was so excited that he began to take his clothes off. The man who told the story was not there.

The tablet had come from Nineveh ("NIN-eh-vuh"), in what is now northern Iraq. About 2,700 years ago Nineveh was the capital of Assyria, and its king was Ashurbanipal ("ah-shoor-BAH-nee-pahl"). Few kings could read. Ashurbanipal could, and he boasted about it, saying that he had learned "the hidden secret of all scribal art" and had looked at writing "on stones from before the flood."

He wanted every tablet worth having. His men went to the cities of his empire, copying tablets and carrying them off, and they brought back hymns, medicine, word lists, stories, and books of omens, which told what the stars, or the liver of a sheep, said about the future. Many of the tablets are stamped with his name.

In 612 BCE, about twenty years after he died, armies of the Babylonians and the Medes captured Nineveh and burned it. Nobody recorded how many people died, and within a few years Assyria was gone. When the palace walls fell in on the tablets, the fire baked some of them harder, and many were smashed.
Archaeologists began digging up the pieces in 1849, and the British Museum now has more than thirty thousand of them. Scholars are still fitting them together.

events.picturesWanted: the Flood Tablet, Gilgamesh Tablet XI (British Museum, K.3375; licence to check); a tablet with Ashurbanipal's library stamp.
references: Jonathan Taylor, "A library fit for a king," British Museum blog, 25 October 2018. The discovery, the stamp, the contents, the fire.
Grant Frame and A. R. George, "The royal libraries of Nineveh: new evidence for King Ashurbanipal's tablet collecting," *Iraq*, 2005. How the tablets were gathered.

Jamie Novotny and Joshua Jeffers, *The Royal Inscriptions of Ashurbanipal, Aššur-etel-ilāni, and Sîn-šarra-iškun, Kings of Assyria*, part 1 (Eisenbrauns, 2018); and Joshua Jeffers and Jamie Novotny, part 2 (Eisenbrauns, 2023). His inscriptions; the boast (K 2694 + K 3050) is in part 2.
Ashurbanipal Library Project, British Museum and Oracc (oracc.museum.upenn.edu/asbp). The count of tablets and fragments.

events.label: First coins

place.name: Sardis, Lydia, western Turkey (38.49 N, 28.04 E). The oldest coins were found at Ephesus (37.95 N, 27.36 E).

events.summary: About 610 BCE. In Lydia, a kingdom in what is now western Turkey, someone began stamping small lumps of gold and silver with a lion's head. They are among the oldest coins anyone has found.

paragraphs: A lump of pale yellow metal, about as big as a lentil, has a lion's head stamped on one side, with its mouth open. On the other side there is only a plain dent, where a punch struck it. It is a coin, one of the oldest anyone has found. It was dug up, with ninety-two others, at the ruins of the temple of Artemis at Ephesus, on the west coast of Turkey, where the coins had been buried more than 2,600 years ago.

Many of the coins, including the lion coins, were made in Lydia ("LID-ee-uh"), a kingdom next door, from electrum, a mixture of gold and silver found in nature in the rivers of Lydia. A few of them carry a word in the Lydian language, walwet, which many scholars think is the name of a king, Alyattes ("al-ee-AT-eez"). He was the king who made peace after an eclipse stopped a battle in 585 BCE.

Before coins, people paid with metal by weighing it, every time. The lion changed that. It said that the piece came from the king and was worth a fixed amount, so nobody had to weigh it. The coins came in fixed sizes, the smallest about as big as a peppercorn.

The stamp did something else as well. When the coins were tested, they turned out to hold less gold than the natural metal from the rivers. The coins were worth what the stamp said, not what was in them, and the king kept the difference.

Later a Lydian king, Croesus ("KREE-sus"), began to make coins of pure gold and of pure silver, and the Greek historian Herodotus wrote that the Lydians were the first people to make coins of gold and silver.
At about the same time, people in China were making coins of their own, in bronze, shaped like little spades. There is no sign that either people knew about the other.

events.picturesWanted: a Lydian electrum coin with the lion's head (British Museum or the Sardis Expedition; licence to check); a Chinese spade coin (Commons; licence to check).
references: John H. Kroll, "The coins of Sardis," Sardis Expedition essay (sardisexpedition.org). The Ephesus coins, their weights and gold, walwet, and the first gold and silver coins.
Robert W. Wallace, "The origin of electrum coinage," *American Journal of Archaeology*, 1987. Why the stamp mattered when the gold in electrum varies.
Herodotus, *Histories*, Book 1, sections 74 and 94. Alyattes and the eclipse; the Lydians as the first to coin gold and silver.
Hao Zhao and others, "Radiocarbon-dating an early minting site: the emergence of standardised coinage in China," *Antiquity*, 2021. The spade coins.

events.label: Eclipse battle

place.name: the Halys river (now the Kızılırmak), central Turkey. The battlefield itself is not known.

events.summary: 28 May 585 BCE. During a battle between two kings in what is now Turkey, the Moon covered the Sun and the day went dark. The armies stopped fighting, and the kings made peace.

paragraphs: Two armies were fighting beside a river in what is now Turkey when darkness fell. It was evening, but the Sun had not yet set. The day had turned into night.

The cause was an eclipse. In this case, the Moon moved in front of the Sun. That cast the Moon's shadow on parts of the Earth, including the battlefield. When the Moon covers the whole Sun, stars come out and birds go silent.
Probably no one in either army knew why the Sun seemed to go out, but the sudden and mysterious darkness stopped the fighting.

The armies belonged to two kings. Alyattes ruled the Lydians, to the west of the river. Cyaxares ruled the Medes, to the east. They had been at war for five years. This was the sixth. No one knows how many soldiers died in those wars or what the fighting cost.

The eclipse ended the fighting that day, and soon afterwards the two kings made peace. The river, called the Halys, became the border between their kingdoms, and a daughter of Alyattes married a son of Cyaxares.

We know about the battle from Herodotus, a Greek historian who wrote a long history about 150 years later. Herodotus also says that a man named Thales had told the Greeks the eclipse would come that year. Most people who study this doubt it. In Thales's time nobody knew how to work out when an eclipse would happen.

We know the day all this happened, though Herodotus did not tell us. The date comes from the sky. The Moon and the Earth move so regularly that astronomers can work backwards and find every eclipse that ever crossed that part of the world. Only one fits: 28 May 585 BCE, in the evening.
The battle is often called the earliest event in history whose exact day we know.

events.picturesWanted: a photograph of a total eclipse of the Sun; a map of the eclipse's path across Anatolia, if a good one with a clear licence exists.
references: Herodotus, *Histories*, Book 1, section 74 (about 430 BCE). The only ancient account. Free online at the Perseus Digital Library.
F. Richard Stephenson, *Historical Eclipses and Earth's Rotation* (Cambridge University Press, 1997). Dating ancient eclipses, and why the Earth's slowing spin matters.

events.label: Pythagoras

place.name: Crotone, Calabria, Italy (39.08 N, 17.13 E)

events.summary: About 530 BCE. A man named Pythagoras moved from the Greek island of Samos to Croton, in southern Italy, and gathered followers. He left no writings that we know of. What he actually discovered, nobody knows for sure.

paragraphs: We think Pythagoras ("pih-THAG-or-us") was born on the Greek island of Samos about 570 BCE, and that when he was about forty he moved to Croton, a Greek city on the coast of southern Italy. There he gathered followers and gave them rules: don't eat beans, never walk on the public roads. He taught that after death, a person's soul is born again in another person or an animal.
Things like these, not mathematics, made him famous in his own time.
He wrote no books that we know of. The fullest accounts of his life were written about eight hundred years after he died, and by then he had become a legend.

One old story tells that he was walking past a blacksmith's shop when he heard the hammers ringing out musical notes. He went in to look, and found that the notes depended on how heavy the hammers were. Hammers don't actually work that way, so the story can't be quite right. But the idea behind it is true, and it is easiest to hear with strings.

If you stretch a string tight and pluck it, it shakes the air around it, and you hear a note. A second string, the same in every way but half as long, shakes twice as fast. Its note is an octave higher than the first, and the two blend perfectly. A string two thirds as long also blends well with the first string, and so does one three quarters as long. Pluck the first string, the half string and the two-thirds string together, and you hear a chord. A great deal of music is built on those simple fractions.
Pythagoras's followers wrote these fractions down. The first one known to have done it was Philolaus ("fil-oh-LAY-us"), who lived about a hundred years after Pythagoras.
Did Pythagoras find these fractions himself? Nobody knows for sure. He became a legend in Greece, and the trouble with legends is that you never know when to believe them.

events.picturesWanted: a single string held at its middle (to be drawn for CW; a live version belongs with the Sound lab); the coast at Crotone (Commons; licence to check).
references: Carl Huffman, "Pythagoras," *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy* (revised 2024; plato.stanford.edu). Nearly everything here: dates, the rules, no books, the late biographies, the hammers.
Carl Huffman, "Philolaus," *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy*. The ratios in numbers.
Walter Burkert, *Lore and Science in Ancient Pythagoreanism*, trans. E. L. Minar (Harvard University Press, 1972). Pythagoras as a teacher of the soul, and the mathematics as later.
Leonid Zhmud, *Pythagoras and the Early Pythagoreans* (Oxford University Press, 2012). The case that the early Pythagoreans did do mathematics.

events.label: Athens votes
events.kindNote: not in the closed list (sky, earth, crop, craft, object, place, person, text); kept as written

place.name: Athens, Greece; the Pnyx marks it (37.97 N, 23.72 E), though the assembly may have met in the Agora at first

events.summary: 508 BCE. The people of Athens trapped a Spartan king on their city's hill and brought back a man named Cleisthenes, whose new rules put the city in its citizens' hands. Most people in Athens were not citizens.

paragraphs: For two days, a king of Sparta and his soldiers were trapped on the Acropolis ("uh-KROP-uh-lis"), the rocky hill in the middle of Athens, surrounded by the ordinary people of the city. On the third day the king gave up and was allowed to leave.

How had it come to this? Two years earlier, with help from Sparta, the Athenians had thrown out Hippias, the man who ruled them alone. Then two powerful Athenians fought over what should come next. One of them, Isagoras, called in the king of Sparta to help him take charge. The other, Cleisthenes ("KLYS-thuh-neez"), had promised the ordinary people a share in running the city. The people would not have Isagoras. They trapped him on the hill with the king, and they brought Cleisthenes back.

Then Athens changed. Every citizen was put into one of ten new groups, called tribes, and each tribe mixed men from the city, the coast and the countryside. Each tribe sent fifty men to a council of five hundred, which ran the city's business. The big decisions were made by an assembly, where any citizen could come, speak and vote. Before long it met on a hillside called the Pnyx ("pnicks").

Who was a citizen? Only free men. Most came from Athenian families, though Cleisthenes added some newcomers. Women could not vote, enslaved people could not, and neither could foreigners who lived and worked in Athens. Most of the people of Athens had no vote at all. But inside the assembly, a poor farmer's vote counted for exactly as much as a rich man's.

One of the new rules let the citizens vote to send a powerful man away from Athens for ten years, though it was first used about twenty years later. Each voter scratched a name on a broken piece of pottery. In an old well below the Acropolis, archaeologists found 191 of these pieces, almost all bearing the same name, Themistocles, and written in only about fourteen different hands. It looks as though someone had prepared them in advance.

events.picturesWanted: an ostrakon with Themistocles's name (Agora Museum, Athens; American School of Classical Studies; licence to check); the Pnyx with its speakers' platform (Commons; licence to check).
references: Herodotus, *Histories*, Book 5, sections 66–78. The siege on the Acropolis and Cleisthenes's return.
Aristotle (or his school), *The Constitution of the Athenians*, sections 20–22. The ten tribes, the council of five hundred, and ostracism.
Josiah Ober, *The Athenian Revolution: Essays on Ancient Greek Democracy and Political Theory* (Princeton University Press, 1996). The people's uprising as the start.
Mabel L. Lang, *Ostraka* (The Athenian Agora, vol. 25, American School of Classical Studies at Athens, 1990). The 191 ostraka from the well.

events.label: Confucius

place.name: Qufu, Shandong, China (35.61 N, 117.00 E)

events.summary: About 500 BCE. In the state of Lu, in China, a teacher named Kongzi, whom Europeans later called Confucius, taught how to live and how to govern. He wrote nothing. His students wrote down what he said.

paragraphs: In the town of Qufu ("choo-foo"), in eastern China, there is a graveyard with more than a hundred thousand graves. Almost everyone buried there belongs to one family, the Kong family, the descendants of one man.
His name was Kong Qiu ("kong chyoh"). He came to be called Kongzi or Kong Fuzi, Master Kong, and long afterwards European missionaries turned Kong Fuzi into Latin as Confucius.

He was born about 551 BCE in or near Lu, one of many states in a China that was divided and often at war. He wanted to help a ruler govern well. He held a few posts in Lu, then travelled from state to state looking for a ruler who would take his advice, and when he did not find one, he came home and taught.
He taught how to behave well toward your parents, your friends and the people you rule, and he taught how to study. Two of the things he is remembered as saying are these:

paragraphs.quote: When I walk with two others, I'm bound to find my teacher there.
To know when you know something, and to know when you don't know, that's knowledge.

paragraphs: He wrote no book. After he died, his students, and then their students, wrote down what they remembered of him: short sayings, answers to questions, little scenes. Over two or three hundred years these were gathered into a book called the Analects, and nobody knows how many of the sayings are really his. For two thousand years after that, the Analects was one of the most widely read books in China, and later in Korea, Japan and Vietnam.

His family has kept track of itself for centuries. An edition of the Kong family tree printed in 2009 fills eighty books and names more than two million people across eighty-three generations. It is said to be the longest family tree in history.

events.picturesWanted: the Temple of Confucius at Qufu (UNESCO; Commons; licence to check); a page of the Analects in an old printed edition (public domain).
references: "Confucius," *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy* (plato.stanford.edu). His dates, his posts in Lu, his travels, how the Analects was put together.
Robert Eno, *The Analects of Confucius: An Online Teaching Translation* (2015). The saying on knowing.
Burton Watson, trans., *The Analects of Confucius* (Columbia University Press, 2007). The saying on walking with two others.
UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Temple and Cemetery of Confucius and the Kong Family Mansion in Qufu" (inscribed 1994). The graveyard.
Library of Congress, "An extensive tree," *Library of Congress Information Bulletin*, December 2010. The family tree.

events.label: Aeschylus

place.name: the Theatre of Dionysus, Athens, Greece (37.97 N, 23.73 E)

events.summary: 499 BCE. In Athens, a young man named Aeschylus entered the city's contest for new plays for the first time. He would put a second actor on the stage, so that two characters could talk to each other.

paragraphs: In Athens, people sit on wooden benches, looking down on a flat floor where the chorus will dance. It is spring, and the city is holding its festival for Dionysus, a god of wine. For several days the city watches new plays, and judges choose the best.
In 499 BCE a young man of about twenty-five named Aeschylus ("ESS-kuh-lus") entered the contest for the first time. He did not win; his first win came fifteen years later.

A play then had a chorus, a group of men who sang and danced together, and a single actor, who wore a mask and could play several characters by changing masks. The actor spoke, and the chorus answered. But the actor had nobody else to talk to.

Aeschylus added a second actor. Now two characters could stand face to face, argue, lie to each other, or change each other's minds. We know this from the philosopher Aristotle, who wrote about plays some 160 years later. He says that the next great playwright, Sophocles, added a third.
Aeschylus wrote between seventy and ninety plays, and seven have survived.

He was also a soldier. In 490 BCE he fought at Marathon, where the Athenians defeated a Persian army that had landed in Greece, and where his brother was killed. The Greek historian Herodotus says that 192 Athenians and about 6,400 Persians died there.

Aeschylus died in Sicily as an old man. The words on his grave said who he was and where he came from, and that the grove of Marathon could tell of his courage. They said nothing about his plays. One ancient writer says Aeschylus wrote those words himself; another says the people of the town where he died wrote them. Nobody knows which is right.

events.picturesWanted: the Theatre of Dionysus today (Commons; the stone seats are later, so the caption must say so); a Greek theatre mask on a painted vase (licence to check).
references: Aristotle, *Poetics*, section 4 (1449a), trans. S. H. Butcher. The second actor, and Sophocles's third.
*Life of Aeschylus*, trans. S. Burges Watson (ToposText). His battles, his plays, and the epitaph, said to be written by the people of Gela.
Pausanias, *Description of Greece*, Book 1, section 14.5. The epitaph, said to be written by Aeschylus himself.
Herodotus, *Histories*, Book 6, sections 114 and 117. His brother's death at Marathon; the numbers of dead.
Anthony J. Podlecki, "Aeschylus," *Encyclopaedia Britannica*. His dates, first contest, first win, number of plays.

events.label: Anaxagoras

place.name: Athens, Greece (37.97 N, 23.73 E)

events.summary: About 450 BCE. In Athens, a teacher named Anaxagoras said that the Sun was a red-hot stone bigger than southern Greece, and that the Moon's light was borrowed from the Sun. Athens grew nervous.

paragraphs: Around 467 BCE, a stone fell out of the sky at a place called Aegospotami ("ee-gos-POT-uh-my"), on the narrow strait between Europe and Asia that is now called the Dardanelles. Plutarch, a Greek writer who lived more than five hundred years later, says people believed the stone was huge, and that it was still being shown in his own day.

Stones were not supposed to be up there. But a man named Anaxagoras ("an-ak-SAG-er-us") thought they were. He came from Clazomenae, a Greek city on the coast of what is now Turkey, and he moved to Athens and taught there for many years. Nobody is sure when he arrived: scholars' guesses run from about 480 to about 456 BCE.

To many Greeks the Sun was a god. Anaxagoras said it was a mass of red-hot stone, or perhaps red-hot metal, larger than the Peloponnese ("PEL-uh-puh-neez"), the great peninsula that makes up the south of Greece. He said the Moon was made of earth, with hills and valleys, and that it had no light of its own: it shone with light from the Sun.

That one idea explains eclipses. When the Moon passes between us and the Sun, it blocks the Sun. When the Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon, the Moon goes dark. Anaxagoras is the first Greek known to have explained eclipses this way. And if the Sun was a stone, then a stone could fall out of the sky.

Athens grew nervous. Plutarch says a law was proposed against anyone who taught about the heavens and did not believe in the gods, and that Pericles, the leading man of the city and a friend of Anaxagoras, sent the teacher away to keep him safe. Other writers, centuries later, tell four different stories of a trial. Nobody knows which, if any, is true.

Anaxagoras spent his last years at Lampsacus, across the strait from where the stone had fallen. When he was dying, the town asked how it should honour him. He asked that every year, in the month he died, the children be given a holiday.

events.picturesWanted: the strait at Lapseki (ancient Lampsacus) looking across to the Gallipoli shore (Commons; licence to check); a diagram of a solar and a lunar eclipse (to be drawn for CW).
references: John Sisko and Patricia Curd, "Anaxagoras," *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy* (revised 2026; plato.stanford.edu). His dates and the argued chronology, eclipses, the stone, the children's holiday.

Diogenes Laertius, *Lives of Eminent Philosophers*, Book 2, sections 6–15, translated by R. D. Hicks (Loeb, 1925). The Sun larger than the Peloponnese, the Moon's hills and ravines, the four trial stories, his death at Lampsacus.
Plutarch, *Pericles*, sections 32 and 16 (Loeb, translated by Bernadotte Perrin, 1916), and *Lysander*, section 12. The proposed law, Pericles sending him away, and the stone still shown.

Richard Janko, "Eclipse and plague: Themistocles, Pericles, Anaxagoras and the Athenians' war on science," *Journal of Hellenic Studies* 140 (2020), 213–237. One recent view of the dates and the trial.

events.label: Socrates

place.name: Athens, Greece; the Agora (37.975 N, 23.722 E)

events.summary: 399 BCE. In Athens, a jury of citizens sentenced a man named Socrates to death, for not honouring the city's gods and for corrupting the young. He wrote nothing, so we know him only through others.

paragraphs: At a festival in Athens in 423 BCE, the audience watched an actor playing a real, living man, hung up in the air in a basket. The man was Socrates ("SOK-ruh-teez"), and the play was *Clouds*, a comedy by Aristophanes ("air-is-TOF-uh-neez"). It showed Socrates as a crank who gazed at the sky and taught young men tricks for winning arguments they ought to lose. The play came third in the contest.

The real Socrates spent his days in the streets and the marketplace of Athens, asking people questions. What is courage? What is justice? What is a good life? He kept asking until it was plain that the person who had been so sure did not know the answer, and often that Socrates did not know either. He was famously ugly, with a flat, turned-up nose and bulging eyes, and a friend compared him to a satyr, a wild creature from Greek stories who was part man and part horse.

He wrote nothing. Almost everything we know about him comes from three people who knew him, and they disagree. Aristophanes made fun of him. Xenophon ("ZEN-uh-fun"), a soldier, remembered a sensible man full of practical advice. Plato, his pupil, wrote conversations in which Socrates questions people, but Plato often seems to have put his own ideas into his teacher's mouth.
Which is the real Socrates? Nobody can be sure.

In 399 BCE, when he was about seventy, three citizens accused him of not honouring the gods of the city, of bringing in new gods, and of corrupting the young. A jury of about five hundred citizens heard the case. In Plato's account, Socrates says that if thirty votes had gone the other way, he would have been set free. He was sentenced to death, and some weeks later, in prison, he drank a poison. Plato never names the poison; later writers call it hemlock.
Plato describes the death in detail: Socrates calm, talking with his friends to the end. But the friend who tells the story in Plato's book says that Plato was not there that day. He was ill.

events.picturesWanted: a Roman marble head of Socrates, copied from a Greek original (British Museum or Louvre; licence to check); the Agora of Athens today (Commons; licence to check).
references: Debra Nails and S. Sara Monoson, "Socrates," *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy* (revised 2022; plato.stanford.edu). The three witnesses, *Clouds*, his looks, the charges and the dates.
Plato, *Apology* and *Phaedo*, translated by Benjamin Jowett (free online). His age, the thirty votes, the death, and Plato's absence.
Aristophanes, *Clouds* (423 BCE; the text we have is partly revised). Socrates in the basket.

Enid Bloch, "Hemlock poisoning and the death of Socrates: did Plato tell the truth?", *Plato: The Internet Journal of the International Plato Society* 1 (2001). What Plato calls the poison, and whether it was hemlock.

events.label: Kalinga war

place.name: Kalinga (now Odisha), eastern India; Dhauli, near Bhubaneswar, marks it (20.19 N, 85.84 E)

events.summary: 261 BCE. King Ashoka of India conquered the land of Kalinga. Afterwards he had the cost of the war carved on rock, said he regretted it, and changed how he ruled.

paragraphs: A message from a king is carved on a rock face in India. Part of it reads:
"One hundred and fifty thousand people were deported, one hundred thousand were killed, and many times that number perished."
The king is talking about his own war.
His name was Ashoka. Say "a-SHOH-ka." He ruled most of India. About 2,300 years ago, eight years after he became king, he invaded Kalinga, a land on the east coast of India, and won.

Kings of that time carved their victories on stone. Ashoka carved something else. He said the killing and the suffering of the families filled him with sorrow and regret. He said that from then on, the only conquest worth making was a conquest by what he called dhamma: doing right by others. He turned seriously to Buddhism, stopped making war, and had messages carved on rocks and tall stone pillars across his kingdom.
What did his messages say?

Treat servants and workers fairly. Respect your parents. Respect the beliefs of others. Don't kill animals needlessly. Plant trees along roads for shade, and dig wells. He wrote that he had set up care for sick people and sick animals.

What did the war cost? Only Ashoka's own numbers survive. Nobody else counted, and there is no way to check them. We don't know what the war cost in money or effort. We know it made him change how he ruled.
After Ashoka, his writing was forgotten. For two thousand years nobody could read it. In 1837, a scholar named James Prinsep worked out the letters.
The rocks inside Kalinga itself carry Ashoka's messages too. On them, the passage counting the dead is left out.

events.picturesWanted: the Dhauli rock inscription; the lion capital from one of Ashoka's pillars (Sarnath Museum; Commons).
references: Ashoka, Major Rock Edict XIII. Translation in Romila Thapar, *Aśoka and the Decline of the Mauryas* (Oxford, 1961; revised 1997). The numbers and the regret.
Nayanjot Lahiri, *Ashoka in Ancient India* (Harvard, 2015). His life and the edicts.
Charles Allen, *Ashoka: The Search for India's Lost Emperor* (Little, Brown, 2012). Prinsep and the decipherment.

events.label: Eratosthenes
events.kindNote: not in the closed list (sky, earth, crop, craft, object, place, person, text); kept as written

place.name: Alexandria, Egypt (31.20 N, 29.92 E), with Syene (Aswan) to the south

events.summary: About 240 BCE. In Alexandria, in Egypt, a scholar named Eratosthenes worked out the size of the whole Earth from the length of a shadow and the distance between two cities.

paragraphs: In the town of Syene, in the south of Egypt, there was said to be a deep well. On one day a year, at noon, the Sun shone straight down into it and lit the water at the bottom. On that day the Sun was directly overhead, and a stick standing upright cast no shadow at all.
On the same day, at noon, in Alexandria, far to the north, an upright stick did cast a shadow.
Why the difference?

Eratosthenes thought he knew. He was the chief librarian at Alexandria, in charge of the greatest library of the time. Like other Greek scholars, he took it that the Earth is a ball, and that the Sun is so far away that its rays arrive side by side. If the ground were flat, the stick in Alexandria would cast no shadow either. The shadow meant the ground between the two cities curved.

So he measured how much. The shadow in Alexandria showed that the Sun was one fiftieth of a full circle away from straight overhead. So the distance from Alexandria to Syene had to be one fiftieth of the way around the Earth.
That distance was known: about 5,000 stadia. A stadion was a Greek unit of length, about the length of a running track. Fifty times 5,000 is 250,000 stadia. That was his size for the whole Earth.
How close did he come?

Nobody knows exactly. There were several different stadia in use, of different lengths, and nobody knows which one he meant. Depending on the answer, he was within about two percent of the true size, or about sixteen percent too big. Either way, one man with a stick and a known distance had measured the whole Earth without leaving Egypt.
His own book is lost. We know his method from a writer named Cleomedes, who described it about three hundred years later.

events.picturesWanted: a simple drawing of the two sticks and the Sun's parallel rays (to be drawn for CW; a live version belongs on the plane).
references: Cleomedes, *On the Heavens*, Book 1, chapter 7. Translation in Alan Bowen and Robert Todd, *Cleomedes' Lectures on Astronomy* (University of California Press, 2004). The only full account of the method.
Juergen Dutka, "Eratosthenes' measurement of the Earth reconsidered," *Archive for History of Exact Sciences*, 1993. Stadia and accuracy.
Duane Roller, *Eratosthenes' Geography* (Princeton, 2010). His life and lost work.

events.label: Antikythera

place.name: the Antikythera wreck, off the island of Antikythera, Greece (35.89 N, 23.30 E)

events.summary: About 100 BCE. A Greek ship sank carrying a box of bronze gears that showed the movements of the Sun and Moon and predicted eclipses. Nothing like it is known again for over a thousand years.

paragraphs: A lump of green, crumbling bronze sits in a museum in Athens. On one side, if you look closely, you can see the teeth of a gear wheel about as wide as your hand.
Nobody expected gears from ancient Greece.

In 1900, sponge divers sheltering from a storm off the small island of Antikythera found a shipwreck on the sea floor. Over the next year they brought up bronze and marble statues, glass, pottery and coins. The ship had sunk about 2,100 years ago. The lump of bronze came up with everything else, and for months nobody paid it much attention. Then, in 1902, it split open, and an archaeologist named Valerios Stais saw the gear.
What was it?

It took most of the next century to find out. From the 1950s, a scientist named Derek de Solla Price studied it, and in the 1970s he had it X-rayed. In 2005, a team scanned the pieces in layers, the way a hospital scans a body, and read writing on them that had been hidden for two thousand years.

It had been a wooden box about the size of a shoebox, with a handle on the side. Turning the handle turned dozens of bronze gears inside. About thirty survive. On the front, pointers showed where the Sun and Moon were among the stars, and a little ball, half silver and half dark, turned to show the phase of the Moon. On the back, dials showed which months would have an eclipse, and when the great athletic games were held.
Nobody knows who made it. Nobody knows who it was for, or where the ship was going with it.
No machine with gears this fine is known again for more than a thousand years.

events.picturesWanted: the main fragment showing the large gear (National Archaeological Museum, Athens; Commons); a reconstruction drawing (licence to check).
references: Derek de Solla Price, *Gears from the Greeks: The Antikythera Mechanism, a Calendar Computer from ca. 80 B.C.* (American Philosophical Society, 1974). The X-ray work.
Tony Freeth and others, "Decoding the ancient Greek astronomical calculator known as the Antikythera Mechanism," *Nature*, 2006. The 2005 scans and the inscriptions.
Tony Freeth and others, "A Model of the Cosmos in the ancient Greek Antikythera Mechanism," *Scientific Reports*, 2021. The front display.
Alexander Jones, *A Portable Cosmos* (Oxford, 2017). The whole story, readable.

events.label: Pompeii

place.name: Pompeii, near Naples, Italy (40.75 N, 14.49 E)

events.summary: 79 CE. The volcano Vesuvius, near Naples in Italy, erupted and buried the town of Pompeii under ash and stone. A seventeen-year-old named Pliny watched from across the bay and later described it.

paragraphs: A young man is staying in a house across the bay from a mountain. One afternoon his mother points out a strange cloud rising over the mountain. He says it looks like an umbrella pine: a tall trunk, spreading out at the top into branches.
He was seventeen. His name was Pliny.
The mountain was Vesuvius, near Naples in Italy. Few people then thought of it as a volcano. Its slopes were covered with vineyards, and the town of Pompeii sat a few kilometres from its foot.

We know what Pliny saw because, about twenty-five years later, a historian named Tacitus asked him for it, and Pliny wrote two letters. The letters survive. They are the only eyewitness account of the eruption that survives.

His uncle, also named Pliny, commanded the Roman fleet in the bay. He sailed across toward the mountain to rescue people on the shore. He never came back. His nephew stayed behind, and the next day, with his mother, joined the crowds leaving town as ash fell and the ground shook. He writes that the darkness was "not the dark of a moonless or cloudy night, but as if the lamp had been put out in a closed room."

Pompeii was buried under several metres of ash and small stones. Nearby, the town of Herculaneum was buried deeper, under hot flows of ash and gas that ran down the mountain. Many people escaped. Many did not.
Then the towns were forgotten. Digging at Pompeii began in 1748, more than 1,600 years later. The streets, shops, paintings, bread in the ovens and words scratched on walls were all still there.
The date is argued about. Copies of Pliny's letters say 24 August, but a note scratched in charcoal, found in Pompeii in 2018, suggests the autumn.
Volcanologists still call a tall eruption like this one "Plinian," after the young man who described it.

events.picturesWanted: a Pompeii street with Vesuvius behind it (Commons); a wall painting from Pompeii.
references: Pliny the Younger, *Letters*, Book 6, letters 16 and 20, to Tacitus. Translation by Betty Radice (Penguin, 1963). The eyewitness account and the quoted line.
Mary Beard, *Pompeii: The Life of a Roman Town* (Profile, 2008). The town and its rediscovery.
Haraldur Sigurdsson and others, "The eruption of Vesuvius in A.D. 79," *National Geographic Research*, 1985. The eruption's stages.
Massimo Osanna, reports on the 2018 charcoal inscription (Parco Archeologico di Pompei). The date argument.

events.label: Paper

place.name: Luoyang, Henan, China, the Han capital (34.73 N, 112.62 E). The older paper in the More is from Fangmatan, near Tianshui, Gansu (about 34.4 N, 106.0 E).

events.summary: 105 CE. At the Han court in China, an official named Cai Lun showed the emperor paper made from bark, hemp, rags and old fishing nets. History books called him its inventor. But paper is older than that.

paragraphs: In 1986, near the city of Tianshui in northwest China, archaeologists opened a tomb more than two thousand years old. Inside lay a scrap of paper about the size of two postage stamps, with fine black ink lines that seem to show mountains, rivers and roads. It is probably part of a map. The tomb was made between about 179 and 141 BCE.
That is a puzzle, because the history books say paper was invented more than two hundred years later.

Their source is the *Book of the Later Han*, a history put together in the 400s CE. It says that in 105 CE Cai Lun ("tsy LWUN"), an official at the emperor's court, showed the emperor a new writing material made from tree bark, the ends of hemp plants, worn-out cloth and old fishing nets, and that afterwards people everywhere called it Lord Cai's paper.

Read the history closely, though, and it does not say Cai Lun was the first. It says that books had mostly been written on strips of bamboo, which were heavy, or on silk, which was expensive, and that the silk was called *zhi* ("jr"), the same word that was later used for paper. Cai Lun had the idea of making *zhi* from cheap materials.

Paper is made by beating plant fibres in water until they come apart into a soupy pulp. The pulp is spread thin on a fine screen and the water drains away, leaving the fibres tangled into a thin mat, which is pressed and dried into a sheet.

The older paper keeps turning up. At Xuanquan ("shwen-chwen"), a Han postal station near Dunhuang, archaeologists found more than four hundred and sixty pieces of paper, about ten with writing, and seven of those seem to be older than 105 CE. Some historians of paper are not convinced these dates are right.
So did Cai Lun invent paper? Perhaps he found a better, cheaper way to make it. Perhaps he simply brought it to court, so his name went into the history book.
Who made the first sheet, and when, nobody yet knows.

references: *Hou Hanshu* (*Book of the Later Han*), chapter 78, the biography of Cai Lun. The report of 105 CE, his materials, and *zhi* first meaning writing silk. Chinese text on Wikisource.
Tsien Tsuen-Hsuin, *Science and Civilisation in China*, vol. 5, part 1, *Paper and Printing*, ed. Joseph Needham (Cambridge University Press, 1985). The standard history of early paper.
Xiao Congli (肖从礼), "片言纸语｜甘肃简牍博物馆珍藏的古纸（一）" ("Ancient paper in the collection of the Gansu Jiandu Museum, part 1"), 7 May 2021. The finds at Fangmatan, Xuanquan and elsewhere, and how they are dated.
Jonathan Bloom, *Paper Before Print: The History and Impact of Paper in the Islamic World* (Yale University Press, 2001). How paper travelled west.

events.label: Earthquake jar

place.name: Luoyang, China (34.62 N, 112.45 E)

events.summary: 132 CE. At the Han court in Luoyang, China, an astronomer named Zhang Heng built a bronze jar that dropped a ball when the ground shook, even from an earthquake too far away to feel.

paragraphs: A bronze jar nearly two metres across stands in a room at the emperor's court. Around its outside are eight dragons, facing eight directions. Each dragon holds a bronze ball in its mouth. Below each dragon sits a bronze toad, looking up, with its mouth open.
One day a ball drops into a toad's mouth with a clang.
Nobody in the room has felt anything.

The jar was made in 132 by Zhang Heng, an astronomer and mathematician at the court of the Han dynasty in Luoyang, China. Say "JAHNG HUNG." China has many earthquakes, and the court wanted to know about them quickly.

According to the history of the time, the jar was built so that when the ground shook, something inside tipped, and one dragon let go of its ball. The toad that caught the ball showed which direction the shaking came from.
Did it work?

The same history tells this story. One day a ball dropped, and no one had felt any earthquake. The scholars at court said the jar had failed. A few days later a messenger arrived. There had been an earthquake in Longxi, far to the west. After that, everyone believed in it.
What was inside the jar?

Nobody knows. The jar is lost. All that survives is a short description, written down about three hundred years later, and it does not say how the inside worked. Scientists in China and elsewhere have built models since the 1950s, most with a heavy weight hanging inside like a pendulum. Some of the models work. Nobody knows whether any of them is how Zhang Heng did it.
Zhang Heng also made a globe of the stars, turned by water, and counted 2,500 stars in the sky, not including thousands of very faint ones.
All that is left of the jar is one paragraph.

events.picturesWanted: a modern replica of the jar (several museums; Commons; the caption must say it is a modern model).
references: *Hou Hanshu* (Book of the Later Han), biography of Zhang Heng, compiled by Fan Ye in the 400s. The only description and the Longxi story.
Joseph Needham and Wang Ling, *Science and Civilisation in China*, vol. 3 (Cambridge, 1959). Translation and discussion.
Hong-sen Yan and Kuo-Hung Hsiao, "Reconstruction design of the lost seismoscope of ancient China," *Mechanism and Machine Theory*, 2007. The modern models.

events.label: Teotihuacan

place.name: Teotihuacan, State of Mexico, Mexico (19.69 N, 98.84 W)

events.summary: From about 200 to 550 CE, Teotihuacan, in the Valley of Mexico, was one of the largest cities in the Americas, with perhaps 100,000 people. Nobody knows what they called it, or what language they spoke.

paragraphs: A wide, straight avenue runs for kilometres through the ruins of an old city in the Valley of Mexico, less than fifty kilometres northeast of Mexico City. Beside it stands a pyramid sixty-six metres high, as tall as a twenty-storey building, on a base more than two hundred metres along each side.

Every one of those things has a name that someone else gave it. The avenue is the Avenue of the Dead, the pyramid is the Pyramid of the Sun, and the city is Teotihuacan ("tay-oh-tee-wah-KAHN"). All three names are in Nahuatl ("NAH-wah-tl"), the language of the Aztecs, who came to the ruins hundreds of years after the city had emptied. Teotihuacan is usually translated as "the place where the gods were made," though translators disagree.

The city was at its biggest between about 200 and 550 CE. Archaeologists working out how many people lived there start from the large walled apartment buildings, made of stone, where families lived together. In 2019 the archaeologist Michael E. Smith and his colleagues worked from the sizes of those buildings and arrived at about 100,000 people. Older guesses were larger, up to 200,000 in one well-known estimate.

What did those people call their city? What language did they speak? Who ruled them? Nobody knows. They painted signs on walls and pots, but only short groups of signs, never long texts, and nobody can read them for certain. Linguists have suggested several languages. In 2025, two of them, Magnus Pharao Hansen and Christophe Helmke, argued that the signs record an early language from which Nahuatl later grew. That idea is new, and it is too soon to know whether other scholars agree.
About 550 CE, the great buildings along the avenue were burned. Nobody knows who set the fires, whether people of the city or enemies from outside, or why.
The Aztecs believed that the gods had met at Teotihuacan to make the Sun. What the people who built it believed, nobody knows.

events.picturesWanted: the Avenue of the Dead from the Pyramid of the Moon, with the Pyramid of the Sun beside it (Commons; licence to check); a mural from an apartment compound (licence to check).
references: Michael E. Smith, Abhishek Chatterjee, Angela C. Huster, Sierra Stewart and Marion Forest, "Apartment compounds, households, and population in the ancient city of Teotihuacan, Mexico," *Ancient Mesoamerica* 30 (2019), 399–418. About 100,000 people, and the older estimates.
Alejandro Sarabia González, "Los 'túneles arqueológicos' en la pirámide del Sol de Teotihuacán," *Arqueología* 61 (2020), 48–59. The pyramid's height and base.
