events.label: Faraday's ring

place.name: the Royal Institution, Albemarle Street, London (51.510 N, 0.142 W)

events.summary: 29 August 1831. In London, Michael Faraday wound two coils of wire on an iron ring and found that electricity in one coil made electricity in the other, but only when it started or stopped.

paragraphs: The ring is iron, about fifteen centimetres across and nearly as thick as a thumb. Around one side of it, and separately around the other side, Michael Faraday wound coils of copper wire, wrapped in cotton and twine so that the turns would not touch. Some of the wire had been made for bonnets. The ring is still at the Royal Institution in London, where he made it.

Eleven years earlier, a Danish professor, Hans Christian Ørsted ("UR-sted"), had found that an electric current flowing in a wire makes a compass needle near it swing. So electricity could make magnetism. Faraday wanted to know whether magnetism could make electricity, and he had been trying for years.

On 29 August 1831 he joined one coil to a battery. He joined the other coil to a long wire that ran to a compass needle about a metre away. Ørsted's discovery meant that the needle would swing if any current flowed in the second coil. When Faraday connected the battery, the needle swung, wobbled, and settled back where it had been. When he disconnected the battery, the needle swung again. While the battery stayed connected, nothing happened.

Here is what was going on. The current in the first coil turned the iron ring into a magnet. While the magnet was growing, and again while it was fading, a current flowed in the second coil. A magnet that stayed the same made nothing at all. What made electricity was a change: magnetism growing or fading, or, as he soon found, a wire moving past a magnet.

Within two months Faraday had shown the same thing more simply, by pushing a bar magnet into a coil of wire and pulling it out. Then he set a copper disc spinning between the ends of a huge magnet, and drew a steady current from it for as long as it turned.
Most of the electricity made in the world today comes from machines that do what his magnet and coil did, over and over: they turn magnets and coils of wire past each other.

events.label: Darwin's tree

place.name: 36 Great Marlborough Street, London (51.514 N, 0.140 W)

events.summary: 1837. In London, Charles Darwin wrote "I think" in his notebook and then drew a small branching tree. It was a guess at how kinds of living things might be related.

paragraphs: On a page of a small notebook, someone has written two words, "I think," and then stopped and drawn instead. The drawing starts at a point marked 1. Lines branch out from it, and branch again, and again. Some of the branches end in a short crossing line, and others just stop. Four of the ends are labelled A, B, C and D.

The notebook belonged to Charles Darwin. He was twenty-eight, and nine months earlier he had come home from almost five years on a navy ship, the *Beagle*, which had sailed around the world while he collected animals, plants, fossils and rocks. Now he lived in central London and was working through what he had found. Inside the cover of this notebook he wrote that he had begun it about July 1837.

The drawing is a guess about where kinds of living things, the species, come from. Suppose every species began as a branch of some older species, and that one as a branch of something older still. Then the species alive today are the tips of the branches. Some branches have died out, and the species on them are gone. Where many have died out between two tips, the two living species look very different, like A and B. Where few have, they look alike, like B and C. Under the drawing Darwin wrote, "Thus between A & B. immense gap of relation, C & B. the finest gradation, B & D rather greater distinction."
Darwin was not the first to draw living things as a branching tree.
Twenty-two years later he published the idea, in a book called *On the Origin of Species*. The book had only one picture in it: a branching tree.

In 2001 the notebook was found to be missing from Cambridge University Library, where it was kept. On 9 March 2022 it came back. Someone left it outside the librarian's office in a bright pink gift bag, with a note that said, "Librarian. Happy Easter. X."

references: Charles Darwin, Notebook B (1837–38), Cambridge University Library MS DAR 121; transcription in *Darwin Online* (darwin-online.org.uk) and images in the Cambridge Digital Library. The date on the cover, the sketch, the words on page 36.

events.label: Daguerreotype

place.name: Institut de France, Paris (48.86 N, 2.34 E)

events.summary: 19 August 1839. In Paris, the French government gave away a way of making pictures with light, invented by Louis Daguerre. Anyone could use it free, except in England, where Daguerre had taken out a patent days before.

paragraphs: On 19 August 1839, in a hall of the Institut de France in Paris, the members of two academies, one for the sciences and one for the fine arts, met together to hear a secret given away. The secret was how to make a daguerreotype ("dah-GAIR-oh-type"), a picture made by light.

Louis Daguerre was a painter who ran a show of huge painted scenes in Paris. For years he had worked on the problem with Nicéphore Niépce, who had made the first photograph from a camera, and after Niépce died in 1833, Daguerre carried on alone.

His method went like this. A copper plate coated with silver was polished until it shone like a mirror, and the vapour of iodine made its surface sensitive to light. The plate went into a camera for several minutes. Then it was held over warm mercury, whose fumes made the picture appear, and washed with a chemical that stopped light from changing it any further. Each picture was the only one. There was nothing to print copies from.

A patent is a government's promise that only the inventor may use an invention, or sell the right to use it. But the French government decided that a method this simple could not be protected, because anyone who had seen it explained could do it. So it bought the method instead. Daguerre was paid 6,000 francs a year for life, and Niépce's son Isidore 4,000. The government's own statement said the method had to belong to everyone or stay unknown.
The news went fast. Within days a Paris shop was advertising the cameras, and by early September they had reached Berlin.

But it did not belong to everyone. A few days before the meeting in Paris, an agent for Daguerre took out a patent in England. Anyone in England who wanted to make a daguerreotype had to pay for the right.

events.label: Paint tubes

place.name: London (51.51 N, 0.13 W)

events.summary: 1841. In London, John Goffe Rand, an American portrait painter, patented a small tube of thin metal for keeping oil paint. Squeezed, it let out a little paint, and it could be closed again.

paragraphs: Before 1841, a painter who wanted to keep oil paint fresh for a few days tied it up in a little bag made from a pig's bladder. To get paint out, you pricked the bladder with a tack and squeezed. The hole could not be properly closed again, so the paint near it dried, and a bladder carried in a pocket or a box could burst. Some painters kept paint in glass tubes or syringes, which kept it better but broke.

John Goffe Rand was born in New Hampshire in 1801, learned to make furniture, painted houses and signs, and then became a painter of portraits. By 1840 he was living in London, where he painted lords and dukes. He also thought about paint.

His answer was a tube of tin, so thin it could be squeezed like a bag, with a cap at one end. You unscrewed the cap and squeezed, and as much paint as you wanted came out. Then you put the cap back, and the paint inside stayed soft, because no air could get in. When the tube was empty, it was flat.
Rand patented the tube in Britain in March 1841, and in the United States that September. By the next year the London colour sellers Winsor & Newton were selling paint in his tubes.
Paint in tubes could go anywhere, and it kept. A painter could carry a dozen colours out into a field, a garden or a street, and come back with them still soft.

Many years later, Jean Renoir, a film director, wrote a book about his father, the painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir. In it he remembered his father saying that without paint in tubes there would have been no Cézanne, no Monet, no Sisley, no Pissarro, and nothing of what journalists later called Impressionism. But painters had carried paint outdoors before. In the 1780s, Pierre-Henri de Valenciennes painted little oil sketches of the sky over Rome. Tubes made it easier.

events.label: Japanese prints

place.name: Champ de Mars, Paris (48.86 N, 2.30 E)

events.summary: 1867. At a world's fair in Paris, Japan took part for the first time, and sent woodblock prints among much else. Over the next twenty years, painters in France collected Japanese prints, and some copied them.

paragraphs: In April 1867 a world's fair opened in Paris on the Champ de Mars, a great open field beside the river Seine, and countries from all over the world showed what they made. For the first time, Japan sent things to show: lacquer, pottery, paintings, and prints.

A Japanese woodblock print was the work of several people. An artist drew the picture. A carver pasted a thin copy of the drawing face down on a block of cherry wood and cut away everything that was not to print. Each colour needed a block of its own, with small marks cut in each block to keep the colours lined up. A printer inked the blocks one at a time and pressed the paper onto each, and a publisher, who had chosen the subject in the first place, sold the prints.

In Paris they looked like nothing else: flat colour, strong outlines, and views from odd places, high above a street or close up behind a branch. Collectors bought them, and in 1872 a critic named Philippe Burty made up a word for the craze, *japonisme* ("zha-po-NEESM").

Twenty years after the fair, Vincent van Gogh, a Dutch painter living in Paris with his brother Theo, collected hundreds of Japanese prints, many of them from the shop of a dealer named Siegfried Bing. In 1887 he copied two prints by the artist Hiroshige in oil paint, a plum orchard and a bridge in the rain.

In 1888 Theo wrote to Vincent about a wave by Hokusai, almost certainly *The Great Wave*, the most famous print of them all. Vincent wrote back and repeated his brother's words: "these waves are *claws*, the boat is caught in them, you can feel it."

events.label: Suez Canal

place.name: Ismailia, midway along the canal, Egypt (30.60 N, 32.27 E)

events.summary: 17 November 1869. The Suez Canal opened in Egypt, joining the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea. Ships between Europe and Asia no longer had to sail around Africa.

paragraphs: Look at a map of Africa and Asia. At the top right corner of Africa, a narrow strip of desert joins it to Asia. On one side is the Mediterranean Sea. On the other is the Red Sea, which leads to the Indian Ocean.
For thousands of years, that strip of sand was in the way.
A ship sailing from London to India had to go all the way around Africa. If you could cut through the strip, the journey would be about seven thousand kilometres shorter.

People had tried before. Egyptian kings, thousands of years ago, dug canals from the Nile to the Red Sea, and those canals filled with sand again. In the 1850s, a French diplomat named Ferdinand de Lesseps got permission from Egypt's ruler to try again, and to cut straight across the desert.
Digging began in 1859. It took ten years.
Who dug it?

For the first years, most of the work was done by Egyptian peasants, forced to leave their villages and dig. Tens of thousands worked at a time, many with nothing but picks and baskets, in the heat, often short of water. Thousands died, of heat, thirst and disease. Nobody knows how many.
In 1864, forced labour on the canal was stopped. After that, most of the digging was done by huge steam machines, some of them designed for the job.
The canal opened on 17 November 1869, with a procession of ships and a party for kings and queens from Europe. It was 164 kilometres long. It has been widened and deepened many times since.
Egypt had paid a large part of the cost. Within a few years, it was so deep in debt that it had to sell its share of the canal to Britain.
The canal has no locks. The two seas are at almost the same height, so the water lies nearly still.

events.picturesWanted: a photograph of the canal under construction, with dredgers (public domain); ships in the canal today, seen from above (Commons or NASA).
references: Zachary Karabell, *Parting the Desert: The Creation of the Suez Canal* (Knopf, 2003). The whole story.
Valeska Huber, *Channelling Mobilities: Migration and Globalisation in the Suez Canal Region* (Cambridge, 2013). The workers and the canal zone.
Suez Canal Authority (suezcanal.gov.eg). Length and figures.

events.label: Impression, Sunrise

place.name: 35 boulevard des Capucines, Paris (48.87 N, 2.33 E)

events.summary: 1874. In Paris, about thirty artists put on an exhibition of their own. A critic made fun of a painting by Claude Monet, *Impression, Sunrise*, and called the painters "Impressionists." The name stuck.

paragraphs: In April 1874, in rooms on the boulevard des Capucines in Paris, hung a small painting of a harbour early in the morning. The harbour is half hidden in mist. There are dark boats on the water, the shapes of ships and cranes behind them, and a small orange sun, with its reflection laid across the water in short strokes of paint.

Claude Monet had painted it from a hotel window in Le Havre, a port in the north of France, probably in November 1872. Now it was in an exhibition that he and about thirty other artists had put on themselves.

In those days the way for a painter in France to be seen was the Salon, a huge exhibition in Paris, held every year, whose judges chose what was hung. The judges had turned down paintings by several of these artists. So they formed a company of their own, rented rooms that had belonged to the photographer Nadar, and hung more than 160 works. The show opened on 15 April and ran for a month.

The catalogue needed a title for the harbour. Monet remembered, twenty-four years later, that the picture could not really pass for a view of Le Havre, so he told them to call it *Impression*. In the catalogue it was *Impression, soleil levant*: Impression, Sunrise.

On 25 April a critic named Louis Leroy wrote a joke review in *Le Charivari*, a newspaper that made fun of things. In it, an imaginary old painter walks round the show getting angrier and angrier, and he says that wallpaper only half made is more finished than this seascape. Leroy called his review "L'Exposition des impressionnistes," the exhibition of the Impressionists.
He meant it as an insult. Four days later another critic, Jules Castagnary, used the same word in praise. By 1877 the painters had taken the name for themselves.

events.label: Galloping horse

place.name: Palo Alto Stock Farm, Stanford, California (37.42 N, 122.18 W)

events.summary: 19 June 1878. In California, Eadweard Muybridge set twelve cameras beside a racetrack and photographed a horse named Sallie Gardner at a gallop. One picture caught all four of her hooves off the ground at once.

paragraphs: On 19 June 1878, a mare named Sallie Gardner galloped down a track at Palo Alto, in California, with a rider on her back. Beside the track stood twelve cameras in a row, and on the far side of the track, facing them, a sloping white screen.

People had drawn and painted horses for thousands of years, but nobody could say for certain what a horse's legs were doing, because they move too fast for an eye to follow. Many painters showed a galloping horse with its front legs stretched out ahead and its back legs stretched out behind, like a rocking horse. People argued about whether a galloping horse ever had all four hooves off the ground.

Leland Stanford, a rich railway owner and a former governor of California, bred horses on his farm at Palo Alto, and he wanted to know. He hired Eadweard Muybridge ("ED-wurd MY-bridge"), an English photographer who lived in San Francisco. Their first try, in 1873, gave a blurred picture of a trotting horse.

By 1878 Muybridge had made shutters fast enough to catch a moving leg. As Sallie Gardner ran past, she set off the cameras one after another. Muybridge said each shutter was open for one two-thousandth of a second.

The pictures came out small and dark, almost shadows. In one of them, all four of her hooves are off the ground. But her legs are not stretched out like a rocking horse's. They are folded up under her belly.
You may read that Stanford paid for all this to win a bet of $25,000. Nobody at the time wrote about a bet, and historians who have looked for one think it never happened.
Muybridge sold the pictures on cards called *The Horse in Motion*, and that October the magazine *Scientific American* put engravings made from them on its cover.

events.label: Krakatoa

place.name: Krakatoa, between Java and Sumatra, Indonesia (6.10 S, 105.42 E)

events.summary: 27 August 1883. The volcanic island of Krakatoa, in what is now Indonesia, blew apart. It made the loudest sound in recorded history, heard nearly 5,000 kilometres away.

paragraphs: On Rodrigues, a small island in the Indian Ocean, the chief of police heard what sounded like the roar of heavy guns, far away to the east. He thought a ship was in trouble.
It was a volcano, nearly five thousand kilometres away.

The volcano was Krakatoa, an island between Java and Sumatra, in what is now Indonesia. It had been rumbling for months. On the morning of 27 August 1883, it blew itself apart in a series of explosions. The biggest came just after ten o'clock.
Is that really the loudest sound ever?

It is the loudest in recorded history. At 160 kilometres away, it was louder than a rock concert heard from the front row. Sailors on a ship about 60 kilometres away wrote that half the crew's eardrums had burst.

Sound is a wave of pressure moving through the air. Most of the Krakatoa wave was too low to hear, but instruments caught it. In cities around the world, weather instruments that measure air pressure showed a jump as the wave passed. Then another jump, hours later, as the wave came back the other way. Some instruments saw it pass seven times, as it went back and forth around the Earth for five days.
The explosions also pushed up huge waves in the sea, which ran up onto the coasts of Java and Sumatra. About 36,000 people died, most of them drowned.
Ash and a fine mist from the eruption spread around the world. For months, sunsets were strangely red. In New York that November, the sky glowed so red that people called out fire engines.
Most of the island was gone. In 1927, a new island rose out of the sea where it had been. It is called Anak Krakatau, "child of Krakatoa," and it is still erupting.

events.label: Van Gogh in Arles

place.name: Arles, France (43.68 N, 4.63 E)

events.summary: 20 February 1888. Vincent van Gogh, a Dutch painter, came by train to Arles, in the south of France, hoping it would look like a Japanese print. It was snowing. In fifteen months there he made about two hundred paintings.

paragraphs: Vincent van Gogh left Paris on the night train on 19 February 1888. All the way south, as he wrote later, he kept watching to see "if it was like Japan yet." He had been collecting Japanese prints, with their bright flat colours, and he hoped the south of France would look like them.

He reached Arles, an old town on the river Rhône, at about ten to five the next afternoon, nineteen hours after leaving. It was snowing. He wrote to his brother Theo that there was "at least 60 centimetres" of snow everywhere, and that the white landscape was "just like the winter landscapes the Japanese did."

Theo sold paintings in Paris and sent Vincent money to live on. Vincent took a room at a small hotel with a restaurant, and when the snow melted he began to paint: orchards in flower, a drawbridge over a canal, fields of wheat, boats on the beach. A few weeks after he arrived he wrote to Theo, "you know, I feel I'm in Japan."
He worked fast. In the fifteen months he lived in Arles he made about two hundred paintings, which is a painting every two days or so, and more than a hundred drawings.

In September he began painting outdoors at night. He painted a café terrace in a square in the middle of the town, and then the stars over the river, which he said he had "actually painted at night, under a gas-lamp." He wrote to Theo, "It often seems to me that the night is much more alive and richly coloured than the day."
You may read that he stuck candles round the brim of his hat to see by. That story first appeared in print more than thirty years after he died, and it is very unlikely to be true.
In May 1889 he moved to Saint-Rémy, a town about twenty kilometres away, and there, the next month, he painted *The Starry Night*.

references: Leo Jansen, Hans Luijten and Nienke Bakker, editors, *Vincent van Gogh: The Letters* (Van Gogh Museum and Huygens ING, 2009), letters 577, 585, 676, 691 and 706 and their notes, at vangoghletters.org. Every quotation here, in the edition's translation.

Monica Bowen, "Artists and Candle Hats," *Alberti's Window* (blog, December 2021). Where the candle story comes from.

events.label: Eiffel Tower

place.name: Champ de Mars, Paris (48.86 N, 2.29 E)

events.summary: 1889. For a world's fair in Paris, Gustave Eiffel's company built a tower of iron 300 metres tall, the tallest thing anyone had built. It was meant to come down after twenty years.

paragraphs: In February 1887, while workers were digging the foundations of a tower on the Champ de Mars in Paris, a newspaper called *Le Temps* printed a protest signed by about forty artists and writers. Among them were the writer Guy de Maupassant, the composer Charles Gounod, and Charles Garnier, who had designed the Paris opera house. They called the tower useless and monstrous, and compared it to a gigantic black factory chimney.

The tower was being built for a world's fair, to open in 1889, a hundred years after the French Revolution. Two engineers in Gustave Eiffel's company, Maurice Koechlin and Émile Nouguier, had the first idea for it, and an architect, Stephen Sauvestre, worked on how it would look. It was chosen from 107 designs.

It went up in a little over two years. In Eiffel's workshops outside Paris, 18,038 pieces of iron were cut and drilled, each to a drawing. They were carried to the site, where between 150 and 300 men fastened them together with two and a half million rivets. A rivet is a metal pin, pushed red-hot through holes in two pieces and hammered flat at the end, so that as it cools and shrinks it squeezes the pieces tight together. The iron alone weighed 7,300 tonnes.

When it was finished, at the end of March 1889, it was 300 metres tall, nearly twice the height of the Washington Monument, the tallest thing built before it. Nothing people built was taller until the Chrysler Building in New York, in 1930.

Eiffel's permit was for twenty years. After that, the tower belonged to the city of Paris, which could pull it down. So Eiffel looked for ways to make it useful. He set up experiments on the weather and on falling objects, and he paid for experiments with radio, and in 1909 the army set up a radio station at the tower. A tower that could send messages a long way was worth keeping. In 1910 the city let it stand.

place.name: Saint-Rémy

events.summary: 1889. He painted it from memory and imagination, in the daytime, in a room where he was not allowed to paint at night. The village is invented. The sky is not.

events.label: Montparnasse train

place.name: the old Gare Montparnasse, now Place du 18-Juin-1940, Paris (48.84 N, 2.32 E)

events.summary: 22 October 1895. In Paris, an express train came into the Montparnasse station too fast, ran through the end of the line, crossed the station hall and broke through the wall. The engine fell to the street below.

paragraphs: Express number 56 left Granville, on the coast of Normandy, at a quarter to nine on 22 October 1895. It was due at the Montparnasse station in Paris at five to four in the afternoon, and it was running a few minutes late.

At Montparnasse the tracks ended inside the station, on a floor about ten metres above the street. At the end of each track stood a buffer stop, a heavy frame built to stop a train that rolled too far. Beyond the buffers was the station's hall, almost thirty metres across, and beyond the hall was the front wall, looking out over a square called the Place de Rennes.

The train came in far too fast. It had an air brake. A pipe full of compressed air ran the length of the train, and when the driver let air out of the pipe, the brakes on every carriage pressed on at once. That afternoon the brake did not stop the train in time.

The engine smashed through the buffers, crossed the hall, broke through the wall and fell to the square below, where it stuck, nose down in the ground, with the carriages still up in the station behind it. The station clocks stopped at four.
A woman who sold newspapers in the square was killed by falling stone. A few people on the train were hurt.

The engine stood on its nose in the square for several days. Crowds came to look, and photographers came to take its picture. To get it down, about fifty men tried pulling, and then a team of horses, and in the end it took winches and jacks. When the engine was examined, it was found to be hardly damaged.

At the trial the next spring, the driver, Guillaume-Marie Pellerin, was fined fifty francs and given two months in prison, a sentence he did not have to serve unless he broke the law again. The old station was pulled down in the 1960s, and a tower of offices, the Tour Montparnasse, now stands near where it was.

events.label: Lumière show

place.name: Grand Café, 14 boulevard des Capucines, Paris (48.87 N, 2.33 E)

events.summary: 28 December 1895. In a room below a café in Paris, ten short moving pictures made by Louis and Auguste Lumière were shown to an audience that had paid to see them. Each film lasted about fifty seconds.

paragraphs: On the evening of 28 December 1895, about thirty people each paid a franc and went down the stairs into the Salon Indien, a room beneath the Grand Café on the boulevard des Capucines in Paris. What they saw there was ten films, each about fifty seconds long, thrown onto a screen by a machine called the Cinématographe.

The brothers Louis and Auguste Lumière, who ran a factory in Lyon that made photographic plates, had patented the machine that February. It was a wooden box that could film, print and project, and it weighed less than five kilograms. They had already shown their films to small invited audiences. This was the first show in Paris that anyone could pay to see.

Here is the programme of that evening, in order. Workers leaving the Lumière factory at the end of the day. A man trying, again and again, to get up onto a horse. A baby fishing for goldfish in a bowl. Photographers stepping off a boat near Lyon. Blacksmiths at work. A gardener watering his garden, and a boy who steps on the hose. A baby eating breakfast. Men tossing someone in a blanket. A busy square in Lyon. Boys jumping into the sea.
There is no train on the programme.

You may have read that when the Lumières showed a film of a train coming into a station, the audience screamed and ran. The first known showing of a train film was in Lyon a month later, in January 1896, and the best-known version seems to have been filmed in 1897. Martin Loiperdinger, a German historian of film, points out that no report of a panic can be found in the newspapers of the time.

In the summer of 1896, the Russian writer Maxim Gorky saw the Lumières' films and wrote about the train: "Suddenly something clicks, everything vanishes and a train appears on the screen. It speeds straight at you — watch out!" Then he imagined it crashing into the room. He did not say that anyone ran.

events.label: Radium

place.name: École municipale de physique et de chimie industrielles, rue Vauquelin, Paris (48.84 N, 2.35 E)
place.short: École municipale de physique et de chimie industrielles

events.summary: 26 December 1898. In Paris, Marie and Pierre Curie, with the chemist Gustave Bémont, announced a new element, hidden in a black rock called pitchblende. They named it radium, from the Latin word for a ray.

paragraphs: In 1896 a physicist in Paris named Henri Becquerel found that uranium, a metal, gives off rays that nobody can see, which pass through black paper and fog a photographic plate. Marie Curie, a young physicist from Poland who was working in Paris, chose those rays as the subject of her doctorate.

The rays had a useful habit. Where they passed through air, they let a little electricity leak through it. Her husband, Pierre Curie, and his brother Jacques had built an instrument that could measure very small amounts of electricity, so she could measure the rays from a sample by how much electricity they let through.
In 1898 she tested every substance she could get. Two minerals that contained uranium, pitchblende and one called chalcolite, gave off far more rays than the uranium in them could explain.

So she made chalcolite herself, in the laboratory, from pure ingredients. Her chalcolite gave off no more rays than any other compound of uranium. The chalcolite from the ground must have something in it that hers did not. In April she wrote that the minerals might contain an element much more active than uranium.

That spring Pierre put his own work aside to join her. They ground pitchblende, dissolved it, and split it into its parts, measuring each part for rays. In July they announced one new element, which they named polonium, after Poland. In December, with Gustave Bémont, they announced a second, radium. They called substances like these radio-active.

They had no radium to show yet. There was so little of it in pitchblende that it took four more years, and tonnes of leftover ore, worked in a leaky wooden shed with a glass roof, to get a pinch of radium chloride, about a tenth of a gram. Marie Curie remembered going back to the shed in the evening and seeing their radium samples, set out on tables and shelves, glowing faintly in the dark.

events.label: Tunguska

place.name: near the Podkamennaya Tunguska River, Siberia, Russia (60.89 N, 101.89 E)

events.summary: 30 June 1908. Over a forest in Siberia, something from space exploded in the air. It flattened millions of trees. No crater has ever been found.

paragraphs: At a trading post in the Siberian forest, early on a summer morning, a man was sitting on the porch. Suddenly the sky to the north seemed to split in two, and fire appeared over the forest. He felt heat so strong that his shirt seemed to be burning. Then a blast threw him off the porch.
The explosion was about sixty kilometres away.

It happened on 30 June 1908, over a forest near the Tunguska River in Siberia. Almost no one lived there. The blast flattened millions of trees across an area bigger than a large city, all lying with their tops pointing away from the middle. At the very middle, strangely, trees were left standing, stripped of their branches, like telegraph poles.
Nobody reached the place for nineteen years.

In 1927, a scientist named Leonid Kulik led an expedition into the forest. He expected to find a crater and a huge meteorite. He found the flattened trees, and the standing poles at the centre. He found no crater. He searched for years and never found the meteorite either.
So what was it?

Most scientists now think it was a piece of rock, or perhaps part of a comet, a few tens of metres across. It came in from space at tremendous speed. The air in front of it pushed back so hard that it heated up and burst apart several kilometres above the ground, before it could hit. The blast did the damage. Almost nothing was left to land.
For a few nights afterwards, the sky over Europe glowed so bright that people in London could read a newspaper outdoors at midnight.
Nobody has ever found a piece of it large enough to be sure.

events.picturesWanted: Kulik's 1927 or 1929 photograph of flattened trees (public domain); a map showing the pattern of fallen trees.
references: Vladimir Rubtsov, *The Tunguska Mystery* (Springer, 2009). The expedition, the evidence, the explanations.

events.label: Leavitt's rule
events.kindNote: not in the closed list (sky, earth, crop, craft, object, place, person, text); kept as written

place.name: Harvard College Observatory, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA (42.38 N, 71.13 W)

events.summary: 1912. At Harvard College Observatory, Henrietta Leavitt found that certain flickering stars reveal their true brightness by how fast they flicker. Her rule let astronomers measure distances far across the universe.

paragraphs: A glass plate the size of a book is covered with thousands of tiny black dots. Each dot is a star. The plate is a photograph of the sky, taken in Peru, with the colours reversed so the stars show dark.
Henrietta Leavitt spent her working days studying plates like this one.

She worked at the observatory of Harvard University, in the United States, as one of a group of women the astronomers called "computers." Their job was to measure the stars on the plates. It was careful work, and badly paid.

Leavitt was looking for variable stars: stars that get brighter and dimmer, over and over. She compared plates of the same patch of sky taken on different nights. She found more than two thousand variable stars.
Some of them were in the Small Magellanic Cloud, a hazy patch of stars in the southern sky. And some of those were a particular kind, which brighten and dim in a steady rhythm, like a slow heartbeat.
What did she notice?
That the brighter ones had slower heartbeats. A star that took many days to brighten and dim was brighter than one that took only a few.
All the stars in the Cloud are about the same distance from us. So the difference in brightness was real, not a trick of distance. That meant the rhythm told you how bright a star really was.
And that is a ruler. A candle looks dimmer the farther away it is. If you know how bright a star really is, and you measure how bright it looks, you can work out how far away it is.
She published her rule in 1912. Other astronomers used it to measure the size of our galaxy, and then to find other galaxies.
She died in 1921. In 1925, a Swedish mathematician wrote to her, wanting to put her name forward for a Nobel Prize. He did not know she had died.

events.picturesWanted: Leavitt at her desk (Harvard College Observatory, public domain); a photographic plate of the Small Magellanic Cloud.
references: Henrietta Leavitt and Edward Pickering, "Periods of 25 variable stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud," *Harvard College Observatory Circular* 173, 1912. The rule.
George Johnson, *Miss Leavitt's Stars* (Norton, 2005). Her life and work.
Dava Sobel, *The Glass Universe* (Viking, 2016). The women computers at Harvard.

events.label: Ramanujan's letter

place.name: Madras (now Chennai), India (13.08 N, 80.27 E)

events.summary: 16 January 1913. Srinivasa Ramanujan, a clerk in Madras, India, with almost no university training, mailed pages of astonishing mathematics to a stranger in Cambridge, England. The stranger, G. H. Hardy, recognised genius.

paragraphs: A letter arrives at Trinity College, Cambridge, from India. It begins politely: "Dear Sir, I beg to introduce myself to you as a clerk in the Accounts Department of the Port Trust Office at Madras on a salary of only £20 per annum."
The pages that follow are full of formulas.

The man who wrote it was Srinivasa Ramanujan. Say "RAH-mah-NOO-jun." He was twenty-five. He had taught himself mathematics from a few books, and he had failed his university exams twice, because he would study nothing but mathematics. He had filled notebooks with discoveries that nobody around him could check.
The man he wrote to was G. H. Hardy, one of the best mathematicians in England. Hardy got letters from odd people all the time.
What did Hardy make of it?

At first he was not sure what to think. Some of the formulas he knew already. A few were wrong. But some were unlike anything he had ever seen. He wrote later that they "must be true, because, if they were not true, no one would have had the imagination to invent them."

Hardy invited Ramanujan to Cambridge. He arrived in 1914, and for five years the two worked together. Ramanujan was elected to the Royal Society, one of the highest honours a scientist in Britain could receive. But he was often ill in the cold, damp English weather. He went home to India in 1919 and died the next year. He was thirty-two.

Hardy liked to tell one story. He once visited Ramanujan in hospital and said that his taxi had had a dull number: 1729. No, said Ramanujan, it is very interesting. It is the smallest number you can make by adding two cubes together in two different ways.

events.picturesWanted: the photograph of Ramanujan (public domain); a page from one of his notebooks (public domain).
references: G. H. Hardy, *Ramanujan: Twelve Lectures on Subjects Suggested by His Life and Work* (Cambridge, 1940). The letter, "must be true", the taxi.
Robert Kanigel, *The Man Who Knew Infinity* (Scribner, 1991). His life.
Bruce Berndt and Robert Rankin, *Ramanujan: Letters and Commentary* (American Mathematical Society, 1995). The text of the letter.

events.label: Andromeda

place.name: Mount Wilson Observatory, California, USA (34.23 N, 118.06 W)

events.summary: 6 October 1923. At Mount Wilson in California, Edwin Hubble photographed a flickering star in the Andromeda nebula. It showed Andromeda was far outside our galaxy: a whole galaxy of its own.

paragraphs: On a glass photograph of the sky, someone has written a small letter N next to a star, in ink. Then he has crossed the N out, and written beside it, in capitals: "VAR!"
The exclamation mark is the story.

The photograph was taken on the night of 5 October 1923, with the largest telescope in the world, on Mount Wilson in California. It shows part of the Andromeda nebula, a faint oval smudge that you can see without a telescope on a dark autumn night.

At the time, astronomers were arguing about smudges like this one. Some thought they were clouds of gas inside our own galaxy, the Milky Way, which they took to be the whole universe. Others thought they might be galaxies of their own, far outside ours, each made of millions of stars.
The astronomer at the telescope was Edwin Hubble. He was looking for new stars that flare up and fade, called novas, and he thought he had found three. He marked each with N.

Then he compared the photograph with older ones. One of the three was not a nova. It brightened and dimmed, over and over, in a steady rhythm of about a month. It was the same kind of star Henrietta Leavitt had studied at Harvard. So he crossed out the N and wrote "VAR!", for variable.
Why the exclamation mark?

Because of Leavitt's rule. The rhythm told him how bright the star really was. How bright it looked told him how far away it was. The answer was about a million light-years. A light-year is the distance light travels in a year. At that time the whole Milky Way was thought to be about 300,000 light-years across.
So Andromeda was far outside it. It was another galaxy.
Today we know it is even farther, about two and a half million light-years.
The glass plate is kept at the Carnegie Observatories in Pasadena. The "VAR!" is still on it.

events.picturesWanted: the "VAR!" plate (Carnegie Observatories; licence to check); the Andromeda galaxy (NASA, public domain).
references: Edwin Hubble, "Cepheids in spiral nebulae," *The Observatory*, 1925; and "A spiral nebula as a stellar system, Messier 31," *Astrophysical Journal*, 1929. His results.
Gale Christianson, *Edwin Hubble: Mariner of the Nebulae* (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1995). The night and the plate.
Carnegie Science, "Plate Vault: Hubble's M31 VAR! plate" (carnegiescience.edu/resources/historians/plates). The plate itself.
Marcia Bartusiak, *The Day We Found the Universe* (Pantheon, 2009). The argument about the nebulae.

events.label: Chile earthquake

place.name: near Valdivia, Chile (39.8 S, 73.2 W)

events.summary: 22 May 1960. Near Valdivia, in Chile, the ground shook for about ten minutes in the largest earthquake ever measured. The tsunami it made crossed the whole Pacific and killed people in Japan a day later.

paragraphs: In southern Chile, near the coast, there are marshes where dead trees stand up out of the water. Their bark is gone. Their branches are grey. They have been standing like that since 1960.
They used to be a forest on dry land.

On the afternoon of 22 May 1960, the ground under southern Chile shook for about ten minutes. It was the largest earthquake ever measured. A stretch of the Earth's crust about a thousand kilometres long slipped under the coast of South America. Along the coast, some land rose, and some sank by up to two metres. The sea came in, and forests drowned.

How many people died? Nobody knows exactly. Estimates run from about a thousand to about six thousand. In the days before, a smaller earthquake had frightened many people out of their houses, which may have saved lives.
The earthquake also pushed up the sea floor, and that made a tsunami: a wave caused not by wind but by the ground under the sea.
Out in the open ocean, a tsunami is low and fast, moving about as fast as a jet plane. Ships barely notice it. When it reaches shallow water near land, it slows down and piles up.

About fifteen hours after the earthquake, the tsunami reached Hawaii, more than 10,000 kilometres away. It killed sixty-one people in the town of Hilo. About twenty-two hours after the earthquake, it reached Japan, on the far side of the Pacific. Nobody there had felt anything. More than a hundred people died there.
Two days after the earthquake, a volcano in Chile called Cordón Caulle began to erupt, and kept erupting for weeks.
The dead trees are still standing in the marsh.

events.picturesWanted: the "sunken forest" near Valdivia (Commons); the tsunami damage in Hilo (USGS or NOAA, public domain).
references: US Geological Survey, "M 9.5 – 1960 Great Chilean Earthquake (Valdivia Earthquake)," earthquake.usgs.gov. Size, length of rupture, deaths.
Brian Atwater, Marco Cisternas and others, *Surviving a Tsunami: Lessons from Chile, Hawaii, and Japan*, USGS Circular 1187 (1999, revised 2005). The drowned trees and the times to Hilo and Japan.
Marco Cisternas and others, "Predecessors of the giant 1960 Chile earthquake," *Nature*, 2005. The sunken forest at Maullín.
NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, Global Historical Tsunami Database. Deaths in Hilo and Japan.

events.label: Moon landing

place.name: the Sea of Tranquility, on the Moon. On the map, the launch site stands in for it: Kennedy Space Center, Florida, USA (28.61 N, 80.60 W)

events.summary: 20 July 1969. Two American astronauts, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin, landed on the Moon and walked on it. They were the first people ever to stand on another world.

paragraphs: In a grey plain of dust on the Moon, there is a footprint. It is the print of a boot, with ridges across the sole. It has been there since 1969.
There is no wind on the Moon to blow it away, and no rain to wash it out.

The boot belonged to Buzz Aldrin, and he photographed the print on purpose, to see how the dust behaved. Minutes before, Neil Armstrong had stepped off the ladder of their landing craft and become the first person to stand on the Moon.

They had come from Earth in three days, on top of the biggest rocket that had ever flown, with a third astronaut, Michael Collins. He stayed in orbit around the Moon while the other two went down, and waited for them.

The landing was nearly a failure. As the landing craft came down, Armstrong saw that the computer was steering it toward a field of boulders. He took over, flew it himself across the boulders, and set it down with less than a minute of fuel left for landing.
What did they do there?

They walked around for about two and a half hours. They set up experiments, collected about twenty-one kilograms of rock and dust to bring home, planted a flag, and took photographs. Hundreds of millions of people on Earth watched them on television.
On the leg of the landing craft they left a metal sign. It says: "Here men from the planet Earth first set foot upon the Moon, July 1969 A.D. We came in peace for all mankind."
Over the next three and a half years, ten more people walked on the Moon. The last left in December 1972.
The footprints are still there. Nobody has walked on the Moon since.

events.picturesWanted: Aldrin's bootprint (NASA, AS11-40-5878, public domain); Earth seen from the Moon (NASA, public domain).
references: NASA, *Apollo 11 Mission Report* (1969) and the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal (hq.nasa.gov/alsj). The landing, the time outside, the samples, the plaque.
Andrew Chaikin, *A Man on the Moon* (Viking, 1994). The whole story.
Michael Collins, *Carrying the Fire* (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1974). The view from orbit.

events.label: Green Belt

place.name: Nairobi, Kenya (1.29 S, 36.82 E)

events.summary: 1977. In Kenya, Wangari Maathai began paying women a small sum for every tree seedling they grew that survived. The Green Belt Movement she started has planted tens of millions of trees.

paragraphs: On 5 June 1977, in a park in Nairobi, Kenya, a small group of people planted seven trees.
That was the beginning.

The woman who organised it was Wangari Maathai. Say "wan-GAH-ree ma-TIE." She had grown up in the Kenyan countryside, near a stream where she used to watch frogs' eggs. She went on to study biology in the United States and Germany, and in 1971 she became the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate.

In the 1970s, she listened to women from the countryside. They told her their streams were drying up. They had to walk farther and farther to find firewood. Their soil was washing away, and their families did not have enough to eat.
Maathai saw that all of these had one cause. The forests were being cut down.
What could one person do about that?

Her answer was simple. Women already knew how to grow plants. So she paid them to grow trees. A woman who raised seedlings from seeds, and planted them, was paid a small amount for each tree that was still alive a few months later. The trees gave shade, firewood and fruit, held the soil in place, and kept water in the ground.
The idea spread from village to village. The group became known as the Green Belt Movement.
It was not always peaceful work. When Maathai stood up against plans to build on a park in Nairobi, and to sell off a forest, she was arrested and beaten. She kept going.
In 2004 she was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. She was the first African woman to receive it.
By the time she died in 2011, the Green Belt Movement had planted more than thirty million trees. Today the count is more than fifty million.

events.picturesWanted: Wangari Maathai planting a tree (Commons or Green Belt Movement; licence to check); women with tree seedlings.
references: Wangari Maathai, *Unbowed: A Memoir* (Knopf, 2006). Her own account: the stream, the women, the seedlings.
Wangari Maathai, *The Green Belt Movement: Sharing the Approach and the Experience* (Lantern, 2003). How the movement works.
The Nobel Prize, "Wangari Maathai – Facts" (nobelprize.org). The prize, 2004.
Green Belt Movement (greenbeltmovement.org). Current tree count.

events.label: Last smallpox

place.name: Merca, Somalia (1.71 N, 44.77 E)

events.summary: 26 October 1977. In Merca, Somalia, a hospital cook named Ali Maow Maalin fell ill with smallpox. He recovered. He was the last person in the world to catch the disease in the ordinary way.

paragraphs: In October 1977, a young man named Ali Maow Maalin was working as a cook in a hospital in the town of Merca, in Somalia. He agreed to ride in a car with two sick children, to show the driver the way. The ride took about fifteen minutes.
The sick children had smallpox.

Smallpox was one of the deadliest diseases there has ever been. It spread from person to person, it covered the body in blisters, and it killed about three out of every ten people who caught it. In the 1900s alone, it killed an estimated three hundred million people.
But there was a way to stop it. A vaccine protected people from smallpox, and it had existed since 1796.
So why was smallpox still around in 1977?

Because vaccinating everyone in the world is hard. In 1967, the World Health Organization began a campaign to end smallpox everywhere. Instead of trying to vaccinate everyone, teams hunted down every case. When they found one, they vaccinated everyone around it: family, neighbours, people who had visited. The disease had nowhere to go. Country by country, it disappeared.
By 1977, Somalia was the last place it survived.
Ali Maow Maalin had never been vaccinated. About ten days after the car ride, he fell ill. Teams found everyone he had met, and vaccinated all of them. He recovered. Nobody caught smallpox from him.
He was the last person in the world to catch smallpox in the ordinary way. In 1980, the World Health Organization declared smallpox gone. It is the only human disease that has ever been wiped out.
Ali Maow Maalin spent his later years working to vaccinate children in Somalia against another disease, polio.

events.picturesWanted: a smallpox vaccination team in the 1970s (WHO or CDC, public domain); the WHO certificate of eradication.
references: Frank Fenner and others, *Smallpox and Its Eradication* (World Health Organization, 1988). The whole campaign, and Merca.
D. A. Henderson, *Smallpox: The Death of a Disease* (Prometheus, 2009). How the teams worked.
World Health Organization, "Smallpox" fact sheet and the 1980 declaration. Eradication.

events.label: First web page

place.name: CERN, Meyrin, near Geneva, on the border of Switzerland and France (46.23 N, 6.05 E)

events.summary: 1990. At CERN, a laboratory for physics near Geneva, Tim Berners-Lee put the first page of the World Wide Web on a computer where others could read it. The page explained the web. Nobody has a copy.

paragraphs: In March 1989, Tim Berners-Lee, an English computer scientist, wrote a proposal at CERN ("SERN"), a great laboratory for physics that straddles the border between Switzerland and France, near Geneva. Thousands of people came and went at CERN, and information got lost: who had written which program, which notes went with which experiment. He suggested a way of linking documents, on any kind of computer, so that a reader could jump from one to another. His boss, Mike Sendall, wrote on the cover: "Vague but exciting…"

In the autumn of 1990 Berners-Lee wrote the programs to make it work, while Robert Cailliau, a Belgian engineer, helped him win support for it at CERN. There were three parts. Every page has an address, and a page can hold links, words that fetch the page at another address when you choose them. A server is a computer that keeps pages and hands them out when asked. A browser is a program that asks for pages and shows them.

By Christmas 1990 it all worked, on a NeXT computer at CERN. On the computer a label said: "This machine is a server. DO NOT POWER IT DOWN!!" The first website was at the address info.cern.ch, and its first page was about the web itself: what it was, and how to take part.
In August 1991 Berners-Lee told people outside CERN about it, in a message to an online discussion group. In April 1993 CERN gave the web's programs away, free, for anyone to use.

Nobody has a copy of the first page as it was in 1990. A page on a server is changed by writing over it, and the old version is gone. In 2013 CERN put back the oldest copy it could find, from a year or two later, at the old address, where you can still read it. CERN said it would keep looking for older ones.

events.picturesWanted: the NeXT computer with its label (Wikimedia Commons, Coolcaesar 2005, GFDL / CC BY-SA, credit needed); a screenshot of the restored page at info.cern.ch (CERN holds the rights; low risk, but check).
references: CERN, "A short history of the Web" and "Web History," Web@30 (web30.web.cern.ch). The proposal, the first server, the 1993 release.
Tim Berners-Lee, "Information Management: A Proposal," CERN, March 1989 and May 1990 (info.cern.ch/Proposal.html). The proposal itself.
Tim Berners-Lee and Robert Cailliau, "WorldWideWeb: Proposal for a HyperText Project," CERN, 12 November 1990.
Max Froumentin, "Vague but exciting," W3C Web History Community Group (blog, 30 October 2012). Mike Sendall's note.
CERN, "Where the web was born" (home.cern). The first website, the label, and why no screenshots exist.
